open.title: open_c2_004

items.sub_competency: C2.5 · Data validation, quality & leakage checks

open.question:
You inherit a loan-default model. On 5-fold cross-validation it scores 0.96 ROC-AUC, but across its first month in production it holds at roughly 0.71. You review the team's setup:

- Data: ~200k loan applications spanning 2019–2023, one row per application. Some borrowers appear multiple times (repeat applicants share a `borrower_id`).
- Features include applicant income, requested amount, credit score at application, a high-cardinality `employer_name`, and `num_collections_calls` (calls the collections team logged about the loan).
- `employer_name` is mean-encoded against the default label once over the entire dataset before cross-validation.
- Median imputation values and a `StandardScaler` are computed on the full dataset, then `cross_val_score` is run with `KFold(shuffle=True)` over the resulting matrix.

Explain why cross-validation is so optimistic relative to production. Identify each distinct leakage mechanism, describe precisely how each one inflates the CV score, and lay out a corrected validation-and-feature setup you would actually trust to estimate production performance — including how you would verify the leakage is gone.
open.answer_format: A structured written explanation, ~250–400 words. Enumerate each distinct leakage mechanism with (a) the causal mechanism by which it inflates CV and (b) its fix, then describe the integrated corrected validation design and at least one verification method. Bullet/numbered structure is fine.
open.reference_answer:
The 0.96 CV score is an artifact of at least five distinct leakage mechanisms; production (~0.71) is the honest number.

1) Post-outcome / target-proxy feature. `num_collections_calls` is generated *after* a loan becomes delinquent — it is a downstream consequence of the label, not a predictor available at application time. At scoring time for a new application it is unknown (usually 0), so the model has learned a near-deterministic shortcut. Fix: enforce point-in-time (as-of) feature availability — every feature must be knowable at the prediction cutoff (application time); drop `num_collections_calls` and any other post-decision field.

2) Target (mean) encoding over the full dataset. Encoding `employer_name` with the default rate leaks the label directly into a feature: each row's encoded value is computed using its own label (and the validation rows' labels). With high cardinality (employer near one-to-one with borrower) this approaches memorizing the target. Fix: compute the encoding out-of-fold / nested inside CV, fit only on the training partition, with smoothing/regularization for rare employers.

3) Preprocessing fit on the full dataset. Imputation medians and scaler statistics include the validation rows, leaking distributional information. Fix: wrap impute → scale → encode in an sklearn `Pipeline` and pass the Pipeline to `cross_val_score`, so each fold fits preprocessing on its training split only.

4) Group leakage. `KFold(shuffle=True)` scatters a repeat borrower's applications across train and validation, letting the model memorize borrower-specific risk. Fix: `GroupKFold`/`StratifiedGroupKFold` keyed on `borrower_id` so a borrower never spans folds.

5) Temporal leakage. Random shuffling trains on 2023 to predict 2020, whereas production always predicts the future. Fix: a time-ordered split — `TimeSeriesSplit` / forward-chaining, or a hard out-of-time holdout (train ≤2022, validate 2023) — and keep borrower groups from crossing the temporal boundary.

Corrected setup: a point-in-time feature table with an application-time cutoff; all preprocessing/encoding inside a Pipeline that fits per fold; a time-ordered, group-aware split; final estimate on an out-of-time holdout as the production proxy.

Verification: ablate suspicious features and watch CV collapse toward 0.71; audit feature importances for a single dominating feature; run adversarial validation (train-vs-production classifier) to detect distribution shift; and confirm the corrected CV estimate ≈ out-of-time holdout ≈ production.
expected_answer_points: Identifies num_collections_calls as post-outcome/target-proxy leakage — its value only exists after default and is unavailable at scoring time — and fixes it via point-in-time feature availability (drop post-decision features).

Identifies the full-dataset mean/target encoding of employer_name as target leakage (each row's encoding uses its own label), and fixes it with out-of-fold/nested encoding fit only on training folds, with smoothing for rare categories.

Identifies imputation medians and StandardScaler fit on the full dataset as train/validation contamination, and fixes it by putting all preprocessing in an sklearn Pipeline so it fits per fold on training data only.
Identifies group leakage from repeat borrowers under KFold(shuffle=True) and fixes it with GroupKFold/StratifiedGroupKFold keyed on borrower_id.

Identifies temporal leakage from random shuffling (training on the future to predict the past) versus production's train-past/predict-future, and fixes it with a time-ordered split or out-of-time holdout.

Proposes an integrated corrected validation that mirrors production: point-in-time features, pipeline-inside-CV, and a time-ordered, group-aware split with an out-of-time holdout as the production proxy.
Describes at least one detection/verification method (feature-ablation, importance audit, adversarial validation, or comparing corrected CV to an out-of-time holdout) to confirm leakage is removed.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Every identified mechanism and fix is technically correct: the post-outcome feature is excluded on prediction-time availability grounds; target encoding must be out-of-fold; preprocessing must fit per fold; grouping is on borrower_id; the split must be time-ordered. Full marks require no false claims (e.g., that regularization, more data, or a random holdout would fix leakage, or that target encoding 'on training data only' is inherently safe).

Covers all five distinct leakage sources present (post-outcome feature, full-data target encoding, full-data preprocessing, repeat-borrower group leakage, temporal leakage) plus an end-to-end corrected validation and at least one verification method. Score scales with how many distinct, correct sources and remedies are found; missing the higher-impact ones (post-outcome feature, temporal, group) costs more than missing the scaler-in-pipeline point.

Explains the causal mechanism by which each source specifically inflates CV — leaking the label, future information, or validation-fold statistics — and justifies why the proposed split mirrors the production train/predict boundary, rather than merely listing fixes by name.

Well-organized, cleanly separates diagnosis from remediation, and uses precise terminology (out-of-fold encoding, point-in-time/as-of correctness, GroupKFold, TimeSeriesSplit, out-of-time holdout, adversarial validation) correctly and economically.

common_pitfalls: Attributing the gap to ordinary overfitting or model complexity and recommending regularization / hyperparameter tuning instead of fixing the leaked features and validation design.
Treating the target encoding as safe because it is 'on training data,' missing that it must be computed out-of-fold or it leaks each row's own label.
Fixing only the textbook scaler/imputer-in-pipeline issue and overlooking the higher-impact post-outcome feature (num_collections_calls), the temporal split, and the repeat-borrower group leakage.

Recommending StratifiedKFold or a random train/test holdout as the remedy, not realizing the same leakage contaminates a random holdout and that group and temporal structure must be respected instead.
Failing to recognize num_collections_calls as a consequence of the label — treating it as a legitimate predictor — and so never enforcing point-in-time feature availability.
Confusing data leakage with covariate/distribution shift, or proposing to 'collect more data' rather than removing the label/future information from features and folds.

open.title: open_c2_005

open.question: In a design review, a colleague presents a card-fraud classifier. The dataset is 3M transactions with a 0.2% fraud rate (~1 in 500). Their pipeline: (1) apply SMOTE to the entire dataset to balance it to 50/50, (2) do an 80/20 random train/test split, (3) train a gradient-boosted model (XGBoost), (4) report test ROC-AUC = 0.97, and (5) ship with a fixed 0.5 decision threshold. In production the fraud team can manually review at most ~200 flagged transactions per day out of ~50,000 daily transactions. Critique this methodology step by step, then design a corrected training-and-evaluation pipeline. Be specific about: which steps are methodologically wrong and why, which metrics you would report instead of ROC-AUC, how you would handle the imbalance, what rebalancing does to the model's predicted probabilities and the 0.5 threshold, and how you would validate that the shipped model actually satisfies the 200-review/day capacity constraint.
open.answer_format: A structured critique-and-design in prose (~250-400 words). Walk through the flaws in each pipeline step, then lay out the corrected pipeline, naming the specific metrics, the resampling/weighting choice, the calibration/prior-correction step, and the threshold-under-budget logic. Bullet points plus a short justifying paragraph are fine.
open.reference_answer:
The methodology is broken in three compounding ways, and the headline 0.97 is not trustworthy.

1) SMOTE before the split is data leakage. SMOTE interpolates each synthetic minority point between a real minority sample and its nearest minority neighbours. Doing this on the full dataset means synthetic points in the test set are built from training points (and vice-versa), so the test set is contaminated. Resampling must happen only on the training partition, and inside each CV fold — the validation/test sets must keep the true 0.2% prior. Fix this first: split (ideally an out-of-time / temporal split, since fraud patterns drift and a random split leaks future behaviour), then resample only the training side.

2) ROC-AUC is the wrong headline metric here. With 99.8% negatives, the FPR denominator is enormous, so thousands of false positives barely move FPR — ROC-AUC can sit at 0.97 while precision at any reviewable alert volume is terrible. Report PR-AUC / average precision, and, decisively, operating-point metrics tied to the budget: recall (frauds caught) when the alert volume is capped at ~200/day (~0.4% of 50k), i.e. precision@200 and recall@200. This is really a ranking-under-budget problem: rank transactions by score and see how many true frauds fall in the top ~200.

3) Rebalancing to 50/50 destroys probability calibration and makes 0.5 meaningless. The model now learns P(fraud|x) under a 50/50 prior and massively over-predicts fraud relative to the real 0.2% base rate, which is exactly why production alerts explode. Either prior-correct the scores in log-odds space (subtract the training prior log-odds, add the true prior log-odds) or recalibrate (Platt/isotonic) on a held-out set that has the true distribution. Then do NOT use 0.5: tune the threshold (or take top-k) on a true-prior validation set to fill the ~200/day budget while maximising recall.

Corrected pipeline: temporal split → within training folds, handle imbalance via cost-sensitive weighting (XGBoost scale_pos_weight) or modest resampling, and benchmark it against doing nothing but threshold-tuning, since SMOTE adds no real signal and misbehaves with categorical/high-cardinality features. Evaluate on the untouched, true-prior (and out-of-time) test set using PR-AUC and precision/recall at the 200-alert budget. Calibrate, pick the operating threshold to hit the budget, and in production monitor calibration and precision@budget over time (accounting for delayed fraud labels).
expected_answer_points: Applying SMOTE (or any resampling) before the train/test split leaks synthetic points across the split and inflates the reported metric; resampling must be confined to the training partition / inside each CV fold, with validation and test kept at the true prior.

ROC-AUC is misleading under 0.2% prevalence because the vast negative count keeps FPR low despite many false positives; report PR-AUC / average precision and budget-tied operating points (precision@~200/day and recall at that alert volume) instead.

Rebalancing to 50/50 shifts the base rate the model learns, so predicted probabilities are inflated/miscalibrated versus the true prior and must be prior-corrected in log-odds space or recalibrated (Platt/isotonic) on true-distribution data.

The fixed 0.5 threshold is invalid after rebalancing/calibration; the operating threshold (or top-k) must be tuned on a true-prior validation set to fill the ~200 review/day budget while maximising recall — a ranking-under-budget framing.

Consider cost-sensitive learning / class weights (e.g. XGBoost scale_pos_weight) as an alternative to SMOTE, and benchmark against threshold-tuning alone, noting SMOTE pitfalls (no new signal, poor behaviour with categorical/high-dimensional features, noisy borderline synthetics).

Evaluate on an untouched test set with the real prior, and for fraud specifically prefer a temporal / out-of-time split over a random split to avoid future-information leakage and reflect concept drift.
Address production validation/monitoring: track calibration and precision/recall at the review budget over time, accounting for delayed/uncertain fraud labels.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly diagnoses the resample-before-split leakage, why ROC-AUC misleads under extreme imbalance (huge TN base keeps FPR low), and the base-rate/calibration distortion from 50/50 rebalancing, with an accurate fix (prior correction or recalibration on true-prior data). No incorrect claims (e.g. that 'balancing fixes' the threshold, or that ROC-AUC is fine here). Full marks require accurate mechanisms, not just naming the right buzzwords.

Covers all four asked dimensions — flawed steps, replacement metrics, imbalance handling, and probability/threshold-under-budget validation — and ties the metric and threshold explicitly to the ~200-review/day constraint. Loses points for skipping calibration/prior-correction, the budget-linked operating point, or the evaluation-on-true-prior/temporal-split point.

Justifies each recommendation with the underlying mechanism (why leakage inflates the score, why FPR stays low, why 50/50 over-predicts, why a budget makes it a ranking problem) rather than asserting best-practice labels. Credit for weighing SMOTE vs class weights vs threshold-tuning rather than reflexively picking one.

Organised as a clear critique-then-redesign that a review audience could act on, using correct vocabulary (leakage, PR-AUC/average precision, precision/recall@budget, calibration, prior shift, scale_pos_weight, out-of-time split) precisely and concisely.

common_pitfalls: Focuses only on 'SMOTE vs undersampling' and misses that the primary error is resampling before the split, which is what actually inflates the 0.97.

Accepts ROC-AUC (or proposes accuracy/F1 at 0.5) as the reporting metric, failing to explain why FPR-based metrics look great at 0.2% prevalence, and never connects the metric to the 200-alert/day budget.

Treats the 0.5 threshold as fine 'because the data is now balanced', ignoring that rebalancing inflates predicted probabilities and that calibration / prior correction is required before any threshold is meaningful.
Tries to fix bad production precision with more aggressive resampling instead of threshold-tuning / top-k ranking against the fixed review capacity.
Uses a random split for fraud data, overlooking temporal leakage and concept drift that an out-of-time split guards against.
Gives generic advice ('get more data', 'try deep learning', 'use class weights') without engaging the budget-constrained operating point or the calibration consequence of resampling.

open.title: open_c2_006

items.sub_competency: C2.7 · Data versioning, lineage & access control

open.question: Your team ships a fraud-scoring model to production. Six months later an auditor demands that you (a) reproduce the exact model that scored a specific transaction and (b) show which raw source data flowed into it. Your current setup: pipeline code lives in Git, and each retrain reads a single `s3://features/latest/` folder of Parquet that the ETL job overwrites in place; the trained model is copied to `s3://models/fraud/prod.pkl`. You cannot reproduce the old model and cannot say which upstream tables fed it. As a design-review write-up, diagnose why this setup fails reproducibility and auditability, propose a data versioning and lineage design, compare at least two concrete versioning approaches with a justified choice for this S3/Parquet context, and explain how a past run would then be reproduced.
open.answer_format: A short written design-review answer, roughly 220-340 words: diagnose the gap, propose a versioning + lineage design, compare at least two concrete tools with a justified choice tied to the S3/Parquet context, and describe the reproduction procedure. A structured explanation, not code.
open.reference_answer:
Root cause: the dataset is mutated in place. Git version-controls the code, but the model artifact has no durable pointer to the exact bytes it trained on, and 'latest/' overwrites destroy every prior state. Plain Git and Git-LFS can't efficiently version multi-GB Parquet, nor express which upstream tables produced it. So neither the exact inputs nor the transformation history survive.

Design:
1) Store training data in an immutable, versioned layer so each dataset state gets a stable id (content hash / commit / snapshot). Candidates: DVC (content-hashes the data, commits a small pointer file into Git, pushes blobs to S3); lakeFS (git-style branches/commits/tags over the same S3 buckets with zero-copy branching); or an Iceberg/Delta table with ACID snapshots and time travel.
2) Pin data to each run. In an experiment tracker (e.g. MLflow) log the dataset version id, code commit SHA, hyperparameters, library versions and random seeds against the model artifact, making artifact <-> data <-> code a resolvable triple. Stop overwriting prod.pkl; store versioned artifacts.
3) Capture transformation lineage. Emit lineage from the pipeline (OpenLineage -> Marquez, dbt, or a data catalog), ideally column-level, so each feature traces back to its raw source table and transform.

Choice: for a team that already keeps Parquet in S3 and wants audit-grade, engine-agnostic branching without copying data, I'd pick lakeFS; DVC is simpler for a small file-based team; Iceberg/Delta time travel is lowest-friction only if they already run a lakehouse, but it's table-format-bound and limited by snapshot expiration/VACUUM.

Critically, extend retention so the audited version survives the compliance window: disable premature Delta VACUUM / Iceberg snapshot expiry and S3 lifecycle deletion, and treat old versions as immutable.

open.question:
You own a real-time credit-card fraud model — an XGBoost gradient-boosted tree served behind a low-latency scoring API. On a temporally held-out test set it reaches 0.94 ROC-AUC and precision@100 of 0.82. The day it goes live, production precision@100 sits at ~0.55 and stays there: it is not sloping downward over the following weeks, it is simply bad from the first hour. Training features are built by a nightly Spark job over the warehouse; serving features are computed in the Python scoring service from Redis counters plus the incoming request. Two features matter here: `txn_count_24h` (the cardholder's transaction count in the trailing 24 hours) and `merchant_avg_ticket` (the merchant's average transaction amount), looked up from a table that is missing for ~30% of merchants at serving time.

Explain what is most likely happening and why the offline-online gap has this shape (flat and present from launch, rather than a slow decline). Identify the concrete mechanisms of training-serving skew this setup invites, describe how you would confirm the root cause, and lay out how you would fix it and prevent recurrence. Be specific about feature computation, point-in-time correctness, and monitoring.
open.answer_format: A structured written explanation, ~250-400 words, moving from diagnosis (drift vs skew) through root-cause confirmation to fix and prevention. Short bullet lists are fine. Must name specific mechanisms (dual code path, point-in-time correctness / leakage, missing-value distribution mismatch) and concrete tooling/methods (feature logging, PSI/KS, feature store, as-of joins).
open.reference_answer:
Signature first. A gap that is present in the very first hour and stays flat — rather than sloping downward over weeks — is the fingerprint of training-serving skew and/or an optimistic offline evaluation, not data drift. Drift is temporal: the live distribution slowly moves away from training, so performance decays gradually. A constant day-one gap means the model is being fed different feature values in production than it learned from, or the offline number was never honest.

Mechanisms this setup invites:
- Two code paths. Features are built twice — nightly Spark/SQL over the warehouse for training, and online Python over Redis for serving. The two implementations inevitably diverge on null handling, 24h window boundaries, time zones, rounding and type coercion, so the same cardholder yields a different vector offline vs online.
- `txn_count_24h` — point-in-time correctness. If the Spark job counts over the whole day's table without a strict as-of cutoff, the training feature peeks at transactions that occurred after the scored one. That is leakage: offline AUC is inflated by information not causally available at serving. Conversely the online Redis counter can be stale (eventual consistency / TTL), so serving sees a weaker value than training.
- `merchant_avg_ticket` — missingness mismatch. 30% missing at serving but (near-)complete in the backfilled warehouse means training almost never saw the default/imputed value that a third of live rows now receive. The trees split on a region of feature space they never learned, and error concentrates on those rows.

Confirm the root cause. Turn on feature logging to capture the exact vectors served. Sample live scored transactions, re-run the training pipeline for the same entity and as-of timestamp, and diff row-by-row — non-trivial diffs localize the skew per feature. Complement with per-feature PSI / KS between the training set and the logged serving features; the skewed features light up. Re-evaluate offline with strictly point-in-time features to expose the leakage.

Fix and prevent. Kill the dual code path: put feature definitions in a shared transformation layer / feature store (Feast, Tecton) so offline and online compute identically, and generate training data with point-in-time-correct (as-of) joins. Better still, train on the logged served features so the training distribution equals the serving distribution by construction. Make missingness first-class — impute consistently in both paths, add an `is_missing` indicator, and ensure the training data carries the same missing rate rather than a backfilled complete table. Finally, stand up continuous skew monitoring (served-vs-recomputed feature diffs, PSI, per-feature missing-rate alerts) and shadow/canary new models before full rollout.
expected_answer_points: Correctly diagnoses this as training-serving skew (and/or a leaky offline eval), NOT data drift, justified by the signature: a flat gap present from launch versus the gradual temporal decline that would indicate drift.

Identifies the dual-code-path mechanism — nightly Spark/SQL for training vs online Python/Redis for serving — producing divergent feature values for the same entity via null handling, window boundaries, time zones, rounding or type coercion.

Diagnoses `txn_count_24h` as a point-in-time-correctness problem: either training leaks future transactions (no strict as-of cutoff), inflating offline AUC, or the online counter is stale relative to training.

Diagnoses the ~30% missing `merchant_avg_ticket` as a train/serve distribution mismatch: training rarely saw the default/imputed value that a third of serving rows now get, concentrating error on those rows.

Proposes a concrete confirmation: feature logging plus recompute-and-diff (re-run the training pipeline for the same entity and as-of timestamp, compare vectors row-by-row) and/or per-feature PSI/KS between training and logged serving features.

Proposes eliminating the dual code path via a shared transformation layer or feature store (Feast/Tecton) with point-in-time-correct (as-of) training joins — ideally training on logged served features so distributions match by construction.

Adds prevention: consistent missing-value handling with an explicit missingness indicator and matching missing rate in training, plus continuous skew monitoring and shadow/canary comparison of served vs recomputed features before rollout.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly attributes the flat, launch-time gap to training-serving skew (and/or leaky offline evaluation) rather than drift, and accurately describes the mechanisms — dual computation paths diverging on edge cases, point-in-time/leakage or staleness on txn_count_24h, and the missing-value distribution mismatch on merchant_avg_ticket — with no technical errors. Deduct for calling it drift, for claiming retraining on recent data fixes it, or for garbling point-in-time correctness.

Full marks: covers all four stages — diagnosis (skew vs drift), root-cause confirmation, fix, and prevention — and addresses both named features plus the shared code-path issue. Partial credit if one stage (typically confirmation or prevention/monitoring) or one of the two features is omitted.

Full marks: justifies WHY a flat-from-launch signature implies skew not drift, WHY future-peeking or a complete-table backfill inflates offline metrics, and WHY 30% default imputation concentrates error — and ties each proposed fix to the specific mechanism it addresses. Partial credit for correct conclusions asserted without the underlying reasoning.

Full marks: an organized diagnose -> confirm -> fix -> prevent narrative usable in a design review, using precise vocabulary (point-in-time correctness, feature store, feature logging, PSI/KS, as-of join). Deduct for a disorganized list of buzzwords or vague, unattributed claims.

common_pitfalls: Misdiagnoses the problem as data drift and prescribes retraining on recent data — but a flat gap present from hour one is skew (or a leaky eval); retraining does not close a code-path or leakage gap.
Blames model overfitting and reaches for regularization or more data, ignoring that the offline metric came from a held-out set and the gap is about feature computation, not variance.

Treats the 30% missing merchant_avg_ticket as merely 'needs imputation' without recognizing the train/serve distribution mismatch — imputing at serving to a value the training data almost never contained does not help.

Overlooks point-in-time correctness for txn_count_24h and proposes to 'just recompute the same feature online' without noticing the training pipeline may be leaking future data and inflating offline AUC.
Offers only monitoring/alerting (drift dashboards, PSI) as the fix — detection without correcting the dual code path or the leakage.
Suggests making serving match training (e.g., adding the future-window count online), which is causally impossible, instead of making training reflect the causal serving reality.

open.question: You are reviewing a colleague's training script. They fit a logistic-regression model with plain (full-batch) gradient descent implemented by hand in NumPy: `w <- w - eta * grad`. Two of the features are `age` (roughly 0-90) and `annual_income` (roughly 0-200000); the rest are similar mixes of scales, and none are normalized. They report that with `eta = 1e-6` the training loss drops but crawls downward for thousands of iterations, and every time they raise `eta` to speed it up the loss starts oscillating and then blows up to NaN. They ask you: 'Is my gradient buggy?' Diagnose what is actually happening in terms of the loss-surface geometry, then propose at least two concrete fixes with their justification and trade-offs, and say which you would reach for first and why.
open.answer_format: A short written diagnosis plus design discussion, roughly 200-320 words: explain the geometric root cause, then give at least two justified fixes with their trade-offs and a first-choice recommendation. Referencing the Hessian / condition number and the stability bound on the step size earns full marks; formulas are welcome but prose is fine.
open.reference_answer:
The gradient is almost certainly fine; the symptom is classic ill-conditioning caused by unnormalized features on wildly different scales. Because `income` spans ~200000 and `age` ~90, the loss surface is a long, narrow valley: the Hessian of the loss has a very large condition number kappa = lambda_max / lambda_min, meaning curvature is steep along one axis and nearly flat along another.

Plain gradient descent uses one global step size for every coordinate. For stability it must satisfy roughly eta < 2/lambda_max, i.e. eta is pinned by the steepest (largest-curvature) direction. At `1e-6` the step is small enough to be stable, but progress along the flat (small-lambda) direction is proportional to eta*lambda_min, so it crawls; the per-step contraction factor is about (kappa-1)/(kappa+1), which approaches 1 as kappa grows. When they raise eta past 2/lambda_max, the steep direction overshoots and amplifies each step -> oscillation -> divergence to NaN. So no single eta both moves the flat direction fast and keeps the steep direction stable. That is a conditioning problem, not a bug.

Fixes:
1. Standardize/normalize the features (subtract mean, divide by std). This makes the curvature roughly isotropic, collapses kappa toward 1, and lets a much larger stable eta work. Cheapest, most effective, and should be the default -- the only cost is remembering to apply the identical transform at inference (fit the scaler on train only).
2. Momentum / Nesterov. Accumulating a velocity term damps the oscillation in the steep direction and accelerates the flat one, improving the effective rate to depend on sqrt(kappa) instead of kappa. One extra hyperparameter and a velocity buffer.
3. Adaptive per-coordinate methods (Adam/RMSProp) give each parameter its own effective step from running gradient-magnitude estimates, so they are largely robust to feature scale. Cost: ~2x parameter memory for the moment buffers and occasionally slightly worse generalization.
4. Second-order / preconditioning (Newton, L-BFGS): rescale the gradient by the inverse Hessian, making the step scale-invariant, but full Newton is O(d^3) per step and stores a d x d Hessian -- impractical at high dimension.

I would reach for feature standardization first: it is one line, addresses the root cause directly, and makes every downstream optimizer behave better, whereas momentum/Adam merely paper over the bad conditioning.
expected_answer_points: Correctly identifies the root cause as ill-conditioning from unnormalized features of very different scales, producing an elongated/anisotropic loss surface (Hessian with large condition number kappa = lambda_max/lambda_min) rather than a gradient bug

Explains the stability constraint: a single global step size must satisfy roughly eta < 2/lambda_max, so eta is bounded by the steepest-curvature direction, and exceeding it causes the observed oscillation and divergence to NaN

Explains the slowness: with eta pinned small, progress along the flat/low-curvature direction is tiny; convergence rate degrades as kappa grows (per-step factor ~ (kappa-1)/(kappa+1) -> 1), so no single eta serves both directions
Proposes feature standardization/normalization as the direct fix that reduces kappa toward 1 and permits a larger stable eta, noting the transform must be fit on train and reapplied at inference

Proposes at least one optimizer-side remedy -- momentum/Nesterov (damps oscillation, rate improves to ~sqrt(kappa)) and/or adaptive per-coordinate methods (Adam/RMSProp) that are robust to feature scale
Notes second-order/preconditioning (Newton, quasi-Newton/L-BFGS) as scale-invariant in principle but O(d^3)/memory-costly, i.e. a trade-off against cheap normalization
Gives a justified first choice (normalization) because it fixes the underlying geometry cheaply, versus optimizer tweaks that only compensate for bad conditioning

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly attributes the behavior to ill-conditioning (large-condition-number Hessian from unscaled features), states the eta < ~2/lambda_max stability bound tying the step size to the steepest direction, and correctly links large kappa to slow convergence and eta-raising to divergence. Proposed fixes and their mechanisms (normalization lowering kappa, momentum ~sqrt(kappa), Adam per-coordinate steps, Newton scale-invariance/cost) are technically correct. Deduct for a wrong mechanism, a reversed relationship (e.g. thinking large kappa means small lambda_max), or claiming it must be a gradient bug.

Full marks: covers the diagnosis (geometry + why both slow and unstable), at least two concrete fixes with justification, their trade-offs, and a first-choice recommendation. Deduct for giving only one fix, omitting trade-offs, or skipping the diagnosis and jumping straight to remedies.

Full marks: the fixes are justified by the diagnosed cause (e.g. normalization chosen because it lowers kappa at the source) rather than listed generically, and the first-choice recommendation is defended by a real trade-off argument. Deduct for unsupported assertions or fixes that do not connect back to the conditioning explanation.

Full marks: clear, well-organized answer that a colleague could act on, using correct vocabulary (condition number, curvature/Hessian, step size, oscillation/divergence). Deduct for disorganized, vague, or jargon-without-meaning writing.

Claims Adam or Newton is a strict free-lunch upgrade, ignoring Adam's extra optimizer-state memory / generalization caveats or Newton's O(d^3) cost and Hessian storage

open.question:
You own a binary classifier (a fine-tuned neural network) that outputs a probability p that a support ticket is "urgent". Downstream, an automated router treats p as a literal probability: it computes expected cost = p x (cost estimate) and routes any ticket above a dollar threshold to a human agent. The model's held-out ROC-AUC is 0.92, but the operations team reports that among tickets the model scored around 0.80, only ~55% actually turned out urgent, and this over-prediction pattern is consistent across score bands (predicted rate > observed rate almost everywhere).

Explain what is going wrong in terms of calibration versus discrimination, how you would rigorously diagnose it, how you would fix it (name a concrete method appropriate to this model and at least one alternative with its trade-off), and what the fix will and will not change about the model's behavior and the AUC. Be specific about the data you would use.
open.answer_format: A short structured written explanation, roughly 200-320 words, ideally organized as: (1) what is wrong (calibration vs discrimination), (2) how to diagnose it, (3) how to fix it with a justified method choice, and (4) what the fix does and does not change. Correct use of the field's vocabulary (reliability diagram, ECE/Brier, temperature/Platt/isotonic scaling) is expected.
open.reference_answer:
This is a calibration failure, not a discrimination failure. ROC-AUC measures only how well the model ranks positives above negatives, and it is invariant to any strictly monotonic transform of the scores, so a model can rank almost perfectly (AUC 0.92) while its numeric probabilities are systematically inflated. Because the router uses p as a literal probability in an expected-cost calculation, miscalibration directly corrupts routing even though the ordering is fine. The consistent over-prediction matches the well-documented tendency of modern neural nets (trained with NLL/softmax) to be overconfident.

Diagnosis: on a held-out split never used for training or tuning, build a reliability diagram - bin the predictions (e.g. 10-15 equal-frequency bins), plot mean predicted probability (x) against observed positive frequency (y) per bin. A calibrated model sits on the diagonal; this one will sit below it. Summarize with Expected Calibration Error (weighted mean of |confidence - accuracy| across bins) and/or the Brier score, and report the bin count since ECE is binning-sensitive.

Fix: fit a post-hoc calibration map on a dedicated held-out calibration set (never the training data, which yields optimistic maps). For an overconfident neural net the standard cheap fix is temperature scaling - learn a single scalar T>1 by minimizing NLL, then divide the logits by T before the sigmoid. Alternatives: Platt scaling (a logistic fit on the scores) or isotonic regression (non-parametric, more flexible but data-hungry and prone to overfit small calibration sets). I would prefer temperature scaling here for its single low-variance parameter, reserving isotonic for when data is plentiful and residual miscalibration remains.

What changes and what does not: all three are monotonic maps, so the ranking and therefore ROC-AUC are unchanged - calibration corrects the probability values, not the ordering, which is exactly what the expected-cost router needs. It will not improve the model's ability to separate urgent from non-urgent (accuracy/AUC stay the same), and the router's dollar threshold should be re-derived afterwards because the score-to-probability mapping has shifted. I would also monitor calibration over time, since drift can re-introduce it.
expected_answer_points: Identifies this as a calibration problem distinct from discrimination/ranking, and explains that ROC-AUC is invariant to monotonic score transforms, so high AUC and poor calibration coexist
Notes the systematic over-prediction is consistent with modern neural nets being overconfident, and that the downstream expected-cost use makes correct probabilities (not just ranking) essential
Diagnoses with a reliability diagram (binned mean-predicted vs observed frequency) plus a scalar metric such as ECE and/or Brier score, computed on a held-out set
Fixes with post-hoc calibration fit on a separate held-out calibration split, explicitly not the training data

Names temperature scaling (a single scalar T on the logits) as the appropriate fix for an overconfident NN, and gives at least one alternative (Platt or isotonic) with its trade-off (e.g. isotonic is flexible but overfits small data)
States the fix is a monotonic map, so ranking and ROC-AUC are unchanged; it corrects the probability values, not the ordering
Notes it will not improve discrimination/accuracy, and that the router's decision threshold should be re-derived after calibration

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly separates calibration from discrimination, states that AUC depends only on ranking and is invariant to monotonic transforms, accurately describes the reliability diagram and ECE/Brier, and correctly characterizes temperature/Platt/isotonic scaling (including that monotonic maps preserve ranking). No technical errors such as claiming calibration raises AUC or conflating it with accuracy.

Addresses all four asked parts: root cause (calibration vs discrimination + NN overconfidence), diagnosis (reliability diagram + metric on a held-out set), a concrete fix with a named alternative, and what does/does not change (AUC unchanged, threshold re-derivation). Also specifies fitting the calibration map on a separate held-out split.

Justifies the method choice (why temperature scaling suits an overconfident NN, and the isotonic/Platt trade-off) and explains why a monotonic calibration map restores the downstream expected-cost routing while leaving ranking intact, rather than merely listing techniques.
Clear, well-structured explanation using correct terminology (calibration, reliability diagram, ECE/Brier, temperature scaling) with precise cause-and-effect reasoning that a reviewer could act on.

Proposes only lowering the routing threshold; this shifts the operating point but does not make p a valid probability, so the expected-cost math stays wrong
Fits the calibration map (temperature/isotonic/Platt) on the training set, or measures ECE on the same data used to fit it, causing leakage and optimistically good calibration
Claims temperature scaling or isotonic regression will improve AUC or accuracy, not recognizing that monotonic maps preserve ranking and leave AUC unchanged
Confuses post-hoc temperature scaling of logits with the LLM sampling temperature or with 'setting temperature to 0 for determinism', which are unrelated
Offers a single accuracy or AUC number as evidence of calibration instead of a reliability diagram / ECE / Brier score

open.question: You are the ML engineer on a consumer-lending model that outputs a risk score p in [0,1] used to approve or deny loan applications. Two protected groups, A and B, have materially different default base rates. A fairness audit reports two findings that Product treats as contradictory: (1) the model is well-calibrated within each group (among applicants scored s, the observed default rate is approximately s for both A and B), yet (2) among applicants who ultimately repaid, group B is denied at a substantially higher rate than group A -- i.e., the false-positive rate (denying a creditworthy applicant) differs between groups, violating equalized odds. Product asks you to 'fix the model so it is both calibrated AND has equal error rates across groups.' In a design review, explain whether that request is achievable and why, and lay out a principled, legally-aware plan for how to proceed and what trade-offs the organization is actually choosing.
open.answer_format: A written explanation of roughly 250-400 words. A strong answer names the fairness criteria precisely, states the impossibility result and its mechanism (ideally with the base-rate identity linking PPV/FPR/FNR to prevalence), explains why the two audit findings are mutually consistent rather than a bug, and lays out a justified, legally-aware remediation plan that makes the trade-off explicit.
open.reference_answer:
This is the classic fairness-impossibility situation, not a bug. Three families of group-fairness criteria are in play: independence / demographic parity (equal approval rate), separation / equalized odds (equal TPR and FPR across groups), and sufficiency / calibration (a score means the same default probability in each group; the stronger form is equal PPV / predictive parity). The audit found calibration holds while FPR differs -- and given unequal base rates, those two facts are mutually consistent and mathematically forced.

Why: for a group with prevalence p, the confusion-matrix rates are tied together by
FPR = (p/(1-p)) . ((1-PPV)/PPV) . (1-FNR).
If you hold PPV (calibration/predictive parity) and FNR equal across groups but p differs, FPR must differ. Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan and Chouldechova prove the general result: calibration and equalized odds (balance for both classes) cannot both hold unless the classifier is perfect or the base rates are equal. So 'retrain until both are satisfied' is impossible short of a perfect model; more data or threshold tuning only slides you along the trade-off curve, it does not remove it.

What to actually do:
1. Treat it as a value decision, not metric optimization: choose the governing criterion by the dominant harm. Here the salient harm is denying credit to applicants who would have repaid (false positives on the 'good' outcome), which argues for prioritizing error-rate balance (equalized odds) even at some calibration cost -- and documenting that choice.
2. Post-processing (Hardt-Price-Srebro) can equalize odds via group-specific thresholds/randomization, but in US lending, race-conditional thresholds raise disparate-treatment concerns under ECOA / Regulation B, so flag the legal tension rather than shipping it blindly; weigh group-blind levers (better features, a reject-option review band).
3. Interrogate the label: 'default' may be a biased proxy (measurement/label bias, differential access to forbearance), so equalizing metrics on a biased target can entrench harm -- investigate target and data quality.
4. Evaluate rigorously: report subgroup and intersectional metrics with confidence intervals and adequate sample sizes, and monitor under distribution shift over time, not on one snapshot.
5. Communicate transparently that no model is 'fair' in the absolute -- the organization is selecting an explicit fairness definition and accepting a stated trade-off.
expected_answer_points: Names the fairness families precisely and maps the audit: calibration/sufficiency holds while equalized-odds/separation (equal FPR) is violated.
States the impossibility result: calibration and equalized odds cannot both hold when group base rates differ, except for a perfect classifier (Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan / Chouldechova).
Explains the mechanism -- PPV, FPR, and FNR are algebraically tied to prevalence (ideally the identity FPR = (p/(1-p)).((1-PPV)/PPV).(1-FNR)) -- so the two findings are consistent, not a defect.
Concludes that 'just retrain / add data / tune thresholds' cannot satisfy both objectives; those only move the model along the trade-off, never off it.
Selects a governing fairness criterion justified by the specific harm asymmetry (denying creditworthy applicants argues for error-rate balance) and frames the choice as a documented value decision.
Names post-processing (Hardt et al. group-specific thresholds) but flags the disparate-treatment / fair-lending (ECOA/Reg B) legal tension of race-conditional decision rules.

Adds rigor: questions whether the label is a biased proxy, reports subgroup/intersectional metrics with confidence intervals and adequate sample sizes, monitors under distribution shift, and communicates the trade-off transparently.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly distinguishes independence/demographic parity, separation/equalized odds, and sufficiency/calibration; correctly states the calibration-vs-equalized-odds impossibility under unequal base rates; and accurately explains the base-rate mechanism (the PPV/FPR/FNR-prevalence linkage). Full marks require no false claims (e.g., not asserting both can be jointly achieved by a non-perfect model, not misdefining the metrics).

Covers: (a) why the two audit findings are consistent, (b) the impossibility/mechanism, (c) that retraining cannot satisfy both, (d) a chosen governing criterion with a remediation path, and (e) at least one of label-bias scrutiny, evaluation rigor (CIs/subgroups/monitoring), or the legal constraint. Deduct for omitted dimensions.

Justifies the recommended fairness criterion using the concrete harm/error asymmetry rather than asserting it, explains why the naive 'fix both' request fails, and reasons about the legal/deployment tension of group-conditional thresholds instead of proposing them uncritically.

Explanation is well structured and uses fairness vocabulary precisely (calibration, PPV, FPR/FNR, equalized odds, base rate), and clearly frames fairness as an explicit value choice with a stated trade-off suitable for a stakeholder design review.

common_pitfalls: Treats the FPR disparity as a straightforward bug to be 'debugged out,' not recognizing it is the mathematical consequence of equal calibration plus unequal base rates.
Claims both calibration and equalized odds can be achieved with a better model, more data, or threshold tuning -- missing that only a perfect classifier or equal base rates escapes the trade-off.
Conflates the three fairness families (demographic parity/independence, equalized odds/separation, calibration/sufficiency) or uses the terms interchangeably.
Recommends group-specific (race-conditional) thresholds as the fix without acknowledging the disparate-treatment / fair-lending (ECOA/Reg B) legal problem.
Picks a fairness criterion by fiat ('use equalized odds') without justifying it via the specific harms and error costs of this lending context.
Assumes the 'default' label is clean ground truth, ignoring that a biased target makes metric-equalization entrench rather than remove harm.
open.prompt: You are the ML engineer on a consumer-lending model that outputs a risk score p in [0,1] used to approve or deny loan applications. Two protected groups, A and B, have materially different default base rates. A fairness audit reports two findings that Product treats as contradictory: (1) the model is well-calibrated within each group (among applicants scored s, the observed default rate is approximately s for both A and B), yet (2) among applicants who ultimately repaid, group B is denied at a substantially higher rate than group A -- i.e., the false-positive rate (denying a creditworthy applicant) differs between groups, violating equalized odds. Product asks you to 'fix the model so it is both calibrated AND has equal error rates across groups.' In a design review, explain whether that request is achievable and why, and lay out a principled, legally-aware plan for how to proceed and what trade-offs the organization is actually choosing.
open.title: open_c3_011

open.question: Your team is building a fraud-detection classifier on a tabular dataset (~200k rows, ~80 mostly numeric features). The first model, a scikit-learn RandomForestClassifier with fully grown trees, reaches training AUC 0.97 and held-out validation AUC 0.86. A colleague replaces it with XGBoost configured as n_estimators=2000, learning_rate=0.3, max_depth=10, and no early stopping; it reaches training AUC 0.99 but validation AUC 0.82. In the design review you are asked to: (a) explain mechanistically, in bias-variance terms, why the two ensembles produce such different train-vs-validation gaps; and (b) give a concrete, ordered plan to retune the gradient-boosted model so it closes the gap and ideally beats the random forest. Name the specific hyperparameters you would change and justify each one.
open.answer_format: A structured written explanation, roughly 250-400 words, in two parts: (a) a mechanistic bias-variance contrast of bagging vs boosting that accounts for the differing train-validation gaps, and (b) an ordered retuning plan that names specific XGBoost hyperparameters and justifies each change. Prose or a short justified step list are both acceptable.
open.reference_answer:
(a) Mechanism. A random forest is a bagging ensemble: it trains many deep trees in parallel, each on a bootstrap sample of rows with a random feature subset considered at each split. Individual deep trees are low-bias but high-variance; because bootstrapping and feature subsampling decorrelate them, averaging their outputs sharply reduces variance while leaving bias roughly unchanged. Crucially, adding more trees only makes the variance estimate converge, so n_estimators is not an overfitting knob for a forest — hence its train-validation gap stays controlled (0.97 vs 0.86).

Gradient boosting is an additive, sequential model: f_m = f_{m-1} + eta * h_m, where each new shallow tree h_m is fit to the negative gradient (pseudo-residuals) of the loss under the current ensemble. Each stage reduces bias by correcting the ensemble's current errors. Because it greedily drives down training loss, n_estimators IS an overfitting knob: with learning_rate=0.3 (large steps), max_depth=10 (high-capacity learners, not weak learners), 2000 rounds, and no early stopping, the model keeps fitting noise. The 0.99/0.82 gap is classic high-variance overfitting from an over-long, over-flexible boosting run.

(b) Retuning plan (ordered):
1. Turn on early stopping: pass a validation set / watchlist with early_stopping_rounds and lower learning_rate to ~0.01-0.05, keeping a large n_estimators cap so early stopping picks the optimal round count. Lower eta needs more trees — the eta x n_estimators trade-off.
2. Reduce learner capacity: cut max_depth to ~3-6, and/or raise min_child_weight and gamma (min split-loss) so splits need more evidence.
3. Add stochasticity: set subsample (~0.7-0.9) and colsample_bytree (<1) — stochastic gradient boosting decorrelates trees and lowers variance.
4. Add explicit regularization: reg_lambda (L2) and reg_alpha (L1) on leaf weights.
5. Tune with cross-validation and watch the train-vs-validation loss curves; for the fraud class imbalance consider scale_pos_weight.

Expectation: a well-regularized GBM should match or beat the forest's 0.86 because boosting reduces bias, but it demands more careful tuning; the random forest is the more robust default when tuning budget is limited.
expected_answer_points: Frames bagging/Random Forest as variance reduction: averages many decorrelated deep (low-bias, high-variance) trees trained in parallel on bootstrap samples plus random feature subsets, cutting variance without materially changing bias

Frames boosting as bias reduction: an additive, sequential model where each shallow tree is fit to the negative gradient / pseudo-residuals of the loss, greedily correcting the current ensemble's errors
Explains that n_estimators is an overfitting knob in boosting (more rounds keep chasing residuals/noise) but not in bagging (more trees only converge variance and do not overfit)

Diagnoses the 0.99/0.82 XGBoost gap as high-variance overfitting caused by high learning_rate, deep trees, too many rounds, and no early stopping, versus the forest's controlled gap from variance averaging
States the learning_rate <-> n_estimators trade-off and prescribes low eta + large n_estimators cap + early_stopping_rounds on a validation set
Names concrete complexity/regularization controls with correct direction: lower max_depth, raise min_child_weight/gamma, add subsample & colsample_bytree, add reg_lambda/reg_alpha
Judgement: a properly regularized GBM can match or beat the forest because boosting lowers bias, while the forest is the more robust low-tuning default

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Bias-variance mechanisms are correct and not swapped: bagging reduces variance by averaging decorrelated trees, boosting reduces bias by sequentially fitting gradients/residuals; correctly asserts n_estimators overfits boosting but not forests; every hyperparameter change moves in the overfitting-reducing direction (lower eta, shallower trees, subsampling, more regularization). No false claims (e.g. that more forest trees overfit, or that raising eta/depth fixes overfitting).

Covers both the mechanistic contrast (part a) and an actionable retuning plan (part b); the plan touches the main levers — learning_rate + early stopping, tree-complexity controls, stochastic subsampling, and explicit L1/L2 regularization — rather than fixing only one knob.

Ties each recommendation back to bias-variance reasoning and the specific symptom (0.99 vs 0.82 gap), explains the eta x n_estimators coupling, and reaches a defensible judgement about when GBM beats a forest versus when the forest is the safer default.

Uses precise ensemble vocabulary (bagging, boosting, bootstrap, pseudo-residuals, early stopping, subsample/colsample, reg_lambda) correctly; the plan is ordered and easy to follow; distinguishes the two ensembles cleanly without hand-waving.

common_pitfalls: Claims adding more trees overfits a random forest the same way it does boosting, conflating how the two ensembles relate to n_estimators
Describes boosting as many independent trees voting or trains them in parallel, missing the sequential negative-gradient / residual-fitting mechanism
Swaps bias and variance: says the forest reduces bias or that boosting reduces variance
Prescribes fixes in the wrong direction, e.g. increasing learning_rate or max_depth, or 'just reduce n_estimators' without early stopping and without lowering eta
Lowers learning_rate without increasing the n_estimators budget, ignoring the eta x n_estimators coupling, or omits a validation-based early-stopping criterion entirely
Offers only generic advice (add more data, cross-validate) without naming the concrete XGBoost regularization levers (min_child_weight, gamma, subsample, colsample_bytree, reg_alpha/reg_lambda)

open.question: A teammate trains a binary classifier to flag fraudulent credit-card transactions. In the dataset, about 0.5% of transactions are fraud. In the design review they proudly report that the model reaches 99.5% accuracy on the test set and propose shipping it. As the reviewer, explain why accuracy is the wrong headline metric here, name the metrics you would ask to see instead and why, and describe at least two concrete techniques you would use to improve the model's ability to actually catch fraud. Be explicit about any trade-off the team must decide on.
open.answer_format: A short written explanation in prose, roughly 150-250 words. A complete answer covers three things: (1) why 99.5% accuracy is misleading given the base rate, (2) which evaluation metrics to use instead and why, and (3) at least two concrete remedies, with the key trade-off named. Naming real tools/terms (precision, recall, PR curve, SMOTE, class weights, threshold tuning) is expected.
open.reference_answer:
Accuracy is meaningless here because the classes are extremely imbalanced. A trivial model that predicts "not fraud" for every transaction already scores 99.5% accuracy, so that number just reflects the 0.5% base rate and tells us nothing about whether the model catches fraud. I'd ask to see the confusion matrix and minority-class metrics: precision (of the transactions we flag, how many are truly fraud) and recall (of all actual fraud, how much we catch), summarized as F1, and ideally the precision-recall curve / PR-AUC, which is far more informative than ROC-AUC under severe imbalance because ROC is dominated by the huge true-negative count and can look deceptively strong.

The core trade-off the team must decide is recall vs precision, driven by business cost: a false negative is missed fraud (expensive), while a false positive blocks a legitimate customer (annoying, support cost). That decision also sets the operating threshold rather than a default 0.5.

Concrete remedies: (1) cost-sensitive learning via class weights, e.g. class_weight="balanced", so the loss penalizes minority errors more; (2) resampling the training data, e.g. SMOTE oversampling of the minority or undersampling the majority; and (3) tuning the decision threshold on a validation set. Crucially, resampling and threshold tuning must be done only on training folds, and the test set must keep the true 0.5% distribution (stratified split) so the reported metrics reflect production reality.
expected_answer_points: A trivial classifier that always predicts the majority class ("not fraud") already achieves ~99.5% accuracy, so accuracy merely reflects the base rate and says nothing about fraud-detection ability
Recommends minority-class-focused metrics: precision, recall, and F1 (and the confusion matrix), rather than overall accuracy
Recommends the precision-recall curve / PR-AUC and notes it is more informative than ROC-AUC under severe imbalance (ROC-AUC can look deceptively high because true negatives dominate)

Names the precision vs recall trade-off explicitly and ties it to business cost of false negatives (missed fraud) vs false positives (blocking legitimate customers), which also drives threshold choice
Remedy: cost-sensitive learning / class weights (e.g. class_weight="balanced")
Remedy: resampling the training set (e.g. SMOTE oversampling of the minority or undersampling the majority) and/or tuning the decision threshold away from 0.5
Insists resampling/threshold tuning happen only on training data and the test set preserve the true class distribution (stratified split), so reported metrics reflect production

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly explains the majority-class-baseline argument (a trivial negative predictor reaches ~99.5%), correctly defines/uses precision and recall, and accurately recommends PR-based evaluation over ROC/accuracy for heavy imbalance. Proposed remedies (class weights, SMOTE/resampling, threshold tuning) are technically valid and correctly applied. Full marks require no incorrect claims (e.g. mixing up precision and recall, or claiming ROC-AUC is unaffected by imbalance).

Covers all three required parts: (1) why accuracy misleads, (2) better metrics with justification, and (3) at least two concrete remedies. Full marks also mention the correct evaluation hygiene (resample only training data, keep a stratified/realistic test distribution). Partial credit if one part is missing or only a single remedy is given.

Explicitly connects the metric choice and threshold to the business cost of false negatives vs false positives and names the precision/recall trade-off as a decision the team must make, rather than just listing techniques. Full marks tie the 'why' of each recommendation to the imbalance and the fraud context.

Well-organized review-style explanation using correct terminology; distinguishes precision from recall clearly and states recommendations a teammate could act on. Deduct for vague, disorganized, or jargon-dropping answers that never explain the reasoning.

common_pitfalls: Accepting or defending the 99.5% accuracy, or failing to point out that an always-'not-fraud' baseline already achieves it
Recommending ROC-AUC as the primary metric without recognizing that the precision-recall curve is more informative under extreme imbalance, or asserting ROC-AUC is immune to class imbalance
Applying SMOTE/oversampling (or threshold tuning) to the whole dataset before the train/test split, or resampling the test set, which leaks information and inflates reported metrics
Only listing resampling and forgetting other levers such as class weights / cost-sensitive learning and decision-threshold tuning
Maximizing recall with no regard for the resulting false positives, ignoring the precision/recall trade-off and the business cost of blocking legitimate customers
Confusing or swapping the definitions of precision and recall

In the design review they proudly report that the model reaches 99.5% accuracy on the test set and propose shipping it. open.question: A teammate is building the first model for a new binary classification problem: predicting customer churn on a tabular dataset of ~50,000 accounts with an 8% churn (positive) rate and a mix of numeric and categorical features. Skipping any baseline, they went straight to tuning an XGBoost model and now report 'ROC-AUC 0.82, and 93% accuracy — let's ship it.' You are running the design review. Explain what baselines should have been established before trusting that XGBoost result, walk through the sequence you'd build from trivial to competitive, justify each, and describe how you'd interpret the 0.82 against them and what conditions must hold for the comparison to be valid.
open.answer_format: A structured written explanation (~250-350 words), ideally with a short ordered list of baselines each with a one-line justification, followed by a paragraph on interpretation and comparison validity.
open.reference_answer:
Before trusting any single number I'd insist on a ladder of baselines, each evaluated on the identical CV split, preprocessing, and metric as the XGBoost model.

1. Trivial / naive baseline: a majority-class (always-predict 'no churn') predictor, plus a base-rate or stratified-random guesser. This sets the absolute floor. Crucially, on an 8% positive rate the majority classifier already scores ~92% accuracy, so the teammate's '93% accuracy' is almost meaningless — it barely beats predicting nothing. This exposes accuracy as the wrong headline metric under imbalance; I'd switch the conversation to ROC-AUC and, given the rarity of the positive class, PR-AUC / F1 or recall at a fixed precision, since a trivial model gets ROC-AUC ~0.5 and near-zero PR-AUC.

2. Simple-model baseline: a regularized logistic regression (with basic one-hot encoding + scaling) or a shallow tree. This is the 'reasonable-effort' reference the complex model must beat to justify its cost and opacity.

3. Incumbent / heuristic baseline: whatever rule or human process currently flags churn today. Lift over this is what actually justifies the project to the business.

Interpretation: 0.82 is meaningful only as lift, not in isolation. A large gap over the trivial baseline plus a clear gap over logistic regression confirms real signal and that the extra model complexity is earning its keep; if XGBoost barely beats logistic regression, ship the simpler, more maintainable model. Baselines are also diagnostics: if a trivial baseline scores surprisingly high, or XGBoost looks implausibly good, suspect target leakage or a broken split.

Validity conditions: every model must share the same train/validation folds (or CV scheme), the same preprocessing fit only on training folds, the same metric, and a fixed seed. I'd also report cross-validation variance (or bootstrap CIs) so the lift is judged against noise, not a single lucky fold.
expected_answer_points: Establish a trivial/naive floor first — a majority-class predictor (and/or base-rate / stratified-random guess) — to define the absolute lower bound before any learned model

Recognize the imbalance trap: with 8% positives the majority classifier already achieves ~92% accuracy, so '93% accuracy' is near-worthless and accuracy is the wrong metric; prefer ROC-AUC and especially PR-AUC / F1 / recall-at-precision for the rare class
Add a simple, low-tuning model baseline (regularized logistic regression or shallow tree with basic preprocessing) as the 'reasonable-effort' reference the complex model must beat
Include an incumbent/heuristic or human baseline (the current churn rule or process) because lift over it is what justifies the project to the business
Interpret 0.82 as lift over the baselines rather than in absolute terms — a small gap over logistic regression means the added XGBoost complexity is not justified and the simpler model should win
Use baselines as diagnostics for target leakage or a broken split (trivial baseline scoring too high, or the complex model looking implausibly good)

State the validity conditions: identical CV split/folds, identical preprocessing fit on training data only, same metric, fixed seed, and report variance/confidence (CV std or bootstrap) so lift is judged against noise

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly identifies the majority-class floor and the ~92% accuracy trap under 8% prevalence, names appropriate imbalance-aware metrics (ROC-AUC/PR-AUC/F1), proposes a valid simple-model baseline, and states correct comparison-validity conditions (shared split, leak-free preprocessing, same metric). Deduct for factual errors such as claiming 93% accuracy is strong, misstating what a trivial model scores on ROC-AUC/PR-AUC, or proposing an invalid comparison setup.

Full marks: covers the full ladder — trivial/naive baseline, simple-model baseline, and incumbent/heuristic baseline — plus interpretation-as-lift and at least one diagnostic or variance/uncertainty consideration. Deduct for each missing tier or for omitting the interpretation-as-lift and validity discussion.

Full marks: justifies WHY each baseline exists (floor, reasonable-effort reference, business benchmark), reasons explicitly that 0.82 is only meaningful as lift, and argues the decision consequence (e.g., prefer the simpler model when the gap is small). Deduct when baselines are listed without rationale or when no decision is drawn from the comparison.

Full marks: organized (e.g., an ordered ladder with concise justifications) and readable at design-review altitude, using correct vocabulary. Deduct for disorganized, rambling, or ambiguous explanation that a reviewer could not act on.

common_pitfalls: Accepts or defends the 93% accuracy as good, missing that a majority-class predictor already reaches ~92% under 8% prevalence
Treats a tuned logistic regression or 'another ML model' as the only baseline and skips the trivial majority-class / base-rate floor entirely
Judges ROC-AUC 0.82 as 'good' in absolute terms instead of as lift over the baselines, so never asks whether XGBoost's complexity is justified over a simple model
Compares models evaluated on different splits, metrics, or with preprocessing fit on the full dataset (leakage), invalidating the comparison
Omits the incumbent/heuristic or human baseline that the business actually needs the model to beat
Ignores the diagnostic role of baselines (catching target leakage or a broken split) and reports no variance/confidence, treating a single fold's number as definitive

open.question: Your team serves a 13B-parameter chat model in fp16 on a single A100-80GB GPU behind a REST API. Prompts vary widely (200-4000 tokens) and outputs range 50-800 tokens. The server uses static batching: it waits to collect a fixed batch of 8 requests, pads every sequence to the longest one in the batch, runs generation, and returns all 8 only when the last sequence finishes. In a design review the metrics show: aggregate throughput far below the GPU's theoretical token/sec ceiling, GPU compute (SM) utilization around 25% during generation while HBM is nearly full, and p99 latency dominated by short requests that queued behind long generations. Explain what is happening at the hardware and algorithm level, then propose a concrete plan to improve both throughput and tail latency. Justify each change and state its trade-offs.
open.answer_format: A structured written explanation, roughly 250-400 words: first a diagnosis of the bottleneck (hardware + scheduling), then a prioritized set of concrete optimizations each with its mechanism and trade-off, ending with an explicit throughput-vs-latency framing tied to an SLO. Naming real systems/techniques (vLLM, continuous batching, PagedAttention, AWQ/GPTQ, speculative decoding) is expected.
open.reference_answer:
Diagnosis. Autoregressive inference has two phases with opposite characteristics. Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel as large GEMMs and is compute-bound. Decode emits one token per sequence per step; the math is GEMV-like with very low arithmetic intensity, so each step is dominated by streaming the model weights (and the growing KV cache) out of HBM. Decode is therefore memory-bandwidth bound, which is exactly why SM utilization sits at ~25% while HBM is full: the GPU is waiting on memory, not compute. Static batching compounds this: padding every sequence to the batch maximum wastes compute, the whole batch is held until the slowest generation finishes (head-of-line blocking), and no new request can join mid-flight, so short requests queue behind 800-token generations, inflating p99. HBM being full points to the KV cache as the real concurrency limit.

Plan. (1) Switch to continuous/in-flight batching (vLLM/Orca): schedule at the iteration level so finished sequences exit and queued ones join every step. This raises effective batch size during decode, amortizing each weight load across more sequences, and removes head-of-line blocking, cutting tail latency. (2) Use PagedAttention so KV cache lives in fixed non-contiguous blocks; this eliminates fragmentation and max-length over-reservation, raising the number of concurrent sequences the 80GB can hold. (3) Apply weight-only quantization (INT8/INT4 via AWQ or GPTQ): because decode is bandwidth-bound, moving 4x fewer weight bytes directly speeds decode, and freed memory becomes more KV cache / concurrency. Trade-off: possible accuracy regression (validate on evals) and diminishing benefit in compute-bound, large-batch regimes. (4) Add chunked prefill so a 4000-token prefill is split and interleaved with ongoing decodes instead of stalling them. (5) For latency-sensitive, low-concurrency traffic, consider speculative decoding with a small draft model.

Trade-off framing. Batching maximizes throughput but raises per-request latency, so size max batch and max-num-seqs to the p99 SLO rather than blindly maximizing. Measure prefill vs decode latency, tokens/sec, SM utilization and KV-cache occupancy separately, and pick levers matched to whether the workload is latency- or throughput-bound.
expected_answer_points: Distinguishes prefill (parallel over prompt tokens, compute-bound GEMMs) from decode (one token/step, GEMV-like, low arithmetic intensity) and identifies decode as memory-bandwidth bound because weights + KV cache are streamed from HBM each step, explaining the low SM utilization despite full HBM.

Explains why static/padded batching hurts: wasted compute on padding, head-of-line blocking (short requests wait for the longest generation), and inability to admit new requests mid-flight, which inflates p99 tail latency.

Proposes continuous / in-flight batching (iteration-level scheduling, e.g. vLLM/Orca) so completed sequences leave and queued ones join, raising GPU utilization/throughput and cutting queueing latency.

Identifies the KV cache as the dominant memory consumer and true concurrency limit, and proposes PagedAttention-style block paging to remove fragmentation/over-reservation and increase concurrent sequences.

Proposes weight-only quantization (INT8/INT4, AWQ/GPTQ) and correctly ties the speedup to decode being bandwidth-bound (fewer bytes moved) plus freed memory for more KV cache, while noting the accuracy-risk trade-off and reduced benefit in compute-bound/large-batch regimes.

Articulates the core throughput-vs-latency trade-off: batching amortizes weight loads to boost throughput but raises per-request latency, so batch/concurrency must be tuned to the latency SLO rather than maximized blindly.

Adds at least one further appropriate lever with correct rationale (e.g. chunked prefill to stop long prefills stalling decode, speculative decoding for low-concurrency latency, or tensor parallelism) and mentions measuring prefill/decode latency, tokens/sec, SM util and KV occupancy separately.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly explains prefill-vs-decode and that decode is memory-bandwidth (not compute) bound, correctly attributes the 25% SM utilization / full HBM symptom, and describes continuous batching, PagedAttention/KV-cache limits, and quantization mechanisms accurately. Deduct for physical errors such as calling decode compute-bound, claiming a faster-FLOP GPU or lower temperature fixes utilization, or misstating what quantization/speculative decoding actually do.

Full marks: covers the diagnosis (two-phase + static-batching pathology + KV-cache limit) AND a prioritized multi-lever plan (continuous batching, paged KV, quantization, plus at least one of chunked prefill / speculative decoding / TP) AND the throughput-vs-latency SLO framing. Partial credit if it fixes throughput but ignores tail latency (or vice versa) or omits the KV-cache/memory dimension.

Full marks: each proposed change is justified by the mechanism (e.g. batching helps because it amortizes bandwidth-bound weight loads; quantization helps decode because it is bandwidth-bound) and its trade-off is stated. Deduct when recommendations are asserted as a checklist without linking cause to the observed symptoms or without acknowledging costs.

Full marks: well-organized (diagnosis then prioritized plan then trade-off), uses correct serving vocabulary precisely, and is concise. Deduct for disorganized dumps of buzzwords, vague hand-waving, or terminology used loosely/incorrectly.

common_pitfalls: Treats generation as one monolithic compute-bound operation and never separates prefill from decode, so cannot explain why SM utilization is low while HBM is full.
Diagnoses the low utilization as a compute shortfall and recommends a higher-FLOP GPU or more SMs, missing that bandwidth-bound decode is limited by HBM traffic, not FLOPs.

Suggests simply increasing the static batch size to raise throughput, ignoring that larger batches worsen per-request latency and that static batching's head-of-line blocking is the actual tail-latency cause.
Overlooks the KV cache entirely, assuming model weights are the only memory cost, and so cannot explain the concurrency ceiling or why PagedAttention helps.
Assumes weight-only INT4 quantization always yields a proportional speedup and ignores accuracy risk, dequant overhead, and its reduced benefit in the compute-bound large-batch regime.

Claims speculative decoding boosts aggregate throughput under high concurrency, missing that it primarily reduces latency at low batch and can waste compute on rejected draft tokens when the draft model is poorly aligned.
