open.question:
Your team runs a customer-support triage system for a pan-Arab bank. An intent classifier fine-tuned on Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) call-center transcripts scores 0.91 macro-F1 offline, but in production it drops to about 0.62 on live chat messages. Those messages are overwhelmingly Egyptian and Gulf dialects, with heavy code-switching (Arabizi / Latin-script Arabic and English brand names), inconsistent or absent diacritics, and multiple spellings of the same word (e.g. hamza/alef variants of أريد, and taa-marbuta ة vs haa ه endings). A junior engineer proposes to 'just strip all diacritics and normalize every alef/hamza form to a bare alef' to close the gap.

Explain what is actually causing the train/production gap; evaluate the junior's normalization proposal (where it helps and where it can hurt); and lay out a concrete plan — data, preprocessing/tokenization, model choice, and evaluation — to make the system robust across dialects. Reference the specific Arabic-NLP mechanisms and tools you would use.
open.answer_format: A structured written analysis (~350-500 words) in three parts: (1) a diagnosis of the gap, (2) a two-sided evaluation of the normalization proposal, and (3) a concrete remediation plan covering data, preprocessing/tokenization, model choice, and evaluation. Should name real Arabic-NLP models and tools.
open.reference_answer:
Diagnosis. The dominant cause is diglossia / variety shift, not spelling. The classifier was fine-tuned on MSA but serves Egyptian and Gulf dialectal Arabic (DA), which differ from MSA in lexicon, morphology, clitic patterns and syntax — so the model never learned the dialectal words and constructions that carry intent. On top of that sit two representation problems: (a) tokenizer effects — dialectal terms, Arabizi and English brand names are off-distribution for an MSA-centric subword vocabulary, so they fragment into many high-fertility subwords or hit [UNK], degrading embeddings; and (b) train/serve preprocessing skew — if inference normalizes text differently than training did, the same word maps to different token sequences. A 0.91→0.62 drop is the signature of variety shift plus these effects, not a diacritics bug.

Evaluating the proposal. Diacritic stripping and alef/hamza normalization (أ إ آ → ا) are standard, cheap orthographic hygiene: they collapse spelling variants and reduce sparsity, so they help matching a little. But most Arabic text is already undiacritized, so stripping buys little; normalization is lossy and can conflate distinct words, and over-normalizing (e.g. ة→ه, or ى↔ي) merges semantically different tokens. Crucially, the normalization must match the pretrained model's own scheme and be applied identically at train and inference — inventing an aggressive scheme that diverges from what the model/tokenizer expects can hurt. And none of this touches diglossia: normalization is necessary hygiene, not the cure.

Plan.
- Data: collect and label in-domain production messages stratified by dialect and script; augment the MSA training set with dialectal and Arabizi examples. Add script/dialect identification (e.g. CAMeL Tools DID), transliterate Arabizi into Arabic script, and keep English brand names as-is.
- Model: replace MSA-centric AraBERT with a dialect-aware encoder — MARBERT (pretrained on ~1B Arabic tweets, strong on DA/social text) or CAMeLBERT-Mix (MSA+DA+CA); consider XLM-R where code-switching is heavy.
- Preprocessing/tokenization: adopt one defined normalization plus morphological segmentation scheme (Farasa or CAMeL Tools clitic segmentation of و/ف/ال/ب/ل and pronominal suffixes), matched to the chosen model and applied identically at train and serve.
- Evaluation: report per-dialect and per-script macro-F1 on a stratified set, not just an aggregate, so the dialect gap is visible; monitor production drift and add a confidence-thresholded human fallback.
expected_answer_points: Identifies the core cause as diglossia / MSA-vs-dialect distribution shift — the MSA-trained model lacks dialectal lexicon, morphology and syntax — rather than mere orthography

Names subword-tokenizer fertility / OOV ([UNK]) on dialectal words, Arabizi and English as an off-distribution representation problem, and identifies train/serve preprocessing skew as a distinct contributor

Evaluates the normalization proposal as standard but lossy hygiene: alef/hamza normalization and diacritic stripping reduce orthographic sparsity yet can conflate distinct words and do not fix diglossia
States that any normalization/tokenization scheme must match the pretrained model's own preprocessing and be applied identically at train and inference
Recommends a dialect-aware model (MARBERT or CAMeLBERT-Mix/DA) over MSA-centric AraBERT, and/or XLM-R for code-switching
Prescribes collecting and labelling in-domain dialectal + Arabizi data (augmentation), with dialect/script identification and Arabizi transliteration
Specifies consistent morphological/clitic segmentation and normalization via a real toolkit (Farasa or CAMeL Tools), matched to the model
Prescribes per-dialect / per-script stratified evaluation (per-dialect macro-F1, not just aggregate) plus drift monitoring or a low-confidence human fallback

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly attributes the gap to diglossia/variety shift plus tokenizer fertility/OOV and train-serve preprocessing skew; accurately describes Arabic orthographic normalization (hamza/alef forms, taa marbuta, alef maqsura, diacritics, tatweel) and correctly characterizes real tools/models (MARBERT, CAMeLBERT, AraBERT, Farasa, CAMeL Tools, XLM-R). Deduct for factual errors about Arabic mechanisms or tool capabilities (e.g. claiming AraBERT is dialect-optimized, or that normalization alone resolves dialect).

Full marks: gives the diagnosis, a two-sided evaluation of the normalization proposal, AND all four plan dimensions (data, preprocessing/tokenization, model choice, evaluation) including code-switching/Arabizi handling. Deduct for each missing dimension or a one-sided treatment of normalization.

Full marks: justifies why normalization alone is insufficient, weighs where it helps vs where it hurts, and ties each remediation to the specific failure mode it addresses (e.g. MARBERT for dialect, segmentation for fertility, stratified eval for hidden per-dialect gap). Deduct for assertions offered without mechanism.

Full marks: clear diagnosis/evaluation/plan structure, precise use of Arabic-NLP vocabulary, and concrete examples (specific alef/hamza forms, clitics, named tools). Deduct for vague, disorganized, or jargon-only prose.

common_pitfalls: Treats the problem as purely orthographic and claims the junior's normalization will close the gap, missing that dialectal vocabulary/syntax (diglossia) is the dominant cause

Recommends normalization but ignores train/serve consistency and that the scheme must match the pretrained model's own preprocessing — inventing an aggressive scheme that conflicts with the model's tokenizer
Proposes over-normalization (e.g. taa-marbuta→haa, ya↔alef-maqsura, stripping needed distinctions) without noting it conflates distinct words and is lossy
Keeps the MSA-centric model or names AraBERT as the fix, unaware of dialect-focused models such as MARBERT or CAMeLBERT-Mix
Ignores code-switching / Arabizi entirely, treating the input as monolingual Arabic-script text
Evaluates only with a single aggregate macro-F1, leaving the per-dialect gap invisible — no stratified evaluation or drift monitoring

open.question: Your team trained a binary text classifier that flags toxic comments for moderation. On a held-out test set of 100,000 comments — of which only 3% are actually toxic — the model reports 97% accuracy, and a product manager wants to ship it immediately. Explain why the 97% accuracy figure is misleading for this task, which evaluation metrics you would report instead and why, and how you would choose the model's operating threshold given that this is a content-moderation use case.
open.answer_format: A short written explanation, roughly 150-250 words. It may include a brief list of the specific metrics you would report. It must justify each choice by connecting the metric or threshold to the imbalanced, moderation-specific nature of the task rather than asserting metrics generically.
open.reference_answer:
The 97% figure is nearly meaningless because the classes are heavily imbalanced (only 3% toxic). A degenerate model that labels every comment non-toxic already scores 97%, so accuracy just mirrors the base rate rather than the model's ability to catch toxicity — which is the entire point of the system.

Instead I'd evaluate the positive (toxic) class directly: report precision (of the comments we flag, how many are genuinely toxic) and recall (of the truly toxic comments, how many we catch), their F1, and inspect the full confusion matrix (TP/FP/FN/TN). For a threshold-independent view I'd plot the precision-recall curve and report PR-AUC, which is more informative than ROC-AUC under extreme imbalance: ROC-AUC's huge true-negative pool can make performance look deceptively strong.

Because the model outputs a score, I'd pick the operating threshold from the moderation cost trade-off, not to maximize accuracy. False negatives leave toxic content up; false positives censor legitimate users. If flags go to human reviewers I'd favor higher recall at some precision cost; if the system auto-removes content I'd protect precision to avoid wrongful takedowns. Finally I'd confirm the test set reflects true prevalence and check performance on important slices (e.g., by topic or by dialect/identity terms) so uneven behavior surfaces before shipping.
expected_answer_points: Explains that accuracy is misleading under class imbalance — a trivial all-negative (majority-class) baseline already reaches ~97%, so accuracy reflects the base rate, not toxicity-detection ability.
Recommends reporting precision and recall for the toxic (positive) class specifically, along with F1 and the confusion matrix (TP/FP/FN/TN).
Recommends a threshold-independent metric — the precision-recall curve / PR-AUC — and notes it is preferable to ROC-AUC under heavy imbalance because ROC-AUC can look over-optimistic.
Describes the precision-vs-recall trade-off and ties threshold selection to the asymmetric costs of moderation (missed toxic content vs. over-censoring legitimate users), not to maximizing accuracy.
Notes evaluating on a set reflecting true prevalence and/or on meaningful subgroups/slices to catch uneven behavior before shipping.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly explains that accuracy is dominated by the majority class (an all-negative classifier scores ~97%), correctly defines precision and recall for the toxic class, and correctly recommends precision-recall-based/threshold-independent evaluation (PR curve or PR-AUC) as suited to imbalance. No incorrect claims — e.g., does not confuse precision with recall, does not present ROC-AUC as unproblematic under extreme imbalance, and does not claim accuracy becomes valid simply by adding data.

Addresses all three parts of the prompt: (1) why accuracy misleads, (2) which metrics to report instead — precision, recall, F1, confusion matrix, PR curve/PR-AUC — and (3) how to set the operating threshold, plus at least one supporting consideration such as representative test prevalence or per-slice evaluation.

Justifies metric and threshold choices by explicitly linking them to the imbalanced data and the asymmetric costs of the moderation task (false negatives leaving toxic content up vs. false positives censoring legitimate users), rather than listing metrics as generically 'better'.

Explanation is well-organized and uses correct terminology (precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC, confusion matrix, threshold), and is understandable to a non-specialist stakeholder such as the product manager.

common_pitfalls: Answering with a training-side fix (oversampling, SMOTE, class weights) as if that resolves the objection, when the question is about the misleading evaluation metric, not how to improve the model.
Recommending ROC-AUC as the primary fix without recognizing that under 3% prevalence its large true-negative count can make the model look far better than PR-AUC would show.
Reporting only overall accuracy replaced by overall/macro F1 without singling out recall on the minority (toxic) class, which is the metric that actually matters here.
Treating F1 (equal weight on precision and recall) as automatically correct and never connecting threshold choice to the asymmetric cost of missed toxicity vs. wrongful takedowns.
Confusing precision and recall, or describing the threshold as something to tune to maximize accuracy rather than to hit a target recall/precision for the moderation workflow.
Claiming the 97% accuracy is fine or that the model is 'good enough' because the number is high, missing the majority-class baseline entirely.

open.question:
You are tuning generation parameters for a customer-support assistant built on a hosted LLM. It has two subsystems that share one client wrapper: (1) a field-extraction step that reads a ticket and must emit a small, reproducible JSON object, and (2) a 'suggested reply' drafter that should feel varied across calls. A teammate set temperature=1.5 with top_p=1.0 for BOTH. In production the extraction step intermittently emits malformed/nonsensical output, and the drafts occasionally veer into rare, incoherent tokens.

Explain the mechanism of temperature, top-p (nucleus) sampling, and top-k, and how temperature interacts with the two truncation knobs. Diagnose why temperature=1.5 with top_p=1.0 produces the two symptoms observed. Recommend concrete settings for each subsystem and justify them. Finally, state whether temperature=0 gives you a truly deterministic, reproducible extractor, and why or why not.
open.answer_format: A short written explanation, roughly 200-320 words. Cover: the mechanism of each of the three parameters; how temperature (reshaping) differs from top-k/top-p (truncation) and how they interact; a diagnosis of the two symptoms; concrete recommended settings for the extraction and drafting subsystems with justification; and a precise verdict on whether temperature=0 is genuinely deterministic and reproducible.
open.reference_answer:
Temperature rescales the logits before softmax: each logit is divided by T. T<1 sharpens the distribution toward the highest-probability tokens; T>1 flattens it, pulling probability mass into the long tail of unlikely tokens; T->0 collapses to argmax (greedy). Crucially, temperature only reshapes the probabilities of ALL tokens -- it never removes any candidate.

Top-k and top-p are truncation steps that clip the candidate set before sampling. Top-k keeps the k most probable tokens (fixed count). Top-p (nucleus) keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p, then renormalizes -- an adaptive cutoff that shrinks when the model is confident and widens when it is unsure. So temperature decides the SHAPE of the distribution; top-k/top-p decide how much of the tail you allow to be sampled from.

Diagnosis: temperature=1.5 flattens the distribution, and top_p=1.0 disables truncation, so the entire tail stays eligible. The drafter can therefore sample rare, incoherent tokens -- the 'off the rails' symptom. For extraction, that same flattening plus intact tail lets it pick tokens that break the JSON structure, giving malformed output; extraction should not be sampling creatively at all.

Recommendation: For extraction, use temperature=0 (greedy) -- ideally combined with constrained/structured decoding or a JSON/schema mode -- so structure is enforced rather than hoped for. For the drafter, keep variety but bound the tail: moderate temperature (~0.7-0.9) with top_p~0.9 (or a top_k), not temperature=1.5 with full nucleus. This gives diversity while clipping the incoherent tail.

Determinism: temperature=0 makes decoding greedy and near-deterministic, but not guaranteed bit-for-bit reproducible. Floating-point non-associativity in parallel GPU reductions, varying batch composition, kernel/hardware differences, and MoE routing can flip a near-tie argmax, so identical inputs can occasionally diverge. Pin a seed where the API supports it, but treat 'deterministic' as 'strongly reproducible, not guaranteed'.
expected_answer_points: Temperature divides the logits before softmax: T<1 sharpens toward high-probability tokens, T>1 flattens and raises the long tail, T->0 approaches greedy/argmax; it reshapes probabilities but does not remove any candidate token.

Top-k keeps a fixed number k of the most probable tokens, while top-p (nucleus) keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p and renormalizes -- an adaptive truncation; top_p=1.0 means no truncation.

Correctly distinguishes temperature (reshaping the distribution) from top-k/top-p (truncating the candidate set) and notes they compose: truncation bounds the tail regardless of how much temperature inflated it.

Diagnoses that temperature=1.5 with top_p=1.0 flattens the distribution while leaving the full tail eligible, so rare/incoherent tokens get sampled (drafts veer off) and structure-breaking tokens slip into the extractor.

Recommends temperature=0 (greedy), ideally with constrained/structured or JSON-schema decoding, for the reproducible extraction step, because sampling variety is undesirable there and prompting alone does not guarantee valid structure.
Recommends moderate temperature (~0.7-0.9) plus a bounded top_p (~0.9) or top_k for the drafter, to keep variety while clipping the incoherent tail, rather than temperature=1.5 with full nucleus.

States that temperature=0 is near-deterministic but not guaranteed reproducible due to floating-point non-associativity, batch/kernel/hardware variation, and possible MoE routing effects; a fixed seed helps but does not fully guarantee it.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly describes temperature as logit scaling before softmax (sharpen/flatten/greedy), top-k as fixed-count truncation and top-p as adaptive cumulative-mass truncation, and correctly separates reshaping from truncation. No false claims (e.g. does not say temperature removes tokens, does not conflate top-k with top-p, and correctly qualifies temperature=0 determinism). Deduct for each mechanistic error or unqualified claim that temperature=0 is fully reproducible.

Full marks: addresses all required parts -- mechanism of all three parameters, their interaction, the diagnosis of both observed symptoms, concrete settings for BOTH subsystems, and the determinism verdict. Partial credit loses a point per omitted part (e.g. only recommends settings for one subsystem, or skips the interaction, or ignores the determinism question).

Full marks: settings are justified by the mechanism (e.g. 'top_p<1 clips the tail that high temperature inflated', 'extraction needs no sampling so temperature=0 plus constrained decoding'), not asserted as recipes. The determinism caveat is grounded in a real cause (FP non-associativity / batching / hardware). Partial credit for correct settings with thin or hand-wavy justification.

Full marks: well-organised, uses correct terminology (logits, softmax, nucleus, truncation, greedy) precisely, and clearly separates the two subsystems' recommendations. Deduct for muddled structure, vague wording, or terminology used loosely enough to obscure the mechanism.

common_pitfalls: Claiming temperature=0 is fully deterministic and reproducible, ignoring floating-point non-associativity, batch composition, kernel/hardware differences, and MoE routing that can flip a near-tie argmax.
Conflating top-k and top-p, e.g. describing top-p as keeping a fixed number of tokens rather than an adaptive cumulative-probability cutoff, or thinking they are redundant knobs.
Saying temperature truncates or removes low-probability tokens; in fact it only reshapes the distribution, and truncation is the job of top-k/top-p (so top_p=1.0 leaves the whole tail samplable).
Treating higher temperature as simply 'more creative/better' without recognising that a flattened distribution plus an untruncated tail is exactly what samples rare, incoherent tokens.
Recommending the same or a high temperature for the extraction step, or assuming sampling parameters alone can fix malformed JSON instead of using temperature=0 with constrained/structured decoding.
Recommending temperature=1.5 be kept but 'add top_k later' without explaining that bounding the tail (top_p<1 or top_k) is the actual fix for the incoherent-token symptom.

open.question: Your team ships a RAG assistant over ~4,000 internal engineering docs -- a mix of Markdown runbooks and exported Confluence (HTML) pages -- containing nested headings, numbered step-by-step procedures, code blocks, and wide config tables. The v1 pipeline splits every document into fixed 500-character chunks with 50-character overlap using a naive character splitter, embeds them with a 512-token embedding model, and retrieves top-5 by cosine similarity. Users report two recurring failures: (a) answers to 'how do I do X' procedures are incomplete -- a numbered procedure gets split so retrieval returns steps 1-3 but not 4-6; and (b) queries about config values return chunks where the table header row is separated from the row containing the value, so the model can't tell which parameter the number belongs to. Redesign the chunking strategy to fix both failure modes. Explain what you would change and why, name the concrete techniques you'd use, and call out the main trade-off your design introduces and how you'd tune it.
open.answer_format: A short written design explanation, roughly 200-300 words: a diagnosis of why fixed-size character chunking produces both failures, a concrete redesigned chunking approach that names specific techniques, and an explicit statement of the trade-off it introduces plus how you would tune it.
open.reference_answer:
Both failures share one root cause: fixed 500-character chunking splits at arbitrary offsets that ignore the document's structure, so semantic units (a numbered procedure, a table) get cut in half.

Redesign:

1) Replace the naive character splitter with structure-aware splitting. For Markdown/Confluence, first split on the heading hierarchy (e.g. LangChain's MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter / HTMLHeaderTextSplitter), then within a section use a RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter whose separator list prefers paragraph and list-item boundaries. This keeps a whole 'how do I do X' procedure -- steps 1-6 -- inside one chunk, or at least splits only between logical steps, fixing (a).

2) Treat tables as atomic. Detect tables during parsing and emit each table (with its caption/section heading and header row) as a single chunk; if a table is too large, split by row-groups but repeat the header row with each group so a value is never divorced from its column name. This fixes (b).

3) Measure length in tokens, not characters, using the embedding model's tokenizer (e.g. tiktoken), and size chunks comfortably under the 512-token limit so nothing is silently truncated at embed time. Over-sized sections are sub-split on structural boundaries.

4) Attach metadata to every chunk -- source doc, full heading path, chunk type (prose/table/code) -- for provenance and filtering, and add modest overlap or a parent-document / small-to-big retriever so a matched chunk carries surrounding context.

Trade-off: structure-preserving chunks are larger and more variable in size. That dilutes embedding specificity (a big section embeds to an averaged vector, hurting precision) and consumes more generation context budget per retrieved chunk (fewer distinct hits, higher cost/latency). Tune target chunk size and overlap empirically against a labelled retrieval eval set -- tracking recall@k and end-answer correctness -- rather than guessing a single magic number.
expected_answer_points: Diagnoses the root cause: fixed character-length splitting cuts at structure-blind offsets, fragmenting numbered procedures and separating table header rows from their value rows.

Proposes structure-/heading-aware splitting (e.g. MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter or HTMLHeaderTextSplitter, then RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with structural separators) so section/procedure boundaries are respected and whole procedures stay intact -- fixing failure (a).
Handles tables specially -- keep each table as an atomic chunk and/or repeat the header row with each row-group so values stay bound to their column names -- fixing failure (b).
Measures chunk length in tokens (using the embedding model's tokenizer) against the 512-token embedding limit to avoid silent truncation, sub-splitting oversized sections on structural boundaries.

Specifies an empirical tuning loop against a labelled retrieval/answer eval set (e.g. recall@k, answer correctness) instead of hard-coding one chunk size.

Missing any of these dimensions costs points.

open.question:
You are leading the design review for the retrieval layer of a production RAG system. The corpus is 50 million text chunks, each embedded as a 1024-dimensional float32 vector. The service is multi-tenant: every query must be restricted to a single tenant_id and further filtered by a per-document ACL (an allowed_group list), and tenant sizes are heavily skewed — a few tenants own ~20 million chunks each while thousands of others own only a few hundred. The product requirements are: recall@10 of at least 0.95 relative to exact (brute-force) search, p99 query latency under 50 ms, and the whole per-replica index must fit in a fixed RAM budget of roughly 64 GB.

Walk through your design. Justify (a) the approximate-nearest-neighbour (ANN) index and the specific parameters you would tune, (b) how you would meet the memory budget, (c) how you would enforce the tenant + ACL filtering without wrecking recall, and (d) how you would empirically verify you are hitting the recall and latency targets. Be explicit about the trade-offs and the failure modes you are guarding against.
open.answer_format: A structured design walkthrough (roughly 350-550 words) organized around the four asked sub-parts (index + parameters, memory budget, filtering, verification). It should read like a design-review response: name concrete techniques and parameters, justify each against the numeric constraints, and call out the trade-offs and failure modes. Short prose or bullets are both fine.
open.reference_answer:
Memory first, because it constrains everything. Raw vectors are 50M x 1024 x 4 B ≈ 205 GB — more than 3x the 64 GB budget, and that is before any graph overhead. So keeping full-precision vectors in RAM is off the table; quantization or a disk-backed index is mandatory, not optional.

(a) Index. For <50 ms p99 at high recall I'd default to a graph index (HNSW): traversal gives sublinear query cost and strong recall. The knobs: M (graph degree) and ef_construction control build-time graph quality and memory; ef_search is the query-time dial that trades recall for latency. I'd raise ef_search until recall@10 ≥ 0.95, then confirm p99 is still <50 ms. IVF-PQ (nlist/nprobe) is a lower-memory alternative but usually gives worse recall-vs-latency at this scale; DiskANN/Vamana is the fallback if even quantized vectors won't fit in RAM, since it keeps compressed vectors in RAM and full vectors on SSD.

(b) Memory budget. Use quantization plus two-stage retrieval. Scalar int8 quantization is ~4x (≈51 GB) with small recall loss; product quantization (PQ) or binary quantization compress far more but distances become approximate, so recall drops. Recover it with over-fetch + rescore: the compressed index returns a shortlist (e.g. top 100-200), then those candidates are re-scored against full-precision vectors (held on SSD or a rescore store) to produce the final top-10. Binary/PQ shortlist + int8/full rescore is the standard way to hit an aggressive RAM budget while preserving recall.

(c) Filtering — the crux. Naive post-filtering (global ANN top-k, then drop rows failing tenant/ACL) collapses recall for selective filters: a small tenant's few hundred docs may not appear in the global top-k at all, so you return too few or must over-fetch enormously. Pure pre-filtering (exact scan over the filtered subset) is correct and cheap for the thousands of tiny tenants but O(N) and too slow for the 20M-chunk tenants. So: (1) partition by tenant — a tenant-keyed payload index or per-tenant shard/collection — so each query searches only its tenant's vectors and the graph stays connected within the tenant; (2) within a tenant apply the ACL predicate during graph traversal (filtered/filterable HNSW as in Qdrant/Weaviate/pgvector), with an exact fallback when the filtered cardinality is below a threshold. The failure mode to guard against is that filtering during traversal can disconnect the graph — if too many neighbours are filtered out, the walk stalls and recall tanks — which is exactly why making the dominant filter (tenant) a partition rather than a per-node predicate matters, and why the small-cardinality exact fallback exists.

(d) Verification. Build ground truth by running exact brute-force k-NN over a representative query sample (spanning large- and small-tenant queries and restrictive ACLs), compute recall@10 = |approx ∩ exact| / 10 averaged over queries, and sweep ef_search (and over-fetch depth / nprobe) to the smallest value meeting ≥0.95. Then load-test p99 at production concurrency at that setting; if recall and p99 can't hold together, trade memory (lighter quantization, higher M) for headroom. Re-measure after any embedding-model or data change, and monitor p99 plus periodic exact spot-checks in production. Finally, keep the distance metric consistent (cosine / normalized dot) between the ANN index and the rescore step, or the rerank silently reorders wrongly.
expected_answer_points: Notes that raw float32 storage (≈50M x 1024 x 4 B ≈ 205 GB) far exceeds the 64 GB budget, so quantization or a disk-backed index is mandatory rather than optional

Chooses a graph-based ANN index (HNSW) for the latency/recall target and correctly names the knobs: M and ef_construction at build time, ef_search as the query-time recall-vs-latency dial (or justifies IVF-PQ/DiskANN as alternatives with nlist/nprobe)

Specifies a quantization strategy (int8 scalar, PQ, or binary) with its compression-vs-recall trade-off, AND a two-stage over-fetch + full-precision rescore/rerank to recover recall lost to quantization
Explains that post-filtering collapses recall for selective filters (small tenant may be absent from the global top-k) while a pure exact pre-filter scan is too slow for the 20M-chunk tenants
Proposes tenant partitioning (per-tenant shard/collection or tenant payload index) plus filtered-HNSW for the ACL predicate, with an exact fallback below a cardinality threshold
Identifies the filtered-graph connectivity failure mode (filtering during traversal can disconnect the graph and drop recall) as the reason partitioning the dominant filter matters

Gives an empirical validation plan: build exact brute-force ground truth on representative queries, compute recall@10 vs exact, sweep ef_search to the smallest value meeting ≥0.95, then load-test p99 at that setting
Keeps the distance metric / normalization consistent between the ANN index and the rescore step

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly describes HNSW/IVF/DiskANN mechanics and the precise meaning of M, ef_construction, and ef_search (or nlist/nprobe); the quantization families (int8/PQ/binary) and their compression-vs-recall effects; the ~205 GB vs 64 GB memory arithmetic; and pre-filter / post-filter / filtered-traversal semantics. No false claims — e.g. does not say ef_search is a build-time parameter, that raising M lowers memory, that PQ is lossless, or that post-filtering preserves recall for selective filters.

Addresses all four asked sub-parts (index + parameters, memory budget, filtering, verification) and also covers the two-stage rescore step and the filtered-graph connectivity failure mode. Omitting an entire sub-part, the rescore step, or the recall-collapse issue for selective filters loses marks.

Ties each design choice to the specific numeric constraints (205 GB raw vs 64 GB budget, <50 ms p99, ≥0.95 recall, 100-1000x tenant size skew) and articulates the recall/latency/memory trade-offs, rather than merely listing techniques. Explains why partitioning + exact fallback beats a single global strategy given the skew.

Presented as an organized design walkthrough that another engineer in the review could act on: uses vector-search vocabulary precisely, states assumptions, and keeps index/quantization/filtering/verification cleanly separated.

common_pitfalls: Recommends plain in-RAM HNSW over full float32 vectors without noticing that 205 GB blows the 64 GB budget, so the design is infeasible as stated
Treats metadata filtering as trivial post-filtering and misses that a selective tenant/ACL filter makes the global top-k return too few (or zero) valid hits, collapsing recall
Names a heavy quantizer (PQ or binary) but forgets the two-stage full-precision rescore, leaving the stated ≥0.95 recall unattainable
Mislabels HNSW parameters — e.g. claims ef_search is set at build time, that larger M reduces memory, or conflates ef_construction with ef_search
'Verifies' recall by eyeballing answer quality or by treating the ANN index's own output as ground truth, instead of comparing against exact brute-force k-NN
Applies one global strategy (always exact scan, or one shared graph for all tenants) that ignores the 100-1000x tenant size skew and fails at one end of the distribution

open.question: You are reviewing an enterprise RAG assistant that answers questions over a corpus mixing fully public documents and access-controlled ones (per-user and per-group ACLs), embedded and stored in Qdrant with one point per chunk. A junior engineer implemented permission enforcement like this: run the normal cosine-similarity search for the top k=10 nearest chunks, then in application code drop any returned chunk whose ACL does not include the requesting user, and pass whatever survives to the LLM. In the design review, explain why this retrieve-then-drop (post-filtering) approach is wrong on BOTH correctness and security grounds, and describe how you would re-architect permission-aware retrieval. Concretely address: (a) how ACLs should be modeled in the vector store and pushed into the query; (b) the recall/performance implications of filtering an ANN index and how a system like Qdrant mitigates them; (c) how you keep permissions consistent when a user's group membership changes; and (d) one residual leakage channel that remains even after filtering is correct, and how you would close it.
open.answer_format: A structured design critique of roughly 350-550 words that (1) diagnoses the post-filtering flaw on correctness and security grounds, then (2) walks through the four required dimensions (a)-(d) with concrete Qdrant/RAG mechanisms and at least one explicit trade-off. Prose or headed bullets are both fine; a filter-predicate sketch is a plus but not required.
open.reference_answer:
Diagnosis. Retrieve-then-drop is broken on two axes. Correctness: the ANN search is scored over ALL vectors, so the top-10 window is chosen without regard to permissions. For a restricted user, highly relevant chunks they ARE allowed to see may sit at rank 50 or 5000, while the top-10 fills up with public/other-tenant chunks that then get dropped in app code. The user is left with a silently truncated set (often far fewer than 10) and degraded or empty answers, and there is no fixed over-fetch factor that fixes this because an authorized chunk can be arbitrarily deep. Security: any unauthorized content that is fetched is now inside the process and one bug away from reaching the LLM, the citations, or logs; and observable side channels (how many results were filtered, latency, 'no answer') leak the existence of restricted material. Access control must be a retrieval-layer invariant, not something the LLM is asked to respect via prompt.

(a) Model and push ACLs. Store authorization on each chunk's payload: tenant_id, visibility ('public'/'restricted'), allowed_group_ids (a list), and optionally allowed_user_ids. Create payload indexes on these fields. At query time, resolve the caller's identity into their set of group ids from the IdP/SCIM directory, then push a hard filter INTO the Qdrant search (a pre-filter), e.g. must: tenant_id == T; should: visibility == 'public' OR allowed_group_ids MATCH ANY user_groups OR allowed_user_ids contains user_id. Now ANN scoring only ranks candidates the user may see, so the top-k is both correct and complete.

(b) Filtered-ANN recall. Filtering an HNSW graph is not free: the graph is built over all vectors, so aggressively filtering during traversal can strand the search in a region with few passing neighbours and hurt recall. Qdrant mitigates this with payload-indexed 'filterable HNSW' plus a full_scan_threshold: when the filtered subset is small it falls back to an exact brute-force scan over just those points (guaranteed correct); above the threshold it uses the graph with the filter applied. That is why the filter fields must be indexed and why you tune the threshold rather than assuming a metadata filter is exact and cost-free.

(c) Consistency on membership change. Do NOT denormalize full user lists into every chunk, or a single group change forces rewriting millions of payloads (write amplification) and risks stale grants. Store slowly-changing group_ids on the documents/chunks, and resolve user->groups at query time from the authoritative directory. A revocation then takes effect on the next query with no re-indexing; keep any user->groups cache on a short TTL. When a document's OWN ACL changes, that is a cheap payload update (set_payload) with no re-embedding.

(d) Residual channel. Even with correct filtering, a response/retrieval cache keyed only on the query text will serve one principal's authorized answer to a different, less-privileged principal. Close it by keying caches on (principal or permission-set + query), and add defense-in-depth: re-check the ACL of every chunk at citation/generation time in case cached payloads are stale, and never expose filtered-result counts. (The membership-cache TTL is itself a bounded staleness window after revocation.)
expected_answer_points: Diagnoses the correctness failure of post-filtering: because ANN scores over all vectors, the top-k window is chosen before permissions apply, so authorized-but-lower-ranked chunks are never retrieved and the result set silently shrinks below k, with no fixed over-fetch factor able to guarantee completeness.

Diagnoses the security failure: fetching unauthorized content into the process risks leakage to the LLM/citations/logs and via side channels (filtered counts, latency), and stresses that enforcement must live at the retrieval layer, not be delegated to the LLM through prompt instructions.

Prescribes modeling ACLs in the payload (tenant_id, visibility, allowed_group_ids/allowed_user_ids) with payload indexes, and pushing a hard permission predicate into the vector search as a pre-filter (must tenant + should public/group-intersection/user-match) so ANN only ranks authorized candidates.

Explains that pre-filtering an HNSW index can degrade recall and that Qdrant mitigates it via payload-indexed filterable HNSW plus a full_scan_threshold that falls back to exact search on small filtered subsets — i.e. filters are not free and require indexing/tuning.

Handles membership-change consistency by storing slowly-changing group ids on documents and resolving user->groups at query time (so revocations apply immediately without re-indexing), instead of denormalizing user lists into every chunk (write amplification / stale grants); notes ACL edits are a cheap set_payload with no re-embedding, and bounds any membership cache with a short TTL.

Identifies a concrete residual leakage channel after correct filtering (e.g. a cache keyed only on query text serving one principal's results to another, or the revocation staleness window) and gives a specific mitigation (key caches by principal/permission-set, defense-in-depth ACL re-check at citation/generation time).

Surfaces at least one explicit trade-off, e.g. denormalized user lists (fast queries, painful revocation) vs query-time group resolution (immediate revocation, extra query-time lookup), or filter selectivity vs recall/latency.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: every technical claim is correct — post-filtering truncates results and cannot be fixed by a fixed over-fetch; the pre-filter predicate (tenant/public/group/user with must/should) is well-formed; the filtered-HNSW recall problem and Qdrant's payload-index + full_scan_threshold mitigation are stated accurately; and the query-time group-resolution vs denormalization mechanics (set_payload, no re-embedding on ACL edits) are right. Deduct for invented mechanisms, claiming metadata filters are always exact/free, or asserting membership changes require re-embedding.

Full marks: covers the core diagnosis (correctness AND security) plus all four required dimensions (a) ACL modeling + pushed pre-filter, (b) filtered-ANN recall/perf mitigation, (c) membership-change consistency, and (d) a residual channel with mitigation. Deduct proportionally for each dimension omitted or left superficial.

Full marks: justifies WHY pre-filtering beats post-filtering (ANN ranks the whole space) rather than merely asserting it, and weighs at least one real trade-off (denormalized ACLs vs query-time resolution, or filter selectivity vs recall/latency) with the consequences of each choice. Partial credit for correct choices stated without mechanism-level justification.

Full marks: a well-organized review that separates the diagnosis from the redesign, uses correct vocabulary (pre- vs post-filter, payload/ACL, HNSW recall, tenant isolation) precisely, and is unambiguous about which layer enforces the invariant. Deduct for disorganized, vague, or jargon-name-dropping answers.

common_pitfalls: Proposes 'just over-fetch a much larger k, then filter' as the fix without recognizing it is unbounded — an authorized chunk can sit arbitrarily deep, so no fixed multiplier guarantees a complete result set; only pushing the predicate into the search does.

Treats access control as a prompt problem, e.g. instructing the LLM to 'only use documents the user is allowed to see' or to ignore restricted content, instead of enforcing it as a hard retrieval-layer filter.

Denormalizes full allowed-user lists into every chunk payload and misses the write-amplification / stale-grant fallout when membership changes, or wrongly claims a group change requires re-embedding the affected chunks.

Ignores the filtered-ANN recall interaction entirely — assumes a metadata filter is exact and cost-free, unaware that HNSW traversal over a filtered subset needs payload indexes and a full-scan fallback to stay correct.
Conflates relevance metadata filtering (date, source, language as soft ranking signals) with security filtering, applying ACLs as a re-ranking boost rather than a mandatory must-pass predicate.

Stops at 'add a filter' and never addresses residual channels — shared query-keyed caches, source/citation display, or count/latency side channels — so a technically correct filter still leaks across principals.

open.question: Your team runs a RAG assistant over a 400k-chunk product-docs corpus in Qdrant. Retrieval uses a bi-encoder (dense embeddings): for each query you pull the top-5 chunks by cosine similarity and hand them straight to the LLM. Answer quality is mediocre — when you inspect failures, the passage that actually answers the question is usually *in the corpus and semantically related*, but it lands around rank 15-30, so it never reaches the LLM's top-5 context. A colleague proposes inserting a cross-encoder reranker (e.g. a `ms-marco` / BGE cross-encoder, or Cohere Rerank) into the pipeline. Explain (a) why a cross-encoder can order these candidates more accurately than the bi-encoder alone, in terms of how each model actually computes relevance; (b) how you would restructure the pipeline to use it, being concrete about candidate counts; and (c) the main latency/cost trade-off it introduces and how you would tune it. Note one thing reranking will NOT fix.
open.answer_format: A structured written explanation, roughly 200-320 words, covering three parts: (a) the bi-encoder vs cross-encoder mechanism, (b) a concrete two-stage retrieve-then-rerank design with candidate counts, and (c) the latency/cost trade-off with a tuning recommendation, plus the stated limitation. A rough numeric example for N and k strengthens the answer but prose is fine.
open.reference_answer:
(a) Mechanism. The bi-encoder embeds the query and each document independently into fixed vectors; relevance is just a cosine/dot-product between two precomputed points. Because the query and the document never see each other during encoding, fine-grained term interactions (which entity the question is really about, negation, qualifiers) are collapsed into a single vector and often lost — which is exactly why the right passage lands at rank 15-30 instead of the top 5. A cross-encoder instead takes the (query, document) pair *jointly* as one input and runs full self-attention across both, emitting a single relevance score. Because every query token can attend to every document token, it captures the interaction the bi-encoder averages away, so its ordering of the same candidates is far more accurate.

(b) Pipeline. Make it two-stage. Keep the cheap bi-encoder as a first-stage recall net, but widen the fan-out: retrieve top-N candidates (e.g. N=50-100) from Qdrant instead of 5. Feed all N (query, chunk) pairs through the cross-encoder, sort by its score, and pass only the top k=5 to the LLM. LangChain expresses this as a ContextualCompression/rerank step wrapping the base retriever. Now a chunk the bi-encoder ranked 20th can be re-scored into the final top-5.

(c) Trade-off. A cross-encoder cannot precompute or ANN-index document embeddings — it must run one forward pass per (query, chunk) pair at query time, so latency and cost scale linearly with N. Larger N raises recall (more chance the answer is in the pool) but adds reranker calls and latency. Tune N to the latency budget; mitigate with batching, a smaller/distilled reranker, or a hosted rerank API.

Limitation: reranking only reorders the N candidates the first stage returned — it can never surface a passage that retrieval missed. If the answer isn't in the top-N, no reranker recovers it, so N (and chunking/embedding recall) still sets the ceiling.
expected_answer_points: Bi-encoder embeds query and document independently into vectors and scores by cosine/dot-product over precomputed embeddings, so query and document tokens never interact — fine-grained relevance is lost.

Cross-encoder feeds the (query, document) pair jointly through the model with full cross-attention and emits a single relevance score, capturing interactions the bi-encoder cannot, hence more accurate ordering of the same candidates.

Restructure into two stages: use the cheap bi-encoder to retrieve a wider candidate set of N (e.g. 50-100) rather than 5, rerank those N with the cross-encoder, then pass the top k (e.g. 5) to the LLM.
This surfaces the rank-15-30 passage into the final top-5 because the reranker re-scores a larger pool — directly addressing the observed failure.

The cross-encoder cannot precompute or ANN-index document embeddings; it runs one forward pass per (query, doc) pair at query time, so latency and cost scale with N (and it is therefore a second stage, not a whole-corpus first stage).
Tune N to trade recall against the latency budget, and mitigate cost with batching, a distilled/smaller reranker, or a hosted rerank service.
State the limitation: reranking only reorders the retrieved candidates and cannot recover a passage that first-stage retrieval never returned — N and retrieval recall set the ceiling.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly contrasts independent bi-encoder embedding + vector similarity against a cross-encoder that jointly encodes the pair with cross-attention to produce a score; correctly states the cross-encoder cannot be precomputed/indexed and runs per-pair at query time; the proposed N/k values and two-stage flow are technically sound. Deduct for any incorrect claim (e.g. reranker embeddings stored in Qdrant, reranking boosting recall, cross-encoder run over the whole corpus).

Full marks: addresses all three requested parts (mechanism, concrete pipeline with candidate counts, latency/cost trade-off with tuning) AND names the limitation that reranking cannot recover missed passages. Deduct for each part omitted, for skipping concrete N/k numbers, or for not stating the limitation.

Full marks: explicitly ties the mechanism to the observed symptom (right passage at rank 15-30) and justifies widening N as the fix, and reasons about the recall-vs-latency tension when choosing N rather than asserting a number. Partial credit for correct but shallow justification that states choices without connecting them to the scenario or the trade-off.

Full marks: clear, well-structured answer using correct vocabulary (bi-encoder, cross-encoder, cross-attention, candidate set/N, top-k, two-stage) that a reviewer can follow without rereading. Deduct for vague, disorganised, or jargon-dropping prose that never explains the mechanism.

common_pitfalls: Claims the cross-encoder produces document embeddings that can be stored/indexed in Qdrant like the bi-encoder's — missing that it scores (query, doc) pairs at query time and cannot be precomputed.
Says reranking will improve recall or surface documents that were never retrieved, confusing reranking (reorders an existing candidate set) with retrieval (bounded by N).
Proposes running the cross-encoder over the whole 400k-chunk corpus, ignoring that it is O(N) forward passes and only viable as a second stage over a small candidate pool.
Describes the cross-encoder as merely 'a bigger/better model' without explaining the joint cross-attention over the pair as the reason it ranks better.
Forgets to widen the first-stage fan-out (still retrieves only 5), so the reranker has nothing new to promote and the fix does nothing.
Ignores the latency/cost consequence of N entirely, or confuses reranking with query rewriting / multi-query fusion.

open.question: You maintain a RAG-based support assistant that answers user questions from a set of retrieved help-center passages. In a design review, a colleague worries the model sometimes states things that sound right but aren't actually in the passages it was given. They ask you to (a) define what 'groundedness' (a.k.a. faithfulness) means for this system, distinguishing it from answer correctness, and (b) describe a concrete, repeatable way to evaluate groundedness over a batch of (question, retrieved-context, generated-answer) triples. Also name one failure mode a naive version of your evaluation could miss.
open.answer_format: A short written explanation, ~150-250 words: a definition (with the contrast to correctness), a step-by-step evaluation method, and one named failure mode. Prose or a numbered list is fine.
open.reference_answer:
Groundedness (faithfulness) means every factual claim in the generated answer is supported by — entailed by — the retrieved context actually passed to the model, not by the model's parametric/world knowledge. It is distinct from correctness and relevance: an answer can be perfectly grounded yet wrong if the retrieved passage is wrong, and an ungrounded answer can be coincidentally correct. Groundedness asks only 'is this backed by the provided context?'

A concrete, repeatable method:
1. For each (question, context, answer) triple, decompose the answer into atomic claims (one verifiable statement each).
2. For each claim, run an entailment check against the context — either an NLI model (entailment / neutral / contradiction) or an LLM-as-judge prompted to decide 'supported / not supported by ONLY this context.'
3. Score = supported claims / total claims; average across the batch and surface the specific unsupported or contradicted claims for inspection.
This is essentially the RAGAS faithfulness metric. Validate the automated judge against a small human-labeled sample before trusting the aggregate.

One failure a naive version misses: checking claims against chunks in isolation can mark a claim 'unsupported' when it is only entailed by two chunks combined; conversely, an LLM judge that leans on its own world knowledge will mark fabricated-but-plausible claims as supported — so the judge must be constrained strictly to the provided context.
expected_answer_points: Defines groundedness/faithfulness as: every factual claim in the answer must be supported/entailed by the retrieved context that was passed to the model, not by the model's own parametric/world knowledge.

Distinguishes groundedness from answer correctness/relevance — a grounded answer can still be wrong (if context is wrong), and an ungrounded answer can be coincidentally correct; groundedness only concerns support by the given context.
Method step: decompose the generated answer into atomic, individually verifiable claims rather than judging the whole answer as one yes/no.
Method step: check each claim for entailment against the retrieved context using an NLI model or an LLM-as-judge constrained to the provided context (supported / not supported / contradicted).
Method step: aggregate into a score (fraction of claims supported), average over the batch, and surface the specific unsupported/contradicted claims for review.
Names concrete tooling/framing (e.g., RAGAS faithfulness metric, LLM-as-judge, NLI entailment) and notes the automated judge should be validated against a human-labeled sample.

Names a real failure mode a naive version misses (e.g., claims entailed only by combining multiple chunks judged in isolation; an LLM judge using its own world knowledge to 'support' claims absent from context; or lexical-overlap being mistaken for support).

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly defines groundedness as claim-level support/entailment by the retrieved context (not world knowledge), correctly separates it from correctness/relevance, and describes a technically sound decompose-then-check-entailment method with real tooling. Deduct for conflating groundedness with retrieval quality or answer accuracy, or for asserting incorrect mechanisms.

Full marks: covers the definition, the contrast with correctness/relevance, a concrete step-by-step evaluation (decompose -> per-claim entailment check -> aggregate), some tooling reference, and at least one named failure mode. Deduct proportionally for each missing element.

Full marks: justifies why per-claim entailment against the given context actually measures support (not mere plausibility or lexical overlap) and explains why the named failure mode defeats a naive approach. Partial credit for asserting the method without explaining why it works.

Full marks: clear, well-structured answer using correct vocabulary (faithfulness, entailment, claim decomposition) and concise within the length budget. Deduct for disorganized, vague, or jargon-misusing prose.

common_pitfalls: Conflates groundedness with answer correctness — proposes checking the answer against a gold answer or the open web instead of against the provided retrieved context.
Measures retrieval quality (did we fetch the right documents) rather than generation faithfulness (does the answer stay within what was fetched).
Relies solely on lexical/embedding overlap (ROUGE/BLEU/cosine between answer and context) and treats high overlap as proof of grounding, missing paraphrased hallucinations and unsupported inferences.
Evaluates the whole answer as a single supported/unsupported verdict instead of decomposing into atomic claims, so a mostly-correct answer containing one fabricated fact scores as fully grounded.
Uses an LLM judge but never constrains it to judge strictly from the given context, letting it 'support' claims from its own world knowledge.
Treats the automated groundedness score as ground truth without validating the NLI model or LLM judge against any human-labeled sample.

open.question:
Your team runs a production RAG system over an internal knowledge base (~200k chunks in a vector store); the generator is fed the top-5 retrieved chunks. To choose a retriever, an engineer built an evaluation set by prompting an LLM to generate one question from each of 500 randomly sampled chunks, and treats each question's source chunk as its single relevant document. Retrievers are scored by Recall@20 on this set. Retriever B (hybrid BM25 + dense, with a cross-encoder reranker) beats Retriever A (dense bi-encoder only) at Recall@20 — 0.94 vs 0.88 — so the team ships B. In production, answer quality (user thumbs-up rate) drops relative to A.

In the design review you are asked to (a) explain what is wrong or incomplete about this evaluation methodology, and (b) propose a more rigorous retrieval-evaluation design that would have caught this regression before rollout. Be specific about the labeled set, the metrics and cutoffs, and how retrieval-level evaluation should connect to end-to-end answer quality.
open.answer_format: A structured written critique plus a concrete evaluation design, roughly 250-400 words, ideally split into (a) flaws in the current methodology and (b) the proposed design. Name specific metrics, cutoffs, label-construction methods, and tooling, and give the mechanism by which each flaw could hide the regression.
open.reference_answer:
(a) Flaws. The ground truth is the core problem: labeling only the generating chunk as relevant produces incomplete, single-positive qrels. Other chunks that genuinely answer the question are silently treated as non-relevant, so a retriever that surfaces those is wrongly scored as missing — the labels are noisy in a way that penalizes good retrieval and distorts the difference between systems. Second, the metric and cutoff are mismatched to production: Recall@20 is order-insensitive and measured at k=20, but the generator only sees top-5. B could win at 20 yet lose at 5 (a reranker tuned to pull relevant docs into the top-20 pool tells you nothing about the top-5 ordering the LLM actually consumes). Third, the query distribution is synthetic and single-hop — one question per chunk, answerable from that chunk — so it under-represents real traffic: multi-hop, aggregation, ambiguous, and no-answer queries, and it omits hard negatives. Fourth, recall alone cannot explain a downstream regression: retrieval metrics measure only the retriever's ceiling. B likely raises recall while lowering context precision at k=5, feeding more topically-similar distractors; the generator then degrades via context dilution / 'lost in the middle'. Finally, 0.94 vs 0.88 on 500 items was treated as decisive with no significance test.

(b) Proposed design. Build qrels by pooling candidates from both systems (and BM25) and judging the union with graded relevance (0-3), using human raters or a calibrated LLM-as-judge with measured inter-annotator agreement, so relevant-but-unlabeled docs are captured. Draw queries from real production logs, stratified to include multi-hop and unanswerable cases. Report rank-aware metrics at the production cutoff — nDCG@5, MRR, MAP, and context precision@5 — alongside Recall@5 and Recall@20, using standard tooling (pytrec_eval / BEIR-style qrels). Do paired, per-query comparison with a significance test and confidence intervals. Crucially, run end-to-end evaluation with the generator held constant — faithfulness and answer correctness/relevance (e.g. RAGAS or an LLM judge) plus context precision — to connect retrieval changes to answer quality, and confirm with an online A/B (or interleaving) before full rollout, since offline gains must be shown to transfer.
expected_answer_points: Identifies that single-positive labels (only the generating chunk marked relevant) create incomplete/noisy qrels, so genuinely relevant-but-unlabeled chunks are counted as misses, biasing the comparison; fix with pooling plus graded human/LLM relevance judgments over the union of candidates

Notes the cutoff mismatch: Recall@20 is evaluated at the wrong k when production feeds top-5, and recall is order-insensitive; evaluate at the production k and use rank-aware metrics (nDCG@5, MRR, MAP) because ordering and truncation matter

Explains that LLM-generated one-question-per-chunk queries are single-hop and out-of-distribution vs real traffic (missing multi-hop, aggregation, ambiguous, no-answer queries and hard negatives); use real query logs, stratified

Distinguishes retrieval-level metrics (a ceiling) from end-to-end answer quality, and measures generation with the retriever varied and generator fixed (faithfulness, answer correctness/relevance) to explain the regression

Gives a concrete mechanism for why higher Recall@20 coincides with worse answers: lower context precision at k=5, more distractor chunks, context dilution / 'lost in the middle', or B winning @20 but losing @5
Adds statistical rigor: adequately sized, representative set with paired per-query comparison, significance testing and confidence intervals rather than shipping on a raw 0.94 vs 0.88 gap
Recommends validating offline results online (A/B test or interleaving) before full rollout, and/or names standard tooling (pytrec_eval, BEIR, RAGAS)

rubric_criteria.descriptor: All claims are correct: recall is order-insensitive while nDCG/MRR/MAP are rank-aware; incomplete single-positive qrels bias metrics; the k=20 vs top-5 cutoff mismatch is real; higher recall can coexist with lower context precision and worse generation via distractors / lost-in-the-middle; retrieval metrics bound but do not equal end-to-end quality. No fabricated metric behavior, no claim that higher Recall@k must improve RAG, and any named tools (pytrec_eval, BEIR, RAGAS) are described accurately.

Covers both parts: critiques the label construction, the metric/cutoff choice, and the synthetic query distribution, AND proposes a design spanning pooled graded judgments, production-representative queries, rank-aware metrics at the production k, end-to-end evaluation with the generator fixed, and significance testing / online validation. Full marks require addressing the label/ground-truth flaw and the retrieval-to-answer-quality link, not just listing extra metrics.

Explains the mechanism behind each recommendation — why incomplete labels mislead, why the cutoff mismatch hides the problem, and specifically how B can win Recall@20 yet regress downstream (precision at k=5, distractors, context dilution). Credit is for causal reasoning that ties the methodology flaws to the observed thumbs-up drop, not assertions.

Organized as a critique plus a design, uses retrieval-evaluation vocabulary precisely (qrels, pooling, graded relevance, Recall@k, nDCG@k, MRR, context precision, LLM-as-judge), and is concise and unambiguous for a design-review audience.

common_pitfalls: Only proposing additional metrics (nDCG, MRR, MAP) while never questioning the single-positive ground truth — missing the deepest flaw, that unlabeled-but-relevant chunks are scored as misses
Assuming higher Recall@k must mean better RAG, so being unable to explain how B improves recall yet regresses answer quality (distractors, lower precision@5, lost-in-the-middle)

Conflating retrieval evaluation with end-to-end RAG evaluation — proposing only faithfulness/answer metrics and dropping retrieval-level diagnostics, or vice versa, instead of connecting the two with the generator held constant
Trusting LLM-generated one-question-per-chunk queries as representative of production traffic, ignoring single-hop bias and distribution shift from real user queries
Leaving the evaluation at k=20 when production feeds top-5, or ignoring the cutoff choice and the order-insensitivity of recall entirely
Treating 0.94 vs 0.88 on 500 items as decisive with no significance test, sample-size/representativeness check, or online A/B validation before rollout

open.question: You maintain a RAG assistant over an enterprise knowledge base (SEC filings, internal wikis, HR pages) backed by an embedding model and a Qdrant vector store. The current pipeline embeds the user's question, retrieves the top-k = 8 chunks by cosine similarity, and stuffs them into the LLM context. It handles single-fact lookups well but consistently fails on questions like: 'What is the parental-leave policy of the company that acquired our logistics vendor Rivera Freight in 2023?' The model either hallucinates or says it cannot find the answer, even though the corpus contains (a) a news chunk stating 'Rivera Freight was acquired by Datalink Corp in 2023' and (b) a separate HR chunk describing Datalink Corp's parental-leave policy (which never mentions Rivera Freight). Explain precisely why single-shot top-k retrieval fails here, then design a multi-hop retrieval pipeline that reliably answers such questions. Address how you decompose or iterate, how you decide when to stop hopping, the main failure mode your design introduces and how you'd mitigate it, and how you'd evaluate the result.
open.answer_format: A written design explanation, roughly 200-350 words (prose or a structured list is fine), covering: (1) the failure diagnosis, (2) the multi-hop retrieval design with a concrete two-hop trace on the given example, (3) the stopping rule, (4) the main failure mode plus a mitigation, and (5) how you'd evaluate it.
open.reference_answer:
Why single-shot retrieval fails. The question is answerable only by chaining two facts: (a) Rivera Freight was acquired by Datalink Corp, and (b) Datalink Corp's parental-leave policy. The bridge entity 'Datalink Corp' never appears in the user's question, so when we embed the whole question the HR-policy chunk — which is about Datalink and leave, not Rivera — has low cosine similarity to the query vector and falls outside top-k. Dense retrieval ranks chunks by surface/semantic similarity to the entire query in a single pass; it has no mechanism to first discover the acquirer and then look up that entity. No single chunk contains the full answer, and the completing chunk isn't retrievable until the intermediate fact is resolved. Raising k or swapping the embedding model doesn't fix this — the policy chunk simply isn't 'about' the query until the bridge entity is known.

Multi-hop design. Replace one-shot retrieval with an iterative retrieve-and-reason loop (self-ask / IRCoT / ReAct style) or explicit query decomposition. Hop 1: retrieve on the first answerable sub-question 'Who acquired Rivera Freight in 2023?' -> get the news chunk -> extract the bridge entity 'Datalink Corp'. Hop 2: the LLM reformulates the next query using that resolved entity — 'What is Datalink Corp's parental-leave policy?' -> retrieve the HR chunk. Then synthesize the final answer over the accumulated evidence with citations. The crux is conditioning each new retrieval query on entities discovered in prior hops.

Stopping. Stop when the LLM judges it has sufficient evidence and emits a final answer instead of another sub-question; enforce a hard hop budget (~3-4) and halt if a hop returns no new documents or repeats a query, to bound latency/cost and prevent loops.

Main failure mode + mitigation. Iteration introduces error propagation: a wrong or ambiguous hop-1 entity poisons every downstream hop, and each hop multiplies LLM + retrieval latency and token cost. Mitigate by retrieving several candidates (or keeping a small beam) per hop, grounding/verifying the bridge entity against the retrieved text before reusing it, allowing backtracking, caching sub-question results, and capping hops.

Evaluation. Don't score only final-answer EM/F1. Measure supporting-passage recall across all required hops (did we retrieve BOTH the acquisition chunk and the policy chunk?) and per-hop retrieval accuracy to localise failures; validate on multi-hop QA benchmarks such as HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, or MuSiQue. As an alternative worth noting, a knowledge-graph / Graph-RAG approach that models 'Rivera Freight —acquired_by-> Datalink Corp' as an explicit edge and traverses it sidesteps the semantic gap entirely and is preferable if such relational hops are common.
expected_answer_points: Explains why single-shot top-k fails: the bridge entity ('Datalink Corp') is absent from the query, so the policy chunk has low similarity to the full question and is excluded from top-k; dense retrieval matches surface/semantic similarity to the whole query in one pass and no single chunk contains the full answer.
Notes that this is not fixable by simply increasing k or changing the embedding model, because the completing chunk isn't retrievable until the intermediate fact is resolved.
Proposes an iterative / query-decomposition multi-hop pipeline (ordered sub-questions, or an interleaved retrieve-then-reason loop such as self-ask / IRCoT / ReAct).

Carries the resolved bridge entity forward: hop 1 finds the acquirer, hop 2 reformulates the query using that entity to retrieve the policy chunk, then synthesizes over accumulated evidence — ideally with a concrete two-hop trace.
Defines a stopping criterion and hop budget (LLM emits a final answer when evidence suffices, cap of ~3-4 hops, or halt on no-new-info) to bound latency and avoid loops.

Identifies the introduced failure mode as cascading error propagation (a wrong hop-1 entity corrupts downstream hops) plus multiplied latency and token cost, and gives a concrete mitigation (multiple candidates/beam per hop, verify/ground the bridge entity, backtracking, caching, hard cap).

Specifies multi-hop-appropriate evaluation: supporting-passage recall across ALL required hops (not just final-answer EM/F1) and/or multi-hop QA benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue), plus per-hop retrieval accuracy.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly diagnoses the embedding/semantic reason the second chunk is missed (bridge entity absent from the query -> low similarity -> outside top-k) and proposes a technically sound iterative or decomposition mechanism with correct entity carry-forward and a valid stopping rule. No incorrect claims (e.g., that raising k, lowering temperature, or better prompting alone would recover the missing chunk).

Covers the full arc: failure diagnosis, iterative retrieval design with entity carry-forward, stopping criterion, the introduced failure mode plus a mitigation, and multi-hop-aware evaluation. Loses points for omitting the stopping rule, the error-propagation discussion, or the evaluation angle.

Justifies each choice by mechanism — why decomposition closes the bridge-entity gap, why the next query must be conditioned on the discovered entity, why a hop budget is needed, and why iteration causes error propagation — rather than asserting a recipe without cause.

Clear, well-structured, uses correct vocabulary (bridge entity, sub-question, hop, supporting passages, beam) and ideally walks the two-hop trace on the Rivera Freight / Datalink Corp example so the design is unambiguous.

common_pitfalls: Claims that simply increasing top-k (e.g., k = 50) or swapping to a better embedding model fixes it, ignoring that the policy chunk has no semantic overlap with the full query until the bridge entity is resolved.
Proposes only better prompting ('tell the model to reason step by step') without adding a second retrieval round — the missing chunk is never in context, so no prompt can recover it.
Describes decomposition but treats sub-questions as independent parallel retrievals and never feeds the discovered bridge entity into the next query, so hop 2 still can't find the policy chunk.
Omits any stopping criterion or hop budget, leaving the loop with unbounded latency/cost or a risk of infinite hopping.
Assumes hop 1 is always correct — ignores error propagation and provides no candidate diversity, entity verification, or backtracking.
Evaluates only final-answer exact match and never checks supporting-passage recall, so silent retrieval failures on individual hops go undetected.

open.question: You are the reviewer on a design proposal for a production service backed by a hosted LLM API. The service has two very different code paths. Path A classifies and extracts structured JSON from ~2 million support tickets per day (fixed schema: category, priority, entities) and is on a tight per-request latency and cost budget. Path B is a low-volume (a few hundred calls/day) 'root-cause' agent that reads failing CI pipeline logs, forms hypotheses, and proposes a fix; correctness matters far more than speed. An engineer proposes standardizing BOTH paths on a single reasoning model (e.g. an o-series / DeepSeek-R1 / extended-thinking-style model), arguing 'reasoning models are strictly better, so this simplifies our stack.' Evaluate this proposal. Explain what a reasoning model actually does differently from a standard instruction-tuned model at the mechanism level, then recommend a concrete model strategy for Path A and Path B with justification, including the trade-offs the engineer is ignoring.
open.answer_format: A structured written analysis, ~250-400 words. Start with the mechanism (how reasoning models differ), then give a per-path recommendation (A and B) each with explicit justification and the trade-offs being ignored. Reject or heavily qualify the 'strictly better' framing rather than endorsing it.
open.reference_answer:
The 'strictly better' framing is wrong; reasoning models are a different test-time-compute regime, not a uniformly stronger model, and picking one per workload is the right call.

Mechanism: a reasoning model is post-trained (typically with reinforcement learning, often on verifiable rewards) to emit a long internal chain-of-thought before its final answer, deliberately spending extra test-time compute to plan, self-check, and backtrack. Accuracy scales with how much 'thinking' it does, and most APIs expose a knob for this (reasoning effort low/medium/high, or an explicit thinking-token budget). Crucially those reasoning tokens are generated and billed as output even though the raw trace is usually hidden or summarized, and they add latency and consume the token/context budget.

Those gains are real on hard, multi-step, ambiguous problems and negligible on simple, well-specified ones. So a blanket standardization trades away the strengths of each family.

Path A (2M tickets/day, fixed schema, latency- and cost-bound) should use a fast instruction-tuned (non-reasoning) model, ideally a small one, with structured outputs / constrained decoding to guarantee the schema. The task is format-bound pattern extraction, not multi-step reasoning, so a reasoning model adds latency, per-call cost (hidden reasoning tokens), and rate-limit/throughput pressure while 'overthinking' trivial inputs, with little or no accuracy gain. At 2M/day the cost and latency penalty is enormous.

Path B (low volume, genuinely multi-step debugging, latency-tolerant, correctness-critical) is the textbook case FOR a reasoning model: let it hypothesize and self-correct over logs, tune reasoning effort up, and accept the latency. Volume is low so cost is bounded.

Trade-offs the engineer ignores: billed hidden reasoning tokens, higher TTFT/total latency, overthinking on easy inputs, and prompt differences (reasoning models want simpler prompts, not elaborate few-shot CoT, which is redundant and can hurt). Also verify feature support (structured outputs, tool calling, sampling params) per model. Finally, don't decide by assertion: run an offline eval on representative data comparing accuracy vs latency and cost per path before committing.
expected_answer_points: Explains the mechanism: a reasoning model is trained (typically via RL / RL-on-verifiable-rewards) to spend test-time compute on an internal chain-of-thought before answering, and this 'thinking' is usually tunable via a reasoning-effort or thinking-token budget
Rejects 'strictly better': the accuracy benefit applies to hard multi-step/ambiguous problems and is negligible on simple, well-specified tasks

Names the concrete costs of reasoning: hidden reasoning/thinking tokens are still billed as output, higher latency (TTFT and total), and greater throughput/rate-limit pressure — which is disqualifying for a 2M/day latency- and cost-bound path

Path A recommendation: a fast instruction-tuned (non-reasoning), likely small model with structured outputs / constrained decoding to enforce the schema, because it is format-bound extraction where reasoning adds cost/latency without accuracy gain
Path B recommendation: use a reasoning model (or extended thinking), tuning reasoning effort up, because it is low-volume, genuinely multi-step, latency-tolerant, and correctness-critical

Notes at least one reasoning-model caveat: overthinking trivial inputs, prompting differences (avoid elaborate few-shot CoT), or verifying feature support (structured output/tool calling/sampling params)
Recommends deciding empirically — run an eval comparing accuracy vs latency/cost on representative data per path rather than standardizing by assertion

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly describes the reasoning-model mechanism (test-time compute / trained chain-of-thought, tunable reasoning effort, billed hidden reasoning tokens) and makes technically sound, workload-appropriate model choices; no false claims such as reasoning = temperature/sampling change, reasoning tokens being free, or reasoning models being universally more accurate.

Full marks: addresses both paths distinctly with a concrete recommendation for each, covers the mechanism, the latency/cost/throughput trade-offs, and at least one reasoning-model caveat plus the recommendation to evaluate empirically. Loses marks for a single blanket answer or omitting Path A or Path B analysis.

Full marks: explicitly ties each recommendation to workload properties (volume, latency/cost budget, task complexity) and explains WHY a reasoning model helps Path B but hurts Path A, rather than asserting choices without cause.

Full marks: organized as mechanism then per-path recommendation, uses correct vocabulary (test-time compute, reasoning effort/thinking budget, structured/constrained decoding, instruction-tuned), and reads as a crisp design-review verdict.

Endorses standardizing on the reasoning model for both paths, ignoring that Path A's 2M/day latency and cost budget makes per-call reasoning tokens and added latency disqualifying
Forgets that the hidden/summarized reasoning tokens are still generated and billed as output and eat the latency and context budget
Gives one blanket recommendation instead of distinguishing the format-bound high-volume extraction task from the multi-step debugging task
Suggests heavy few-shot chain-of-thought prompting for the reasoning model, not realizing it reasons internally and that elaborate CoT prompting is redundant and can degrade it
Decides purely by assertion ('reasoning is/ isn't better') without proposing an offline eval on representative data comparing accuracy vs latency and cost
