open.answer_format: An annotated critique-and-redesign: name the schema's failure modes, present the redesigned tool set / JSON Schema using concrete constructs (enum, required, additionalProperties, typed sub-objects), and justify each change by the mechanism it fixes. Should distinguish decode-time guarantees from runtime dispatch checks. Roughly 350-550 words, or an annotated schema plus prose.
open.reference_answer:
The root problem is a single overloaded 'god tool' with an almost type-free schema: the model has no signal for which values are legal and the dispatcher has nothing meaningful to validate against.

1) Split by intent and by side-effect. Replace `manage_ticket` with distinct single-purpose tools: `get_ticket` (read-only), `resolve_ticket`, `set_ticket_priority`, `add_ticket_comment`, etc. The free-form `action` string is the biggest source of wrong verbs (`close` vs `resolve`); when intent is encoded in the tool *name* the model selects it directly and there is no invalid-verb failure mode. Separating reads from writes also means the read path is naturally idempotent and safe, so a status lookup can never accidentally mutate. If you must keep one tool, at minimum make `action` an `enum` of the exact backend verbs.

2) Constrain categorical fields with `enum`. `priority` should be `{"type":"string","enum":["P0","P1","P2","P3"]}`. The enum does double duty: under constrained/structured decoding it makes illegal values like `"urgent"` literally unsampleable, and even without it, it tells the model exactly what is legal, and it gives the validator an exact set to check.

3) Replace the opaque `data: object`. An untyped object lets the model invent arbitrary keys and makes validation vacuous. Give each tool an explicit typed schema for exactly the fields it needs (e.g. `resolve_ticket` takes `ticket_id` and a `resolution_note`), and set `additionalProperties: false` so unexpected keys are rejected rather than silently forwarded.

4) Get `required` and `description` right. Put genuinely mandatory fields (`ticket_id`) in `required` so a call that omits them is invalid rather than reaching the backend as a null. Descriptions are the model's primary signal for tool selection and argument filling: state the ID format, the meaning of each priority, and when to prefer one tool over a sibling, to disambiguate lookalike tools.

5) Use the provider's strict / structured-output mode where available so decoding is grammar-constrained to the schema, guaranteeing well-formed, in-enum arguments rather than merely nudging them. Note the tradeoff: strict modes typically demand `additionalProperties:false` and that every property be listed in `required`, so optional fields must be modelled as nullable unions.

6) Still validate at the dispatch boundary as defense in depth. The schema guarantees shape and enum membership; it cannot guarantee semantics: that the ticket exists, that the caller is authorised, that the ticket isn't already closed, or referential integrity. Validate these at runtime and never trust a model-supplied `ticket_id` blindly, since IDs are frequently hallucinated. Prefer designs where IDs originate from a prior `search`/`list` tool's output rather than being free-typed.

7) Return structured, actionable errors. On rejection, return a machine-readable error naming the field and the allowed values (`{"error":"invalid_priority","allowed":["P0",...]}`) so the model can self-correct on the next turn instead of failing opaquely. For destructive writes, consider a confirm step or an idempotency key so a retried tool call doesn't double-apply.
expected_answer_points: Split the overloaded tool into single-purpose tools keyed by intent (and separate read-only from mutating operations), so intent lives in the tool name and reads stay side-effect-free instead of relying on a free-form action string
Constrain categorical fields (priority -> enum P0-P3, and status/verbs) with JSON Schema `enum`, which both guides the model and makes invalid values unsampleable under constrained decoding
Replace the opaque `data: object` with an explicit typed per-tool schema and set `additionalProperties: false` so arbitrary/hallucinated keys are rejected and validation is meaningful

Mark truly mandatory fields (ticket_id) in `required` and write precise `description`s (ID format, field meaning, when to choose each tool) because descriptions are the model's main signal for tool selection and argument filling

Use the provider's strict / structured-output (constrained decoding) mode to guarantee schema- and enum-conformant arguments at decode time, and acknowledge its tradeoffs (additionalProperties:false, all-required, optional-as-nullable)

Distinguish what the schema enforces (shape, types, enum membership) from what the dispatcher must still enforce at runtime (existence, authorisation, business-rule/state validity), i.e. validate semantics as defense in depth
Do not trust model-supplied IDs blindly (they are hallucinated); prefer IDs sourced from a prior search/list tool's output, and validate existence before acting
Return structured, actionable error messages naming the offending field and allowed values so the model can self-correct, and add idempotency/confirmation for destructive writes

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: every proposed change is technically correct - correct use of enum, required, additionalProperties:false, typed sub-schemas, and an accurate account of what constrained/strict decoding does and its tradeoffs (all-required, nullable optionals). No false claims (e.g. that JSON Schema alone can verify a ticket exists, or that strict mode removes the need for runtime checks). Deduct for schema constructs used wrongly or overstated guarantees.

Full marks: addresses all five observed failures (wrong verb, missing ticket_id, invalid priority, arbitrary data keys, read-through-mutating-path) AND covers both layers - the schema the model sees and the runtime dispatch validation. Partial credit as failures or the dispatch-layer half are left unaddressed.

Full marks: each change is justified by the specific mechanism it fixes (e.g. why intent-in-tool-name beats an action string, why enum helps at decode time, why runtime checks are still needed) and the schema-guarantee-vs-runtime-semantics boundary is argued, not just asserted. Partial credit for correct changes with thin or missing rationale.

Full marks: organised as a clear critique-then-redesign with correct vocabulary (function calling, JSON Schema, enum, additionalProperties, constrained decoding, idempotency) and a concrete redesigned schema or tool list a reviewer could act on. Deduct for vague prose, no concrete schema, or disorganised argument.

common_pitfalls: Keeping the single god-tool and only tightening `action` to an enum, missing the larger win of splitting tools by intent and separating read-only from mutating operations

Claiming that constrained/structured decoding or a strict schema alone makes the agent reliable, ignoring that referential integrity, authorisation, and ticket-state validity are semantic checks JSON Schema cannot express
Leaving `data` as an untyped object (or making it a required-but-vague field) so `additionalProperties:false` has nothing to constrain and arbitrary keys still slip through
Trusting the model-supplied `ticket_id` as valid instead of treating IDs as potentially hallucinated and validating existence or sourcing them from a prior search/list tool

Describing strict mode without its actual constraints - forgetting that it typically forces additionalProperties:false and every property into `required`, so optional fields must be modelled as nullable unions
Treating failed validation as a dead end (raise/return false) rather than returning a structured, field-level error the model can use to self-correct on the next turn

open.question: A teammate is building a customer-support agent on top of an LLM (using something like LangChain/LangGraph). They report two separate complaints from testers: (1) inside a single long chat, once the conversation runs many turns the agent starts forgetting details the user gave near the start of that same chat; and (2) when a customer who was helped last week comes back in a brand-new session, the agent has no idea who they are or what their earlier ticket was about. Explain the difference between an agent's short-term and long-term memory, how each is typically implemented in practice, and map each of the two complaints to the memory type that is failing and how you'd fix it.
open.answer_format: Short written explanation, ~150-230 words. Define short-term vs long-term memory, describe how each is implemented, then explicitly map complaint (1) and complaint (2) to the right memory type with a concrete fix for each.
open.reference_answer:
Short-term memory is the agent's working context for the current session: the running message history (conversation buffer) that is passed back into the model on every call. It lives inside the model's context window, so it is ephemeral and bounded by the token limit — nothing survives once the session ends, and old turns fall out of scope once the history grows past what fits.

Long-term memory is information deliberately persisted OUTSIDE the context window so it can be recalled across sessions. It's stored in an external store — a database, key-value store, or vector store of embeddings — written to explicitly (e.g. a per-customer summary or extracted facts saved after a session) and read back selectively via a keyed lookup or semantic retrieval, then injected into the prompt when relevant.

Complaint (1) — forgetting earlier details within one long chat — is a short-term / context-window failure: the early turns no longer fit. Fix it by managing the buffer: summarize or compress older turns (summary buffer), use a sliding window, or trim/retrieve the relevant history so it stays within the window.

Complaint (2) — not recognizing a returning customer next week — needs long-term memory: persist the customer's identity, past tickets, and a session summary keyed by customer id (or embedded for semantic search), and retrieve and inject the relevant entries at the start of the new session.
expected_answer_points: Short-term memory is the current session's working context — the running conversation/message history passed to the model each turn — held in the context window and therefore ephemeral and bounded by the token limit
Long-term memory is information persisted outside the context window (in a database, key-value store, or vector/embedding store) so it can be recalled across separate sessions
Long-term memory is used selectively: entries are written explicitly and only relevant items are retrieved (keyed lookup or semantic search) and injected into the prompt — not all loaded every turn
Complaint (1), forgetting early details in one long chat, is a short-term / context-window limitation caused by history exceeding the window
Fix for (1): manage the buffer — summarize/compress older turns, use a sliding window, or trim/retrieve so the relevant history fits the context window
Complaint (2), not recognizing a returning customer in a new session, is a long-term memory gap requiring persistence keyed to the customer
Fix for (2): persist customer identity, past tickets, and session summaries in an external store and retrieve/inject them at the start of a new session

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly and precisely characterizes short-term memory as the in-context conversation buffer bounded by the context window and long-term memory as an externally persisted store recalled across sessions; describes real implementation mechanisms (summary/sliding-window buffers; database/vector store with explicit write and selective retrieval) without factual errors such as claiming a bigger context window equals long-term memory or that memory comes from fine-tuning.

Covers both memory types AND both complaints: defines each type, gives an implementation for each, correctly diagnoses complaint (1) as short-term/context and complaint (2) as long-term, and offers a concrete fix for each. Loses marks for skipping a definition, an implementation, a diagnosis, or a fix.

Justifies WHY each complaint maps to its memory type — e.g. that early turns fall out of scope because they exceed the context window, and that cross-session recall requires state persisted outside the window with selective retrieval — rather than merely asserting the mapping.

Clear, well-organized explanation using correct vocabulary (context window, conversation buffer, summarization/windowing, persistence, retrieval/embeddings); the short-term vs long-term distinction and the two mappings are easy to follow.

common_pitfalls: Treats 'memory' as one undifferentiated thing, or claims a larger context window is itself long-term memory, missing that long-term memory must live outside the window and persist across sessions
Maps the complaints backwards — blaming the in-chat forgetting on missing long-term memory, or the returning-customer problem on the context window
Says long-term memory means loading everything the agent ever saw into the prompt every turn, ignoring selective retrieval and the fact that it would overflow the context window
Claims you give the agent memory by fine-tuning the model on the conversation, confusing model weights with runtime state/memory
Hand-waves 'just use a vector database' without explaining the explicit write step, keyed/semantic retrieval, or what short-term memory is
Assumes short-term/conversation memory automatically persists across sessions, so no separate long-term store is needed

open.question: Your team is building a customer-refund handler on top of an LLM. The process is well understood: (1) classify the incoming free-text request, (2) look up the order in the orders DB, (3) check it against the written refund policy, (4) if the request is eligible and the amount is under a $50 threshold, issue the refund by calling the payments API, otherwise (5) escalate to a human agent. In the design review the team lead proposes a fully autonomous agent: hand the model all five tools plus the goal and let a ReAct-style tool-calling loop decide the order and which tools to invoke. Another engineer argues for a deterministic workflow graph (e.g. an explicit LangGraph state machine) in which the LLM is only called at specific nodes. Compare the two approaches for THIS workflow, make a recommendation with justification, and state where — if anywhere — autonomous LLM reasoning belongs and what guardrails you would put around it.
open.answer_format: A structured written comparison plus a scenario-grounded recommendation with justification, roughly 250-400 words. It should contrast the trade-offs of both approaches, commit to a recommendation, say where LLM/autonomous reasoning does and does not belong, and list concrete guardrails.
open.reference_answer:
The two ends of the spectrum differ in who owns the control flow.

Deterministic workflow: the process is modelled as an explicit graph / state machine (LangGraph nodes and edges, or an orchestrator like Temporal/Prefect). Control flow lives in code; the LLM is invoked only at specific nodes for bounded sub-tasks. Pros: reproducible, unit-testable node by node, auditable, predictable cost and latency, and every side effect can be wrapped in its own guardrails and retries. Failures are localised. Cons: you must anticipate the branches up front, so it is more rigid and takes more engineering to encode.

Autonomous agent: give the model the tools plus the goal and let a ReAct/tool-calling loop decide the order and which tools to call. Pros: flexible, less branching code, adapts to unforeseen phrasing. Cons: non-deterministic and hard to reproduce; hard to unit-test; hallucination/errors compound across steps; token cost and latency vary and can blow up; and, decisively here, the loop can invoke a side-effecting, irreversible tool (issue a refund) on the basis of a hallucinated eligibility judgement. Debugging means reading traces, not stepping code.

Recommendation: use a deterministic workflow as the backbone. The process has a small, known set of branches and contains an irreversible, money-moving side effect that must be governed by an explicit, testable policy gate rather than model discretion, and refunds must be auditable and consistent. Encode classify -> lookup -> policy-check -> decide -> act/escalate as the graph.

Where LLM reasoning belongs: at bounded, low-risk, hard-to-hardcode sub-tasks - classifying the request type, extracting the order id and amount from free text, maybe drafting the customer reply - each a single node call returning schema-validated structured output, not an open-ended planning loop. The eligibility decision and the $50 threshold must be deterministic code, not an LLM judgement.

Guardrails: schema-validate every LLM output; use an idempotency key on the payments call so a timed-out retry cannot double-refund; retries with backoff on transient tool failures; route over-threshold or low-confidence classifications to human-in-the-loop; a max-step/max-cost cap on any loop; and full tracing/logging of each node's input and output for audit and debugging. If more flexibility is needed later, a hybrid works: a deterministic outer graph with a constrained agentic sub-loop restricted to read-only tools, never given direct access to the refund action.
expected_answer_points: Characterises the deterministic workflow correctly: control flow fixed in code as an explicit graph/state machine, LLM confined to specific nodes, giving reproducibility, node-level testability, auditability and predictable cost/latency

Characterises the autonomous agent correctly: a ReAct/tool-calling loop that plans its own steps, with the costs of non-determinism, compounding errors/hallucination, variable cost/latency, and trace-based (not step) debugging
Identifies the irreversible side effect - issuing a refund via the payments API - as the decisive risk of letting an autonomous agent choose actions
Recommends the deterministic workflow as the backbone for this well-defined, branchy, money-moving, auditable process, justified from those scenario properties rather than by preference

Places LLM/autonomous reasoning only at bounded sub-tasks (classification, field extraction, reply drafting) with schema-validated structured outputs, and keeps the eligibility/threshold decision as deterministic code
Routes over-threshold or low-confidence cases to human-in-the-loop rather than auto-acting
Specifies concrete guardrails including an idempotency key on the payments call, retries with backoff, output schema validation, a max-step/cost cap, and tracing/logging for auditability
(Optional) Notes a viable hybrid: deterministic outer graph plus a constrained agentic sub-loop limited to read-only tools, never granted the irreversible action

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Accurately describes how deterministic (graph/state-machine, control flow in code, LLM at nodes) and autonomous (self-planning tool-calling loop) workflows actually behave - reproducibility, testability, error accumulation, cost/latency - and correctly frames the payments/refund call as an irreversible side effect. No incorrect claims such as equating 'deterministic' with temperature=0, or asserting an autonomous agent guarantees correct eligibility decisions.

Covers all required facets: trade-offs of both approaches, a definite recommendation for this workflow, correct placement of LLM reasoning at bounded sub-tasks, keeping the policy/threshold decision deterministic, and at least two concrete guardrails (e.g. idempotency key, human-in-the-loop, schema validation, max-step cap, tracing).

Justifies the recommendation by reasoning from the scenario's properties - well-defined branches, an irreversible money-moving action, and the need for auditability/consistency - rather than asserting a preference, and explains why each placement and guardrail follows from those properties.

Presents an organised comparison and a clearly committed recommendation using correct orchestration vocabulary (state machine/DAG, ReAct loop, tool calling, human-in-the-loop, idempotency, tracing); unambiguous and well-structured.

common_pitfalls: Recommends a fully autonomous agent for the whole flow because it is 'more flexible' or 'more modern', ignoring that the loop can trigger an irreversible refund on a hallucinated eligibility judgement
Treats 'deterministic vs autonomous' as being about temperature=0 or deterministic token sampling, missing that the real distinction is who controls the control flow
Lets the LLM make the eligibility decision or apply the $50 threshold instead of encoding that policy as testable, auditable code
Omits idempotency on the payments call, so a retry after a network timeout silently issues a second refund
Produces a generic pros/cons list with no committed recommendation, or a recommendation not tied to the specifics of the refund scenario
Ignores observability and human-in-the-loop - no tracing/logging for audit, no escalation path for low-confidence or over-threshold cases
open.prompt: Your team is building a customer-refund handler on top of an LLM. The process is well understood: (1) classify the incoming free-text request, (2) look up the order in the orders DB, (3) check it against the written refund policy, (4) if the request is eligible and the amount is under a $50 threshold, issue the refund by calling the payments API, otherwise (5) escalate to a human agent. In the design review the team lead proposes a fully autonomous agent: hand the model all five tools plus the goal and let a ReAct-style tool-calling loop decide the order and which tools to invoke. Another engineer argues for a deterministic workflow graph (e.g. an explicit LangGraph state machine) in which the LLM is only called at specific nodes. Compare the two approaches for THIS workflow, make a recommendation with justification, and state where — if anywhere — autonomous LLM reasoning belongs and what guardrails you would put around it.

open.question:
You are hardening a production customer-support agent built on an LLM tool-calling loop (the model proposes a tool call, your runtime executes it and feeds the result back into context, repeat). Its tools include `refund_payment(order_id, amount)`, `search_orders(query)`, and `send_email(to, body)`. Three distinct failure modes show up in production:

A. `refund_payment` intermittently returns HTTP 504 (gateway timeout), and you have confirmed that in some of those cases the refund actually completed on the payment provider's side.
B. The model periodically calls `search_orders` with a malformed filter (e.g. an invalid date range) and the tool responds with HTTP 400 plus a message describing what was wrong.
C. A downstream dependency of `search_orders` goes down for ~2 minutes; during that window every call returns HTTP 503.

Design the tool-failure handling and recovery strategy for this agent. For each of the three modes, explain how you classify it and what recovery action it triggers. Then explain the cross-cutting mechanisms that keep the agent from looping forever, from amplifying the outage, and from causing duplicate side effects. Be specific about where each piece of logic lives: the deterministic runtime wrapper around a tool versus the model's reasoning loop.
open.answer_format: A structured written design, roughly 350-550 words (prose or well-organised bullets). It should address each of the three named failure modes (A, B, C) with a classification and a recovery action, then cover the cross-cutting mechanisms, and state explicitly where each piece of logic lives (deterministic wrapper vs. model loop).
open.reference_answer:
Start from a failure taxonomy and route recovery by class:
- Transient / infrastructure errors the caller can safely re-issue: timeouts, 502/503/504, connection resets, 429.
- Model-correctable errors: the tool rejected the *arguments* (400/422 validation). Re-issuing the identical call is futile; the fix is different arguments, which only the model can produce.
- Permanent / fatal errors: 401/403 auth, 404, hard business-rule rejections. Neither a retry nor a re-prompt helps; abort/escalate.

Mode A (refund_payment 504, possibly-already-succeeded): transient at the transport layer but *mutating*, so a blind retry risks a duplicate refund. The correct fix is idempotency: mint a stable idempotency key once when the agent first decides to refund (e.g. UUID or hash of order_id+amount+attempt-group) and send it on every attempt so the provider deduplicates; then a capped exponential backoff + jitter retry on the 504 is safe. If the provider offers no idempotency, do NOT blind-retry — reconcile first by calling a status/read endpoint (e.g. get_refund_status) and only retry if it did not land. This lives in the deterministic wrapper, not the model loop.

Mode B (search_orders 400 validation): do NOT retry in the wrapper — same arguments will fail again. Surface the structured error (code + provider message) back into the model context as the tool result so the model can correct the filter and re-issue a valid call (model-in-the-loop recovery). Cap self-correction attempts per logical step (e.g. 2-3); after the cap, escalate/abort rather than loop.

Mode C (search_orders 503 outage): transient, but every call fails for ~2 minutes, so uncoordinated per-call retries across sessions become a retry storm that prolongs the outage. Wrap the tool in a circuit breaker: after N consecutive failures, open the breaker and fail fast for a cool-down window, with half-open probes to detect recovery. While open, degrade gracefully (tell the model the tool is temporarily unavailable so it can inform the user or try an alternative) or queue/defer. Backoff must carry jitter to de-correlate retries.

Cross-cutting mechanisms:
- Timeouts on every tool call so a hung dependency can't stall the loop; honor Retry-After on 429/503.
- Keep the two retry layers distinct: bounded deterministic transient retries in the wrapper, and model-driven argument correction in the agent loop. Don't stack them so attempt counts multiply.
- A global termination budget: max tool-call iterations / wall-clock / tokens per task, plus per-tool attempt caps; detect repeated identical failing calls and break. This guarantees the loop halts.
- Return errors to the model as clean, structured observations (not raw stack traces or secrets) so it can reason about them.
- Idempotency keys for ALL mutating tools, not just refunds.
- Observability: log every attempt with its failure class, and define terminal behavior — graceful degradation or handoff to a human — when recovery is exhausted, rather than failing silently or hallucinating success.
expected_answer_points: Establishes a failure taxonomy and routes by it: transient/retriable (timeouts, 5xx, 429) vs. model-correctable argument errors (4xx validation) vs. permanent/fatal (auth, 404, business rejections).
Mode A: identifies the 504-but-succeeded case as a mutating side effect requiring an idempotency key (or a status/reconcile read before retry), and explicitly refuses to blind-retry a mutating call.
Mode B: does NOT retry the 400 in the wrapper; feeds the structured error back to the model so it corrects the arguments (model-in-the-loop recovery), with a cap on self-correction attempts.
Mode C: uses a circuit breaker (open / half-open / closed) with fail-fast and cool-down to prevent a retry storm during the outage, plus graceful degradation while open.
Applies capped exponential backoff with jitter and honors Retry-After for transient retries, and sets timeouts on every tool call.
Distinguishes the two retry layers and where logic lives (deterministic runtime wrapper vs. the model's reasoning loop) and avoids stacking them so attempts multiply.
Enforces a global loop/iteration/token budget and per-tool attempt caps to guarantee termination and stop infinite retry loops.
Defines terminal behavior (graceful degradation or human handoff) and observability, and returns clean structured errors to the model without leaking stack traces or secrets.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly classifies each mode and prescribes the technically right recovery: idempotency key / reconciliation for the mutating 504, model-driven argument correction (not mechanical retry) for the 400, a circuit breaker for the 503 outage, and backoff+jitter plus timeouts for transient retries. No incorrect assertions such as retrying a 400 unchanged, or blind-retrying a mutating call without idempotency.

Addresses all three named failure modes AND the cross-cutting mechanisms (global loop/attempt budgets, the two distinct retry layers and where they live, terminal/degradation behavior, observability). Full marks require both the per-mode handling and the system-level safeguards; deduct for missing pieces.

Justifies choices by mechanism: why idempotency makes mutating retries safe, why retrying a validation error is futile so the model must correct it, why uncoordinated retries during an outage cause a retry storm that a breaker prevents, and why budgets/caps guarantee termination.

Organised so each failure mode and each cross-cutting mechanism is clearly identifiable; states explicitly where logic lives (deterministic wrapper vs. model loop); uses terms precisely (idempotency key, jitter, circuit breaker, Retry-After, self-correction cap).

common_pitfalls: Treats all failures uniformly — applies exponential-backoff retries to everything, including retrying the 400 validation error with identical arguments (which will always fail) instead of routing it back to the model for correction.
Blind-retries the refund 504 without an idempotency key or a status reconcile, causing duplicate refunds; misses that the operation is mutating and may have already succeeded.
Handles the 503 outage with only naive per-call retries, creating a retry storm that worsens and prolongs the outage; never mentions a circuit breaker or fail-fast.
Omits any global termination guarantee (loop/iteration/token budget, per-tool attempt cap), so the agent can loop forever re-issuing failing calls.
Conflates the two retry layers — merges model self-correction with deterministic transient retries, or stacks them so total attempts multiply combinatorially.
Feeds raw stack traces or secrets back into the model context, or defines no terminal behavior (silent failure or hallucinated success) once recovery is exhausted.

open.question:
You maintain a production LangGraph ReAct agent that resolves customer billing disputes. Each turn the model either calls a tool (search_orders, issue_refund, post_ledger_adjustment, escalate_to_human) or emits a final answer; each observation is appended to the message history and the loop repeats. Two incidents happened in production: (a) on some tickets the agent burned the entire token budget repeatedly calling search_orders with slightly reworded queries that all returned nothing useful, then timed out; (b) once it issued the same refund twice after a tool call timed out and was retried. The team's only current safeguard is the graph's recursion_limit=25, which raises GraphRecursionError when the step count is exceeded.

Explain why recursion_limit alone is an inadequate loop-control strategy for this system, then design a layered approach that prevents both non-terminating/thrashing behavior and duplicated side effects. Be concrete about mechanisms and address all four of: (1) how you distinguish the agent looping/thrashing from making legitimate slow progress; (2) what independent stopping conditions you would enforce and why one counter is not enough; (3) how the agent should behave when a limit trips, versus today's GraphRecursionError; and (4) how loop and retry handling must interact with the irreversible issue_refund tool.
open.answer_format: A written design/explanation, roughly 300-450 words, ideally organized around the four sub-questions. Should name concrete mechanisms (fingerprinting, budgets, idempotency keys, interrupts) and justify trade-offs; short bullet lists are fine.
open.reference_answer:
recursion_limit is a necessary backstop but not a strategy. It only counts graph super-steps, so it fires identically whether the agent is progressing or thrashing; it is hard to tune (too low kills legitimately long tickets, too high lets the agent waste tokens and money before it trips); it raises an exception rather than producing a safe outcome; and it does nothing to stop harmful actions that occur mid-loop — the double refund happened well before step 25. It bounds worst-case steps; it neither detects looping early nor terminates safely.

(1) Detecting looping vs. progress. Canonicalize each proposed tool call to (tool_name, normalized_args) and fingerprint it, and also fingerprint the resulting observation. Repeated calls that yield an equivalent (or empty) observation carry no new information — that catches the reworded search_orders case, which collapses to the same normalized call/observation. Track a progress signal (new evidence gathered, a task-state hash) and detect cycles or a window of N turns with no advance. Legitimate slow progress produces new observations/state deltas each turn; thrashing does not.

(2) Independent stopping conditions. Enforce several, because different failure modes exhaust different budgets: an iteration/step cap (backstop), a cumulative token/context budget (incident (a) was token exhaustion), a wall-clock timeout for the ticket SLO, a monetary or tool-call-count cap, per-tool caps (e.g., at most one issue_refund per ticket), and the no-progress/repeated-action threshold, which should trip well before the hard caps. A single counter can't cover a task that is cheap-but-slow, fast-but-expensive, or looping-but-under-budget.

(3) Behavior on trip. Don't let GraphRecursionError propagate to the user and don't fabricate a final answer. Make stopping a first-class terminal edge: emit a structured outcome (status = needs_human / budget_exceeded / no_progress) with partial findings and the trigger reason, route to escalate_to_human, and emit a trace for observability.

(4) issue_refund. Client-side loop control cannot guarantee exactly-once, because a timeout leaves the outcome unknown, so blind retry is unsafe. The real fix is server-side idempotency: derive a deterministic key (ticket_id + order_id + amount) and pass it to the payments API so retries and re-proposals dedupe. Retry only transient/timeout errors, bounded, and don't count sanctioned retries as loop iterations (but cap them so permanent errors don't retry forever). Finally, gate irreversible tools behind a LangGraph interrupt-before/checkpointer human-approval step, and have the loop detector treat a completed side-effecting action as done so it cannot be repeated inside the loop.
expected_answer_points: Explains that recursion_limit is only a blunt backstop: it counts graph super-steps regardless of progress, is hard to tune, raises an exception instead of a safe outcome, and does not prevent mid-loop side effects (the double refund occurred before step 25).

Proposes semantic loop detection by fingerprinting (tool, normalized args) and/or (action, observation) pairs to catch repeated or near-duplicate calls that return no new information — covering the reworded search_orders case.

Adds progress/oscillation detection (track a progress metric or state hash; stop after N turns with no advance or on a detected cycle) and explicitly distinguishes thrashing from legitimate slow progress.

Enforces multiple independent stopping conditions (step cap + token/context budget + wall-clock + cost/tool-call cap + per-tool cap + no-progress threshold) and justifies why one counter is insufficient because different failure modes exhaust different budgets.

Specifies graceful termination: stop into a structured terminal state (status + partial result + reason) and route to escalate_to_human with tracing, rather than letting GraphRecursionError propagate or fabricating a final answer.
Uses server-side idempotency keys for issue_refund as the real fix for the double refund, noting a timeout leaves the outcome unknown so blind retry is unsafe without exactly-once at the API.
Distinguishes bounded retry-with-backoff on transient errors from loop iterations, so sanctioned retries aren't misclassified as loops and permanent errors don't retry forever.
Gates irreversible tools behind a human-approval interrupt-before/checkpointer step and forbids the loop from repeating an already-completed side-effecting action.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Mechanisms are correct and precisely described: recursion_limit semantics (super-step count, GraphRecursionError), action/observation fingerprinting for loop detection, idempotency keys giving exactly-once on retried side effects, the timeout-implies-unknown-outcome reasoning, the retry-vs-loop distinction, and LangGraph interrupt/checkpointer for approval. No false claims (e.g., that a bigger counter, temperature=0, or client-side locks alone fix the double refund).

Addresses all four required sub-parts — loop-vs-progress detection, multiple independent stopping conditions with justification, graceful trip behavior, and the issue_refund/idempotency interaction — each with a concrete mechanism rather than a slogan. Full marks require none of the four to be missing or hand-waved.

Justifies the design choices: why layered defense beats a single counter (different failure modes exhaust different budgets), why a timeout makes blind retry unsafe so idempotency is required, why graceful escalation beats crashing or fabricating, and the tuning trade-off in setting caps too low vs. too high.

Well organized (e.g., around the four sub-questions), uses precise agent/loop-control vocabulary correctly, cleanly separates the distinct mechanisms (detection vs. budgets vs. termination vs. idempotency), and is concrete and actionable.

common_pitfalls: Treats a larger or better-tuned recursion_limit / max_iterations as the whole solution, missing that a blunt step cap neither detects thrashing early nor prevents the mid-loop double refund.

Proposes only exact-duplicate detection and misses that reworded/near-duplicate search_orders calls need semantic or observation-level fingerprinting — or the reverse, deduping so aggressively that legitimate polling or sanctioned retries get killed.
Conflates retry-with-backoff and loop iteration: either counting transient-error retries as loops, or allowing unbounded retries on a permanent error.

Fixes the double refund with client-side loop control alone (dedup sets, in-process locks) instead of server-side idempotency keys, ignoring that a timeout leaves the outcome unknown so exactly-once must be enforced at the payments API.

Has the agent, on hitting a limit, silently return an empty or fabricated final answer, or lets GraphRecursionError propagate to the user, instead of a structured escalation/partial-result terminal state.
Relies on a single global budget (only tokens, or only steps), not recognizing a task can loop while under that budget or die under one budget while fine on every other.

open.question: You maintain a customer-support agent that runs in a tool-use loop. Its tools include search_orders(...) (read), update_ticket(...), send_email(to, body), and issue_refund(order_id, amount). When an underlying tool HTTP call does not return within the timeout, your agent framework automatically retries it. Ops now reports two problems: (1) some customers occasionally receive duplicate emails and duplicate refunds, and (2) once, the model called issue_refund with an amount larger than the order total. First explain the mechanism behind the duplicate irreversible effects, then design a side-effect control layer for this agent. Your design must prevent duplicated irreversible effects under retries, contain a hallucinated/oversized action, and NOT slow down the read-only tools. Justify the main trade-offs.
open.answer_format: A short written root-cause explanation followed by a layered design with justified trade-offs, ~250-400 words: one diagnosis paragraph, then 3-4 named controls each with a one-line justification.
open.reference_answer:
Root cause. The duplicates are a delivery-semantics problem, not a model-sampling one. Retry-on-timeout gives at-least-once execution: a timeout tells you nothing about whether the server actually processed the request — the refund/email may already have committed and only the HTTP response was lost. Because issue_refund and send_email are non-idempotent writes, the blind retry performs the effect a second time.

Design.

1. Idempotency keys. Before the FIRST attempt, mint one deterministic idempotency key per logical action (a UUID stored with the pending action, or a hash of order_id + intent) and send the SAME key on every retry. The backend records keys and, on a replay, returns the stored original result instead of re-executing — making the write effectively exactly-once from the agent's view. Only auto-retry calls that carry such a key; for tools without idempotency support, reconcile by querying current state before re-issuing rather than blind-retrying.

2. Classify tools by side-effect profile. Read-only tools (search_orders) are safe to retry freely and need no gating — keep them on the fast path with no confirmation and cheap retries. Reversible writes (update_ticket) get idempotency plus audit logging. Irreversible / high-impact writes (issue_refund, send_email) get the strongest controls. Applying cost proportionally is what preserves read latency.

3. Human-in-the-loop / policy gate on the risky tail. For destructive or high-value effects (e.g., refunds above a threshold) the agent PROPOSES the action and it is held for human confirmation instead of auto-executing; this is also what catches the hallucinated amount. Pair it with argument guardrails: validate/clamp amount against the order total, allowlist recipients, and enforce a per-run budget / rate cap so a looping or hallucinating model has a bounded blast radius.

4. Observability and compensation. Log every attempted and executed side effect with its idempotency key and approval decision, so duplicates can be reconciled. Because you cannot 'roll back' an external refund or a sent email with a database transaction, provide compensating actions (refund reversal, retraction/notice) for anything that slips through.

Trade-offs: idempotency adds a little backend state and key plumbing but removes duplicates without serializing everything; tool classification and a threshold-based gate deliberately trade a small amount of autonomy/latency on the irreversible tail for safety, while leaving reads untouched.
expected_answer_points: Diagnoses the cause as at-least-once delivery: a timeout is ambiguous (the write may have committed and only the response was lost), so retrying a non-idempotent write repeats the effect
Introduces idempotency keys minted ONCE before the first attempt and reused unchanged across all retries, with server-side dedup returning the original result instead of re-executing
Classifies tools by side-effect profile (read-only vs reversible vs irreversible/high-impact) and applies controls proportionally so read-only tools stay fast/ungated
Adds a human-in-the-loop or policy approval gate for destructive/high-value actions rather than auto-executing them
Adds argument/policy guardrails (validate or clamp amount against order total, allowlists, per-run budget or rate caps) to bound the impact of a hallucinated or oversized action
Distinguishes safe auto-retry (idempotent ops) from unsafe blind retry, e.g. reconciling by querying state before re-issuing non-idempotent calls

Includes auditability (logging each attempted/executed effect with its idempotency key and approval decision) and/or compensating actions, noting external effects cannot be rolled back with a DB transaction

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly identifies retry-on-timeout as at-least-once delivery over non-idempotent writes (not a sampling/prompt problem), and proposes mechanically sound controls: idempotency keys reused across retries with server-side dedup, proportional gating by side-effect class, and guardrails/compensation. No false claims (e.g., that a DB transaction can undo an external refund, or that temperature=0 stops duplicates).

Covers all three required outcomes — (a) no duplicate irreversible effects under retries, (b) containment of the oversized/hallucinated action, (c) reads left fast — and addresses both the delivery cause and the model-error cause plus observability/compensation. Missing one required outcome or the audit/compensation angle caps the score.

Justifies WHY each control fits: why idempotency (not more retries) removes duplicates, why controls are proportional to reversibility rather than uniform, and articulates the autonomy/latency-vs-safety trade-off on the irreversible tail.

Clear diagnosis-then-design structure, correct vocabulary (idempotency, at-least-once/exactly-once, human-in-the-loop, compensating action, blast radius), and controls stated concretely enough to implement rather than as vague slogans.

common_pitfalls: Treats a timeout as proof the call failed and therefore 'safe to retry', ignoring that the refund/email may already have committed server-side
Blames the model and proposes temperature=0 or better prompting to stop duplicates, confusing a distributed-systems delivery problem with a sampling problem
Generates a fresh idempotency key on each retry attempt (or per tool call) instead of minting it once and reusing it, which defeats deduplication
Adds an in-memory 'already sent?' check that does not survive process restarts or concurrent workers and races with the in-flight request
Gates every tool (including reads) behind human approval, needlessly killing read latency instead of applying controls proportional to reversibility
Claims a database transaction / rollback can undo an external refund or a sent email, rather than using idempotency plus compensating actions

open.question:
You maintain a production travel-planning agent built on LangGraph: a ReAct-style loop where an LLM plans and calls tools (search_flights, search_hotels, get_weather, get_user_calendar, book_reservation) until it emits a final itinerary. Your offline suite scores 92% task-completion — the final itinerary matches a gold answer on a 300-example dataset — yet production cost and p95 latency per request have roughly doubled over two releases, on-call sees occasional duplicate bookings that get auto-cancelled, and a PM asks: 'If the final answers are still correct, why evaluate anything else?'

You are asked to add trajectory evaluation. Write a design-review response that (a) explains, with concrete failure modes from THIS system, why task-completion evaluation alone is insufficient and what trajectory evaluation adds; (b) defines precisely what a 'trajectory' is in terms of your traces/spans and what must be instrumented to evaluate it; (c) proposes concrete trajectory evaluation methods, distinguishing reference-based metrics from reference-free (LLM-as-judge) approaches and saying when each applies; and (d) confronts the central difficulty that several different tool sequences can all be correct, explaining how your metrics avoid punishing valid alternative paths. Be specific about metrics and their failure modes.
open.answer_format: A sectioned written design-review response (~350–550 words) addressing all four asks; short headers or bullets are fine. It should name concrete metrics and tracing mechanisms rather than staying at the level of concepts, and tie recommendations to the scenario's evidence.
open.reference_answer:
Task-completion (outcome) evaluation checks only the terminal artifact — does the final itinerary match the gold answer. It is necessary but blind to process, and in this system it cannot see the very defects we're seeing. (1) Redundant/duplicate tool calls: the duplicate bookings that later auto-cancel still fired a real side effect, yet the corrected final answer passes outcome eval. (2) Wasteful re-planning loops that inflate token cost and p95 latency — exactly the 2x regression that persists while accuracy holds. (3) Wrong-but-lucky reasoning that will break on nearby inputs. (4) Unsafe ordering, e.g. book_reservation before get_user_calendar confirms availability. So the PM is right that answers are correct and wrong that nothing else matters: outcome eval answers 'did it arrive?'; trajectory eval answers 'did it arrive the right way?', and cost, latency, and side effects live entirely in the path.

A trajectory is the ordered execution path: the sequence of steps, each being (LLM decision → tool call with name and arguments → observation/result), ending in the final answer. In tracing terms it is the ordered set of spans in the run tree — one span per LLM call and per tool invocation — with inputs, arguments, outputs, tokens, latency, and error status attached (OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, or LangSmith/LangGraph run trees). To evaluate it you must instrument spans to capture tool name, serialized arguments, observation, and status for every step; without arguments and observations you can only count steps, not judge them. Offline datasets are best curated from these production traces.

Reference-based methods (need a gold/reference trajectory) compare the observed tool sequence to an expected one, from strict to lenient: exact ordered match (trajectory_strict_match); in-order subsequence match; order-agnostic set match; and precision/recall/F1 over the set of tool calls — recall catches missing/needed steps, precision catches redundant/duplicate ones (this is what flags the duplicate-booking regression). Single-step evaluation (given a prefix, was the next action correct) localizes errors.

Reference-free methods apply when enumerating gold trajectories is infeasible (most open-ended tasks): an LLM-as-judge reads the whole trace and scores it against a rubric — efficiency (no redundant/duplicate calls), logical ordering, well-formed arguments, error recovery, no hallucinated tools. Also compute cheap quantitative path metrics needing no reference: step count, tool-call count, duplicate-call count, token cost, latency — these directly track the observed regression.

The central difficulty is that many sequences are valid: you may check weather before or after flights, and flight/hotel order is free. Exact-sequence match produces false negatives on valid alternatives. Mitigations: prefer order-agnostic set match or tool-call precision/recall over strict ordering; enforce ordering only where a real dependency exists (confirm-before-book); define equivalence classes of acceptable trajectories rather than one gold path; or use the rubric-based judge, which scores properties instead of string-matching a path. Finally, because agents are stochastic, run each example multiple times (pass^k) to separate flakiness from systematic path errors, and validate the LLM judge against human labels (e.g. Cohen's kappa) before trusting it, watching for length and self-preference bias.
expected_answer_points: Explains that task-completion/outcome eval judges only the final artifact and is blind to process, naming concrete failure modes in THIS system: duplicate bookings (real side effects hidden by a corrected final answer), redundant re-planning loops driving the cost/latency regression, unsafe tool ordering, and lucky-but-wrong reasoning.

Defines a trajectory as the ordered sequence of steps (LLM decision + tool call + arguments + observation) ending in the final answer, and maps it to spans in a run/trace tree (OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions or LangSmith/LangGraph), stating what must be instrumented: tool name, arguments, observation, status, tokens/latency.

Describes reference-based trajectory metrics against a gold trajectory — exact/ordered match, order-agnostic set match, and precision/recall/F1 over tool calls — and correctly explains what precision (redundant/extra calls) versus recall (missing needed calls) each catch.

Describes reference-free evaluation: LLM-as-judge scoring the whole trace against a rubric (efficiency, ordering, valid arguments, error recovery), plus reference-free quantitative path metrics (step/tool-call/duplicate counts, token cost, latency), and says reference-free is needed when gold trajectories can't be enumerated.

Confronts the multiple-valid-trajectories problem: exact-sequence match yields false negatives on valid alternatives; mitigates via set-based/precision-recall metrics, enforcing order only where a genuine dependency exists, equivalence classes of acceptable paths, or rubric-based judging of properties.

Addresses agent stochasticity (multiple runs / pass^k to separate flakiness from systematic errors) and/or validating the LLM judge against human labels (agreement/kappa) and guarding against its biases before relying on it.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly distinguishes outcome/task-completion eval from trajectory eval; accurately describes a trajectory as spans in a run tree and the required instrumentation; states valid reference-based metrics (ordered/set match, tool-call precision/recall) and reference-free approaches (LLM-as-judge, quantitative path metrics) without inventing behavior; correctly explains why exact-sequence match over-penalizes valid paths and gets precision vs recall right. No false claims (e.g., that a correct final answer implies a sound path, or that a single gold trajectory is mandatory).

Covers all four asks: (a) why outcome eval is insufficient with system-specific failure modes, (b) the trajectory/span definition plus instrumentation, (c) reference-based versus reference-free methods with when-to-use, and (d) the multiple-valid-paths difficulty with mitigation. Full marks also acknowledge stochasticity (repeated runs) and/or LLM-judge validation.

Ties each recommendation to the scenario's evidence — links redundant/duplicate calls to the cost/latency doubling and auto-cancelled bookings, and justifies metric choices by exactly what they catch (precision for redundant calls, recall for missing steps) — and reasons about trade-offs (strictness vs false negatives, reference cost vs judge reliability).

Reads as an organized design-review response using precise vocabulary (spans, run tree, trajectory, precision/recall, LLM-as-judge, pass^k); cleanly separates outcome vs trajectory and reference-based vs reference-free; and frames the answer legibly enough to settle the PM's question.

common_pitfalls: Agrees with the PM that correct final answers make process evaluation unnecessary — treats task-completion as sufficient and never explains the invisible cost, latency, and side-effect defects the outcome metric cannot see.

Conflates trajectory evaluation with simply re-running final-answer eval, or proposes only one quantitative signal (e.g., step count) while never checking whether the individual steps/tool calls were actually correct.
Insists on exact ordered tool-sequence match against a single gold trajectory and never confronts that several sequences are valid, yielding an evaluator that fails good runs (false negatives).
Describes an LLM-as-judge over the trace but treats its scores as ground truth — no mention of validating it against human labels or its length/self-preference biases.
Ignores instrumentation: assumes trajectories can be judged without capturing tool arguments and observations in spans, or never mentions tracing (OTel/LangSmith) as a prerequisite at all.
Muddles precision versus recall over tool calls (or reverses them), e.g., claiming recall catches redundant duplicate calls when precision is what flags extras.

Your offline suite scores 92% task-completion — the final itinerary matches a gold answer on a 300-example dataset — yet production cost and p95 latency per request have roughly doubled over two releases, on-call sees occasional duplicate bookings that get auto-cancelled, and a PM asks: 'If the final answers are still correct, why evaluate anything else?'

open.question: You maintain an internal IT help-desk assistant built as a single agent: one LLM running an agentic loop (reason -> call tool -> observe -> repeat) over about five tools (ticket lookup, password reset, KB search, etc.). It works well. Product now wants to add many more capabilities across clearly distinct domains -- HR/payroll questions, device provisioning, and security-incident triage -- and a PM proposes rebuilding it as a multi-agent system with a supervisor that routes to specialized sub-agents. In a design review you are asked to weigh in. Explain how a single-agent architecture differs from a multi-agent one, give the main trade-offs on each side, and recommend an approach for this specific system with justification.
open.answer_format: Short written explanation, ~150-250 words: define both architectures and their coordination mechanism, give concrete trade-offs on each side, and end with a justified recommendation tied to this help-desk scenario.
open.reference_answer:
A single-agent system is one LLM running an agentic loop over a single context and a shared tool set: it reasons, calls a tool, observes the result, and repeats until done. A multi-agent system decomposes the work across specialized agents -- typically an orchestrator/supervisor that routes each request to a sub-agent (an HR agent, a provisioning agent, a security-triage agent), each with its own focused instructions, tool set, and context, coordinating via handoffs or shared state.

Single-agent strengths: simpler to build and reason about; one context so nothing is lost between steps; lower latency and token cost because there are fewer model round-trips; and far easier to trace and debug. Its weakness is that it degrades as scope grows -- a large, mixed tool set hurts tool-selection accuracy, the system prompt bloats with competing instructions, and unrelated domains contend for the same context window.

Multi-agent strengths: each agent stays small and focused, so tool selection and instructions are cleaner; distinct domains are isolated; teams can build, scale, and own subsystems independently. Costs: coordination overhead, more LLM calls (higher latency and spend), harder observability, and the risk of context loss or error propagation across handoffs.

Recommendation: keep the single agent for now, perhaps grouping tools, and introduce a supervisor + sub-agents only once the growing tool count and genuinely distinct domains make one prompt unreliable. Don't add orchestration complexity before the single agent measurably breaks; when it does, decompose along the real domain boundaries (HR, provisioning, security).
expected_answer_points: Defines a single-agent system as one LLM iterating a reason/act/observe loop over a single context with a shared set of tools.
Defines a multi-agent system as an orchestrator/supervisor routing to specialized sub-agents that each have focused instructions/tools and coordinate via handoffs or shared state.
Names a genuine single-agent advantage (simplicity, single unbroken context, lower latency/cost from fewer LLM round-trips, or easier tracing/debugging).
Identifies the single-agent failure mode as scope grows: a large mixed tool set degrades tool-selection accuracy and the prompt/context becomes bloated with competing concerns.
Names a genuine multi-agent advantage (focused per-agent tools/instructions, isolated context per domain, or independent scaling/ownership).
Names a genuine multi-agent cost (coordination overhead, more LLM calls raising latency/cost, harder observability, or context loss / error propagation across handoffs).
Gives a justified recommendation for this scenario: default to the single agent and adopt multi-agent only when tool count/distinct domains justify it, decomposing along real domain boundaries.

Deduct for wrong claims such as multi-agent being inherently cheaper/faster, or conflating the two designs.

Full marks: covers both definitions, at least one real advantage AND one real cost for each side (including the tool-overload failure mode and a handoff/observability concern), and a recommendation. Deduct for covering only one architecture, listing pros without cons, or omitting the recommendation.

Full marks: the recommendation follows from the trade-offs and is tied to this help-desk system's growing tool count and distinct domains (HR/provisioning/security), rather than a generic preference; shows judgement about when the single agent stops being adequate.

Full marks: well-organized and concise, using correct vocabulary (orchestrator/supervisor, sub-agent, handoff, tool-selection, context window) so a reviewer can follow the comparison and the recommendation easily.

common_pitfalls: Treats multi-agent as simply more advanced/better and recommends it by default, ignoring the added latency, token cost, and debugging burden it introduces.
Defines the two designs only superficially ('one bot vs several bots') without the mechanisms -- supervisor/routing, per-agent focused tool sets, handoffs or shared state.
Claims multi-agent is cheaper or faster because work is 'parallelized', when specialist routing typically adds sequential LLM round-trips and token overhead.
Ignores the actual driver of the decision -- that a single agent's tool-selection accuracy and prompt clarity degrade as the tool set grows.
Overlooks handoff-specific risks such as context/state loss between agents, error propagation, and reduced observability.
Gives no recommendation, or one not justified against this scenario's growing and genuinely distinct domains.

open.question: A fintech support team runs a customer-support assistant on a hosted 8B open-weight model. They want two things. (1) Every reply must follow a required structure -- greeting, resolution steps, a compliance disclaimer, an escalation path -- in the company's formal brand tone. (2) Answers must be grounded in their product knowledge base (fees, policies, limits), which is edited several times a week. An engineer proposes: "Let's fine-tune the model every week on a dump of the latest knowledge-base articles plus a few hundred good support transcripts." Evaluate this proposal. Recommend an adaptation strategy (or combination), justify each choice by tying it to the nature of the requirement, explain how you would keep the weekly-changing knowledge current, and state the main risks of the approach you would reject.
open.answer_format: A structured written recommendation, roughly 200-320 words: a verdict on the proposal, a per-requirement strategy mapping (which technique for format/tone vs. for the knowledge base) with justification, a plan for the weekly-changing knowledge, and the key risks of the rejected path.
open.reference_answer:
The proposal conflates two different needs: teaching a behavior (format + tone) and serving factual knowledge (the KB). These call for different adaptation strategies.

Format and tone are stable, learnable behaviors -- a good fit for supervised fine-tuning. On an 8B model I would use a parameter-efficient method (LoRA/QLoRA) rather than full fine-tuning: it is far cheaper, trains in minutes-to-hours, and largely avoids the catastrophic forgetting that full fine-tuning risks. A few hundred curated transcripts that exemplify the required structure (greeting, resolution steps, compliance disclaimer, escalation) and tone are plausibly enough to teach the pattern; I would format them with the model's chat template and mask the loss to the assistant turns.

The weekly-changing KB is the wrong thing to bake into weights. Fine-tuning is an unreliable mechanism for factual recall, and any facts learned go stale the moment fees/policies change -- forcing a full retrain every week, which is slow, costly, and still lags the data. Instead, serve the KB via RAG: chunk and embed the articles, retrieve at inference, and update by simply re-indexing when content changes. This keeps answers current with no retraining and lets you cite sources.

Crucially, combine the two: build the SFT set so examples include retrieved context in the prompt and answers grounded in that context (and that decline when context is missing). That teaches the model both the house format and how to use RAG context.

I would reject the weekly-retrain-on-KB path for its cost, staleness between runs, catastrophic forgetting, and hallucination risk when facts change, and I would evaluate on a hold-out set scoring both format adherence and factual grounding/citation accuracy.
expected_answer_points: Separates the two requirements: format/tone is a stable behavior (SFT-appropriate) whereas the KB is volatile factual knowledge that should not be baked into weights.
Recommends RAG (retrieve at inference, update by re-indexing) for the frequently-changing KB because it stays current without retraining and fine-tuning is an unreliable store for changing facts.
Recommends SFT for the format/tone requirement using a parameter-efficient method (LoRA/QLoRA) on the 8B model rather than full fine-tuning, to cut cost and reduce catastrophic forgetting.
Notes that a few hundred high-quality, correctly-formatted examples (right chat template, loss on completion tokens) can teach style/format but cannot inject an entire knowledge base.

Identifies concrete failure modes of the rejected weekly-retrain-on-KB approach: staleness between retrains, retraining cost/latency, capability regression/catastrophic forgetting, and hallucination when facts change.
Advocates combining SFT + RAG, ideally training on examples that include retrieved context so the model learns to ground answers and to decline when context is absent.
Mentions evaluation on a hold-out set measuring both format adherence and factual grounding/citation accuracy.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly maps volatile factual knowledge to RAG and stable format/tone to SFT; accurately characterizes fine-tuning as an unreliable, quickly-stale store for changing facts and PEFT/LoRA as the cost-appropriate SFT method for an 8B model; makes no false claims (e.g. that RAG reliably imposes output style, or that fine-tuning dependably stores retrievable facts).

Addresses both requirements, gives a concrete combined recommendation, provides a plan for the weekly-update cadence, covers the risks of the rejected path, and touches evaluation; loses points for omitting the knowledge-freshness plan, the risks, or one of the two requirements.

Justifies each technique by tying it to the nature of the requirement (behavior vs. volatile knowledge) and to trade-offs (cost, forgetting, staleness), rather than asserting choices without reasoning.

Delivers a clear, well-structured recommendation a reviewer could act on: an explicit verdict, a clean split of the two concerns, and a stated integration/eval plan, using the field's vocabulary correctly.

common_pitfalls: Endorses fine-tuning weekly on KB dumps to 'teach' the facts, conflating knowledge injection with fine-tuning and ignoring that weights are a poor, quickly-stale store for changing facts.

Treats it as a single problem and picks one technique for both -- 'just fine-tune everything' or 'just use RAG for everything' -- missing that RAG does not reliably enforce output format/tone and SFT does not keep facts current.
Proposes full fine-tuning on the 8B model with no mention of PEFT/LoRA, ignoring the cost and catastrophic-forgetting trade-offs.
Ignores the weekly-update cadence, offering no plan to keep knowledge fresh or assuming retraining latency is negligible.
Recommends RAG but never explains that the SFT data/model must be taught to use retrieved context (and to decline without it), so the two components never actually integrate.
Omits evaluation, or evaluates only format adherence while ignoring factual grounding and citation accuracy.

open.question: Your team must adapt a 13-billion-parameter instruction-tuned model (shipped in bf16) to a specialized legal-document domain, but the only hardware available is a single 24 GB consumer GPU (e.g. an RTX 4090). Full fine-tuning is out of reach, so you choose QLoRA. In a design review you are asked to justify the approach end to end. Explain: (1) with an approximate memory breakdown, why full fine-tuning does not fit on 24 GB but QLoRA does; (2) what NF4 quantization and the frozen 4-bit base weights mean for the forward and backward pass, i.e. where gradients actually flow and where they do not; (3) how you would set the rank r, the alpha scaling, and which modules you attach adapters to, and why the QLoRA paper's finding about target modules matters here; and (4) at deployment, the trade-off of merging the adapter back into the base weights, including the specific wrinkle introduced because the base was trained in 4-bit.
open.answer_format: A structured written explanation, roughly 250-400 words, ideally organized into the four requested parts. A strong answer includes an approximate per-parameter memory arithmetic and uses the correct vocabulary (NF4, compute/dequant dtype, alpha/r scaling, adapter merge).
open.reference_answer:
1) Memory. Mixed-precision full fine-tuning with Adam costs roughly 16 bytes/parameter: a bf16 weight (2) + bf16 gradient (2) + an fp32 master copy (4) + fp32 Adam m and v (4+4). For 13B that is ~208 GB before activations, far beyond 24 GB; the optimizer/master states, not the weights, dominate. QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4-bit NF4 (~0.5 byte/param -> ~6.5 GB, less with double quantization) and only the small LoRA adapters (<1% of params) carry gradients and Adam states, so those cost a few hundred MB. The rest of the budget is activations, cut with gradient checkpointing, plus a paged optimizer that offloads spikes to CPU. It fits.

2) Forward/backward. NF4 is a lossy 4-bit quantile ('NormalFloat') type tuned for zero-centered normal weights. The base is frozen: on each matmul its NF4 weights are dequantized on the fly to the bf16 compute dtype, used, then discarded. The LoRA path runs alongside: h = W_deq x + (alpha/r)·B(Ax), with A,B in bf16 and B initialized to zero (A Gaussian) so at step 0 the adapter is a no-op and training starts exactly at the base model. Backprop computes gradients only for A and B; the quantized base receives no gradient and no optimizer state - that is the whole saving. W_deq is still used to propagate gradients to earlier activations, but dW is never accumulated.

3) Hyperparameters. r (commonly 8-64) sets adapter capacity/param count; alpha enters as the scale alpha/r, so it amplifies the update independent of r (set alpha ~ 2r, then tune). Crucially, the QLoRA paper found that matching full-FT quality depends on attaching adapters to all linear layers (q,k,v,o plus the MLP gate/up/down), not just q and v - the breadth of adapted matrices matters more than a large rank. So prefer many modules at modest rank over few modules at high rank.

4) Merge trade-off. For inference you can fold W_merged = W + (alpha/r)·BA into one matrix, removing the extra adapter matmul and serving a single model. The wrinkle: the adapter was trained to correct one specific NF4-quantized base. If you dequantize, add BA, then re-quantize the merged weights back to 4-bit, you inject a new quantization error the adapter never saw, degrading quality. Mitigate by merging into an fp16/bf16 base (serve in fp16/8-bit, higher memory) or by keeping the adapter unmerged at inference - which also lets you hot-swap multiple adapters on one dequantized base at a small latency cost.
expected_answer_points: Full fine-tuning with Adam costs ~16 bytes/param (bf16 weight + bf16 grad + fp32 master + fp32 Adam m,v), ~200 GB for 13B, so it exceeds 24 GB; the optimizer/master states dominate, not the weights themselves.

QLoRA fits because the base is stored in 4-bit NF4 (~0.5 byte/param, ~6.5 GB) and only the tiny adapters carry gradients and optimizer states; gradient checkpointing and a paged optimizer absorb activations/spikes.
The frozen NF4 base is dequantized on the fly to the bf16 compute dtype for each matmul and discarded; NF4 is a lossy 4-bit quantile type, not an exact store.

Gradients flow only to the LoRA matrices A and B (and their optimizer states); the quantized base gets no gradient/no optimizer state, which is the source of the memory saving; B is zero-initialized so training starts at the base model.
r sets adapter capacity/param count while alpha scales the update as alpha/r (e.g. alpha ~ 2r); they are distinct levers.
Per the QLoRA finding, attaching adapters to all linear layers (attention q/k/v/o and MLP gate/up/down) matters more for matching full-FT quality than pushing rank high; breadth beats depth of rank.
Merging folds W + (alpha/r)BA into one matrix to remove adapter inference latency and serve a single model.

Re-quantizing the merged weights to 4-bit introduces a quantization error the adapter never trained against, degrading quality; mitigate by merging into an fp16 base or keeping the adapter unmerged (which also enables multi-adapter hot-swap).

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks require correct, true claims throughout: the ~16 bytes/param full-FT figure with the components named and the point that optimizer/master states dominate; ~0.5 byte/param for the 4-bit base; on-the-fly dequantization of a frozen NF4 base to the bf16 compute dtype; gradients flowing only to A and B with the base receiving none; the alpha/r scaling and zero-init of B; all-linear-layer targeting; and the merge-then-requantize mismatch. Deduct for false statements such as the base weights being trained/updated, NF4 being lossless, or alpha setting the parameter count.

Full marks require substantive coverage of all four requested parts: (1) the memory breakdown contrasting full FT with QLoRA, (2) forward/backward behavior and where gradients do and do not flow, (3) rank/alpha/target-module choices with the QLoRA target-module finding, and (4) the deployment merge trade-off including the 4-bit re-quantization wrinkle. Missing or only-gestured parts lose marks proportionally.

Full marks require causal justification rather than assertion: why QLoRA fits (the base's gradients and fp32 optimizer/master states are eliminated), why adapter breadth beats large rank, why zero-init B gives a safe start, and why re-quantizing a merged model injects error the adapter never saw. Answers that merely list facts without the underlying mechanism score lower.

Full marks for a well-organized, design-review-appropriate answer that maps cleanly to the four parts, uses precise terminology (NF4, compute/dequant dtype, alpha/r, adapter merge, paged optimizer) correctly, and stays concise. Rambling, disorganized, or jargon-misusing answers score lower.

common_pitfalls: Claims QLoRA's saving comes mainly from shrinking the base weights to 4-bit, missing that the dominant saving is removing the gradients and fp32 Adam/master states for the frozen base.
States or implies the 4-bit base weights are updated during training, rather than only the A and B adapter matrices.
Treats adapter merging as always free and lossless, ignoring that re-quantizing the merged weights to 4-bit introduces error the adapter never trained against.
Recommends maximizing rank r as the primary quality lever, overlooking the QLoRA finding that attaching adapters to all linear layers matters more than large rank.
Confuses alpha with rank, or claims alpha sets the number of trainable parameters, when alpha only scales the update via the alpha/r factor.
Believes NF4 stores weights exactly or that dequantization recovers the original bf16 values, rather than being lossy quantile quantization of normally distributed weights.
