open.question: Your team is instruction-tuning an open-weight base model (e.g., Llama-3-8B *base* — pretrained on next-token prediction only, never instruction-tuned) into a helpful internal assistant. A colleague hands you a folder of ~3,000 raw examples they scraped and asks you to turn it into a proper supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset. Explain (a) how you would structure and format each individual training example, (b) what quality properties the dataset as a whole must have, and (c) why, during training, the loss is computed only on the response tokens rather than over the whole sequence. Ground your answer in how the model actually learns from this data.
open.answer_format: A short structured written explanation (~200-320 words), ideally organised around the three parts (a) per-example structure/format, (b) dataset-level quality, (c) loss masking. Prose or bullets are both fine; include the mechanism (imitation via next-token prediction), not just a checklist.
open.reference_answer:
SFT teaches the base model to imitate ideal responses via ordinary next-token prediction, so the data has to encode exactly the input→output behaviour we want.

(a) Per example: each item is a paired (prompt, target response). I structure it with explicit roles — an optional system message, a user instruction, and the assistant response — and support multi-turn conversations. Crucially I render every example through the model's chat template (its role markers and special tokens) and append the EOS token to the response so the model learns to stop. The training-time formatting must be byte-for-byte what I'll use at inference; any mismatch (different delimiters, missing system prefix) degrades behaviour.

(b) Dataset-level: because SFT is imitation, response quality dominates — responses must be correct, in the desired style/tone, and demonstrate the exact behaviour I want (garbage in, garbage out). I want diversity and coverage of the instruction types the assistant will actually face, not 3,000 near-duplicates. I deduplicate, decontaminate against any eval/benchmark sets to avoid leakage, and sanity-check length and format balance. A smaller, curated, diverse set typically beats a large noisy one (the LIMA finding): with only ~3,000 examples I'd curate hard rather than pad.

(c) Loss masking: the sequence contains both the prompt and the response, but I mask the loss on the system/user (prompt) tokens and compute it only on the assistant response tokens. The goal is to learn P(response | prompt) — to generate good answers given an instruction — not to model or memorise the user's input. Training on prompt tokens wastes gradient signal on text the model will never need to produce and can bias it toward parroting instructions.
expected_answer_points: Each training example is a paired (instruction/prompt, target response), structured with explicit roles (system/user/assistant) and supporting multi-turn conversations

Every example is rendered with the model's chat template / consistent special tokens and role markers, and this formatting must match what is used at inference; an EOS/stop token is appended so the model learns to terminate
SFT is imitation learning via next-token prediction, so response quality/correctness dominates — the model copies whatever it is shown (garbage in, garbage out)
Dataset-level properties: diversity and coverage of the instruction types the assistant will face, plus deduplication and decontamination against eval sets to prevent leakage
Quality over quantity — a smaller curated, diverse set often beats a large noisy one (e.g., the LIMA finding), which is the right call for only ~3,000 examples
Loss is masked on the prompt (system/user) tokens and computed only on the response tokens so the model learns P(response | prompt) rather than modelling/memorising the user's input

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly describes examples as prompt/response pairs with role structure, insists on chat-template + inference-consistent formatting and an EOS token, characterises SFT as imitation via next-token prediction, and correctly states that loss is masked on the prompt and computed only on the response (learning P(response|prompt)). Deduct for wrong loss-masking direction, confusing SFT with RLHF/preference tuning, or inventing formatting that would not match inference.

Full marks: addresses all three parts — per-example structure/format, dataset-level quality (diversity/coverage, dedup, decontamination, quality-over-quantity), and loss masking. Partial credit if one part is thin or a major dataset-quality property (decontamination, diversity, or EOS handling) is missing.

Full marks: ties each choice to the learning mechanism — e.g., quality matters because the model imitates; formatting must match inference or behaviour degrades; masking focuses gradient on the target behaviour. Partial credit for correct claims stated without the underlying 'why'.

Full marks: well-organised (ideally around the three parts), uses correct terminology (SFT, chat template, EOS, loss masking, decontamination) precisely, and is concise and unambiguous. Deduct for disorganised or vague explanation.

common_pitfalls: Frames SFT success as mainly 'get more data' and overlooks that response correctness/style dominates because the model imitates its targets
States or implies the loss is computed over the whole sequence including the prompt, or gets the masking direction backwards (masking the response instead of the prompt)
Omits the chat-template / formatting-consistency-with-inference requirement, or proposes an ad-hoc format that would not match how the model is prompted at serving time
Confuses instruction tuning (SFT) with RLHF / DPO preference tuning — e.g., claims you need a reward model or preference pairs to instruction-tune a base model

Ignores deduplication and decontamination against eval sets, risking benchmark leakage and inflated scores

open.question: Your team is assembling a pairwise preference dataset to train a reward model (later used for PPO, and also directly for a DPO run) for a customer-support assistant. For each prompt you sample two candidate responses from the current SFT model at temperature 0.9, then have annotators (backed by an LLM-as-judge to scale labeling) pick the better one as 'chosen' and the other as 'rejected'. On the held-out eval, the reward model assigns higher scores to longer responses almost regardless of their quality, and after alignment the assistant becomes noticeably verbose and padded. Diagnose the most likely root causes in how the preference data was generated and labeled, and lay out how you would restructure the data-preparation pipeline to fix it. Address candidate generation, labeling, and dataset construction, and note any trade-offs.
open.answer_format: A structured written answer (~250-350 words): first a short diagnosis of the root causes, then a concrete remediation plan organized across candidate generation, labeling, and dataset construction. Bullet points are fine. Should name the confound explicitly, explain the mechanism, and justify each fix rather than just listing techniques.
open.reference_answer:
Diagnosis: response length is a spurious confound that correlates with the 'chosen' label. Both human annotators and LLM-as-judge exhibit a well-documented verbosity bias (they equate length/detail with quality), so the preference labels encode 'longer' as much as 'better'. The reward model then learns length as a cheap proxy for reward, and PPO/DPO exploit it (reward hacking) -- the policy inflates length because that is what the reward signal rewards. Two pipeline choices amplify this: (1) both candidates are drawn from the same model at the same temperature, so pairs are low-diversity and the most salient difference between them is often just length rather than substance; (2) the LLM-judge also carries position/order bias, adding noise and further tilting toward verbose answers.

Remediation:
- Candidate generation: increase pair diversity so the contrast is about quality, not length -- sample from multiple sources/temperatures (and other models), and use best-of-n or varied prompts. Keep generation on-policy (from the current policy) so the reward model is accurate where it will actually be queried.
- Labeling: give annotators an explicit rubric that separates correctness/helpfulness from length; randomize presentation order and average the LLM-judge over both orderings to cancel position bias; calibrate the judge against a human-labeled gold set and track inter-annotator agreement; allow a tie/low-confidence option.
- Dataset construction: measure the correlation between length and the chosen label, then break it -- length-balance the pairs (or subsample so chosen/rejected length distributions match), or apply length-controlled/normalized reward (e.g., a length penalty or length-normalized objective as in SimPO/ODIN-style disentangling). Filter near-tie pairs with small quality margin (they are mostly label noise) and deduplicate.

Trade-off: do not simply hard-penalize length -- sometimes a longer answer is genuinely better. The goal is to remove length as a confound and let quality drive the signal, verified by re-checking the length/reward correlation after the fix.
expected_answer_points: Identifies response length as a spurious confound correlated with the 'chosen' label, and that annotators and LLM-judges have a verbosity bias that encodes 'longer' as 'better'
Explains the mechanism: the reward model learns length as a proxy for reward and PPO/DPO exploit it (reward hacking), producing verbosity
Notes that sampling both candidates from the same model/temperature yields low-diversity pairs where length is the main salient difference, and recommends more diverse candidate generation

Addresses judge/annotator bias: randomize presentation order (and/or average over orderings) to cancel position bias, use a clear rubric separating quality from length, and calibrate the judge against human gold labels / check agreement
Proposes breaking the length-label correlation in the dataset: measure it, then length-balance pairs and/or use length-controlled or length-normalized reward (e.g., SimPO/ODIN-style)
Includes quality controls: filter near-tie / low-margin pairs as label noise, deduplicate, and keep preference data on-policy (from the current policy distribution)
Recognizes the trade-off that length should not simply be hard-penalized because longer answers are sometimes genuinely better; the aim is to remove the confound and re-verify

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly names length as a spurious confound and verbosity bias in annotators/LLM-judges, accurately describes the reward-hacking mechanism (RM learns length proxy; PPO/DPO exploit it), and states valid, real mitigations (order randomization, length-balancing/length-controlled reward, on-policy data, margin filtering, judge calibration) without technical errors. Full marks require the diagnosis and at least two mechanistically-correct fixes.

Covers all three requested areas -- candidate generation, labeling, and dataset construction -- plus a diagnosis. Partial credit if one area (e.g., candidate-generation diversity or on-policy data) is missing or only the diagnosis is given without a concrete remediation plan.

Justifies why each fix addresses the underlying mechanism rather than listing techniques, and surfaces the trade-off that length must not be blindly penalized because longer is sometimes genuinely better. Full marks require causal reasoning tying fixes to the confound and at least one explicit trade-off or verification step.
Well-organized as diagnosis-then-remediation, uses correct preference-data vocabulary (chosen/rejected, pairwise, reward hacking, position/verbosity bias, on-policy), and is concise and unambiguous.

Proposing to simply add a hard length penalty or cap without first measuring the length/label correlation, and without acknowledging that longer answers are sometimes genuinely better
Ignoring LLM-judge and annotator biases (verbosity bias, position/order bias) as a source, or trusting the LLM-judge without calibrating it against human labels
Overlooking that both candidates coming from the same model at the same temperature produces low-diversity pairs, so length becomes the dominant distinguishing feature
Thinking determinism fixes it (e.g., setting temperature to 0) or confusing this with a decoding/sampling problem rather than a data-signal problem

open.question: You are aligning an 8B instruction model with DPO. The preference pairs come from human edits: each rejected response is a lightly edited version of the chosen one, so the two share most of their tokens. You start both the policy and the reference from the same SFT checkpoint and set beta = 0.1. Training looks healthy: the loss falls smoothly and the reward margin (implicit reward of chosen minus rejected) climbs steadily. But you also log the mean per-token log-probability of the *chosen* responses and see it *decreasing* throughout training, and a held-out generation eval shows outputs getting shorter, more repetitive, and worse. Explain mechanistically what is happening, why the standard DPO objective permits a rising margin alongside a falling chosen log-prob, and lay out concrete changes you would make to fix it — giving the trade-off of each.
open.answer_format: A structured written explanation (~250-350 words) in three parts: (1) the mechanism and why the DPO loss permits this, referencing the objective; (2) the role of beta and the shared-token/edit-distance effect; (3) concrete remediations each with an explicit trade-off. Equations may be stated informally.
open.reference_answer:
This is the classic DPO likelihood-displacement / degeneration failure, and the curves are consistent with it rather than a bug.

Mechanism and why the loss permits it: the DPO loss is -log sigma( beta * [ (log pi_theta(y_w|x) - log pi_ref(y_w|x)) - (log pi_theta(y_l|x) - log pi_ref(y_l|x)) ] ). It depends only on the *difference* of the two log-ratios — the margin. Nothing in it pins the absolute likelihood of the chosen response, so the loss keeps falling as long as the rejected log-prob drops faster than the chosen. A rising reward margin with a *falling* chosen log-prob is therefore fully consistent with the objective, not a contradiction. Because your pairs are near-identical edits (small edit distance), chosen and rejected share most tokens; the gradient that suppresses the rejected sequence also pushes down those shared tokens in the chosen sequence, and the displaced probability mass leaks to unseen, off-distribution continuations. That is why generations degenerate (shorter, repetitive) even as the margin looks great.

beta is the only anchor: beta = 0.1 is a weak implicit-KL constraint tying pi_theta to pi_ref, so the policy is free to drift. Raising beta (e.g. 0.3-0.5) tightens the constraint — less degeneration, but smaller preference gains and slower learning.

Fixes with trade-offs:
- Anchor the chosen likelihood: DPO-Positive (DPOP) adds a penalty like max(0, log(pi_ref(y_w) / pi_theta(y_w))) so the chosen log-prob cannot fall below reference; equivalently add a small NLL/SFT loss on y_w (RPO-style). Directly targets the failure; costs a hyperparameter to tune and can shrink the margin if weighted too heavily.
- Curate data: this failure is specifically triggered by low-edit-distance pairs — filter or downweight them, or route them through DPOP.
- Lower the learning rate; DPO degenerates quickly when LR is too high, at the cost of slower convergence.
- Stop trusting margin/loss as the quality signal: log chosen and rejected log-probs separately and KL(pi_theta || pi_ref), and gate promotion on a real generation eval or reward-model score.

Note: a falling chosen log-prob is not intrinsically wrong — only the relative implicit reward matters for the ordering — but here it has gone far enough that mass is escaping the data manifold, so anchoring the absolute likelihood of the chosen response is the correct fix.
expected_answer_points: The DPO loss is a function only of the difference of the two log-ratios (the margin), so it constrains relative ordering, not absolute likelihood — the loss can fall while the chosen log-prob falls, as long as the rejected falls faster.

Because chosen and rejected pairs share most tokens (small edit distance), the gradient suppressing the rejected sequence also pushes down shared tokens of the chosen sequence, displacing probability mass to unseen/off-distribution continuations and causing degeneration.

beta is the only term anchoring the policy to the reference (an implicit KL constraint); beta = 0.1 is weak, so raising beta reduces drift/degeneration at the cost of a smaller margin and slower learning — and correctly notes higher beta means less deviation.

Add an explicit likelihood anchor on the chosen response — DPO-Positive (DPOP) penalty keeping chosen log-prob at/above reference, or an auxiliary SFT/NLL loss on the chosen (RPO-style) — directly fixing the failure, with the trade-off of an extra hyperparameter that can shrink the margin.
Identify low-edit-distance preference pairs as the specific trigger and propose data curation/filtering or routing such pairs to DPOP.

Recognise the reward margin / training loss is not a sufficient quality signal and add guardrails: track chosen and rejected log-probs separately, KL from reference, and a real generation eval or reward-model score.

Note the falling chosen log-prob is not inherently pathological (only relative reward orders the responses) but becomes harmful once probability mass leaves the data manifold — hence anchoring absolute chosen likelihood is the right response.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly states that the DPO loss depends only on the margin (difference of log-ratios) and explains the shared-token/probability-displacement mechanism accurately; gets the direction of beta right (higher beta = tighter to reference/less drift); describes DPOP or an SFT/NLL anchor correctly. No incorrect claims (e.g. that DPO is buggy, that lower beta reduces drift, or that a falling chosen log-prob alone proves an error).

Covers all three requested parts — mechanism, why the objective permits it, and concrete fixes with trade-offs — and touches the beta role, the data (edit-distance) trigger, at least one likelihood-anchoring fix, and the need for eval/KL guardrails rather than trusting the margin.

Justifies each remediation with a mechanism-linked trade-off (e.g. why higher beta trades margin for stability, why anchoring the chosen likelihood targets the exact failure) rather than listing fixes; connects the margin-only objective to the observed symptoms.

Clear, well-structured explanation using correct terminology (implicit reward, log-ratio, margin, implicit KL, reference model); a grader can follow the causal chain from objective to symptom to fix without ambiguity.

common_pitfalls: Claiming DPO is broken or that a decreasing chosen log-prob by itself proves a bug — missing that the objective legitimately constrains only the margin.
Getting the beta direction backwards: suggesting a lower beta to 'strengthen the preference signal', which actually loosens the anchor to the reference and worsens drift.
Attributing the whole problem to overfitting or learning rate without identifying the margin-only objective plus shared-token displacement as the root mechanism.
Recommending a full switch to PPO/online RLHF as the only remedy, overlooking that a cheap explicit anchor (DPOP or an auxiliary SFT loss on the chosen) directly addresses the failure.
Trusting the falling loss and rising reward margin as evidence of success and never proposing generation-quality, reward-model, or KL-from-reference guardrails.
Ignoring the low-edit-distance property of the data, which is the specific documented trigger, and so missing the data-curation and DPOP-routing remedies.

open.question: Your team is compressing a strong 70B instruction-tuned teacher into a 7B student for on-device chat. A junior engineer's recipe is standard token-level knowledge distillation: over a fixed corpus of teacher-generated responses, teacher-force each target sequence and minimize the forward KL D_KL(teacher || student) (equivalently, cross-entropy against the teacher's temperature-softened next-token distribution). Offline the KD loss drops smoothly and validation cross-entropy looks great, but the deployed student is bland and hedging, collapses to safe generic phrasings, and hallucinates confidently on long-tail prompts. Diagnose why this specific recipe produces these symptoms, then design an improved distillation setup. Justify your choice of divergence direction and of sampling regime (on-policy vs off-policy), address temperature and the teacher-student capacity gap, and explain how you would validate that the new student is actually better given that KD/validation loss looked fine.
open.answer_format: A written diagnosis-plus-design (roughly 300-450 words), structured as: (1) a mechanistic diagnosis of the failure, (2) a revised distillation recipe with each key choice justified, and (3) a validation plan. Free-form prose or a short mini design doc; must name the real mechanisms (KL direction, on-policy distillation, temperature/dark knowledge) rather than gesture at them.
open.reference_answer:
Diagnosis. The recipe is token-level, off-policy distillation under a forward-KL objective. Two coupled properties explain the symptoms.

(1) Divergence direction. Forward KL D_KL(teacher || student) is mode-covering / zero-avoiding: it heavily penalizes the student for assigning near-zero probability anywhere the teacher has mass. A 7B student cannot represent the 70B teacher's full distribution, so it is forced to spread probability to cover every mode, becoming an over-smoothed, high-entropy model. That is exactly the bland, hedging, generic behavior; the same smearing leaks mass onto tokens the teacher barely supports, which surfaces as confident hallucination on the long tail. Reverse KL D_KL(student || teacher) is mode-seeking / zero-forcing: the student concentrates on the teacher's dominant modes, producing sharper, more coherent generations (the MiniLLM result). The trade-off is reduced diversity / dropped modes, usually acceptable for an assistant.

(2) Sampling regime. Training only on teacher-forced sequences is off-policy: at inference the student conditions on its own generated prefixes, a distribution it never trained on, so errors compound (exposure bias) - which is why offline loss looks fine but deployed generation degrades. On-policy distillation (GKD) samples sequences from the student during training and scores them with the teacher, removing the train/inference mismatch. Reverse KL on student samples is not directly differentiable through sampled text, so it is optimized with a policy-gradient / on-policy formulation.

Revised recipe. Objective: on-policy generalized KD - sample responses from the student, score token distributions with the teacher, minimize reverse KL (or a generalized JSD early on to stabilize training when the student is far from the teacher). Warm-start / curriculum with some teacher sequences (SeqKD) before going fully on-policy. Temperature: soften both logits with a tuned T to transfer dark knowledge (relative probabilities of non-argmax tokens) and scale the loss by T^2 to preserve gradient magnitude; avoid excessive T, which re-introduces over-smoothing. Capacity gap: if the 70B->7B gap hurts convergence, insert an intermediate teaching-assistant model or add hidden-state/feature matching, and curate the prompt distribution to the target domain.

Validation. KD/validation loss is a poor proxy - low token-level loss coexists with bland generations. Evaluate on held-out prompts with generation-based metrics: win-rate vs the teacher (human or LLM-as-judge), downstream task benchmarks, explicit repetition/degeneracy and hallucination/factuality checks, plus a diversity metric to catch mode collapse from reverse KL.
expected_answer_points: Identifies that the objective is forward KL (soft-target cross-entropy), which is mode-covering / zero-avoiding, and that a low-capacity student forced to cover all teacher modes over-smooths - explaining the bland/hedging outputs and the leaked mass that causes hallucination.

Proposes reverse KL as the fix because it is mode-seeking / zero-forcing (student concentrates on the teacher's dominant modes for sharper coherent generations, e.g. MiniLLM), and acknowledges the trade-off of reduced diversity / mode dropping.
Diagnoses exposure bias / train-inference mismatch from off-policy teacher-forced training, which is why offline loss looks fine while deployed generation degrades.

Recommends on-policy distillation (GKD): sample sequences from the student during training and score with the teacher; notes reverse KL over student samples needs a policy-gradient formulation (not plain backprop through sampled text).
Handles temperature correctly: soften logits to transfer dark knowledge (relative non-argmax probabilities), tune T, scale loss by T^2 to preserve gradient magnitude, and avoid over-high T.
Addresses the teacher-student capacity gap with a concrete mitigation (teaching-assistant / intermediate model, hidden-state/feature matching, or domain-curated prompt distribution).

Specifies a generation-based validation plan (win-rate vs teacher via human/LLM judge, task benchmarks, hallucination and degeneracy checks, diversity metric), explicitly noting KD/validation loss is an inadequate proxy.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly characterizes forward vs reverse KL (mode-covering/zero-avoiding vs mode-seeking/zero-forcing) and maps each to the observed symptoms; correctly identifies off-policy teacher-forcing as the source of exposure bias and on-policy distillation (GKD) as the remedy; states temperature/dark-knowledge and T^2 scaling accurately. Full marks require no reversed KL directions, no invented mechanisms, and a correct note that reverse KL on student samples needs a policy-gradient objective.

Covers all requested facets: mechanistic diagnosis, divergence-direction choice, sampling-regime choice, temperature, capacity-gap mitigation, and a generation-based validation plan. Deduct for each facet omitted or only named without substance.

Justifies each design choice by its underlying mechanism (why forward KL over-smooths a small student, why reverse KL sharpens, why on-policy sampling removes the inference mismatch) and surfaces the trade-offs (diversity loss / mode dropping, JSD for early stability, over-high T), rather than asserting fixes without linking cause to effect.

Organized as diagnosis -> revised recipe -> validation, uses distillation vocabulary precisely (forward/reverse KL, dark knowledge, exposure bias, on-policy/GKD, SeqKD), and reads at a senior design-review register without rambling or hedging.

common_pitfalls: Reverses the KL directions - claims forward KL is mode-seeking or that reverse KL causes the over-smoothing - inverting the core mechanism.
Prescribes only surface tweaks (lower the temperature, train longer, use more teacher data) without addressing the divergence direction or the off-policy/exposure-bias root cause.
Treats distillation as ordinary supervised fine-tuning on the teacher's hard outputs, ignoring soft targets / dark knowledge and thus missing why forward KL behaves as it does.
Proposes on-policy / reverse-KL distillation but forgets you cannot backprop through sampled student text and omits the policy-gradient (GKD-style) formulation, or misstates the objective.
Concludes the 7B student is simply too small for distillation to work, instead of adjusting the objective and data regime.
Declares success on the basis of low KD/validation loss, missing that token-level loss can look great while generations are bland or hallucinated, and provides no generation-based evaluation.

open.question: Your team ran DPO on an 8B chat model. In a pairwise LLM-as-judge evaluation (GPT-4o as judge) against the pre-DPO checkpoint, the DPO model wins 68% of comparisons on a held-out set of instructions. In the ship/no-ship design review, leadership reads '68% win rate' as a clear improvement and wants to release. As the evaluation owner, explain how confident you actually are that this number reflects a genuine quality gain, what specific risks in this measurement could inflate or distort it, and the concrete evaluation steps you would require before signing off.
open.answer_format: A structured written explanation, roughly 250-350 words: a prioritized set of risks in the 68% measurement, each paired with a concrete mitigation, ending with an explicit ship/no-ship gate. Not a yes/no.
open.reference_answer:
A single 68% LLM-as-judge win rate is a signal, not a verdict; I'd validate it along several axes before signing off.

Judge biases. Pairwise LLM judges have systematic biases. Position/order bias: the response shown first is often favored, so I'd evaluate each pair in both orders and only count a win when it survives swapping (or average the two orderings). Verbosity/length bias is the dominant risk here because DPO reliably lengthens outputs and judges reward length; I'd report both models' length distributions and use a length-controlled metric (e.g., AlpacaEval 2.0's length-controlled win rate) so the gain isn't just 'longer.' Self-enhancement/familiarity bias means one judge is not enough, so I'd corroborate with a second judge family plus a human spot-check and report judge-human agreement.

Statistical validity. 68% is uninterpretable without sample size and a confidence interval. I'd compute a bootstrap CI over the held-out prompts and require its lower bound to clear 50% with margin; typically a few hundred prompts.

Representativeness/contamination. I'd confirm the held-out instructions don't overlap the DPO preference data and that they match production traffic, not just easy chat prompts.

Alignment tax/regression. Pairwise chat preference says nothing about knowledge or reasoning, and DPO/RLHF can silently degrade base capabilities. I'd run capability benchmarks on both checkpoints - MMLU, GSM8K/math, HumanEval, IFEval (instruction following) - and gate on no regression. I'd also run safety and over-refusal evals, since preference tuning shifts refusal behavior.

Substance vs style. I'd read a sample of wins to confirm they're driven by correctness and helpfulness rather than formatting, hedging, or tone (reward hacking / Goodhart).

Sign-off gate: a length-controlled, order-swapped win rate with a bootstrap CI whose lower bound clears 50%, no capability or safety regression across the benchmark suite, and human confirmation that wins reflect substance - not just a raw 68%.
expected_answer_points: Position/order bias in the LLM judge: evaluate each pair in both orderings (swap A/B) and average or require the win to hold under swapping, rather than trusting a single fixed order.

Length/verbosity bias is the key confound because DPO systematically lengthens outputs and judges favor longer answers; report length distributions and use a length-controlled win rate (e.g., AlpacaEval 2.0) so the gain isn't just verbosity.
A single judge is insufficient (self-enhancement/familiarity bias): corroborate with a second judge family and/or human spot-checks, and report judge-human agreement.
Statistical significance: 68% needs a sample size and a confidence interval (e.g., bootstrap over the held-out prompts) whose lower bound clears 50% before it counts as an improvement.

Alignment tax / capability regression: pairwise chat preference doesn't capture reasoning or knowledge, so run standard capability benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, IFEval) on both checkpoints and gate on no regression.
Contamination / representativeness: verify the held-out instructions don't overlap the DPO preference data and match the production distribution rather than easy chat prompts.

Substance-vs-style / reward-hacking and safety: inspect wins to confirm they're driven by correctness not formatting/tone, and run safety and over-refusal evals since preference tuning changes refusal behavior.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly names real LLM-as-judge biases (position/order, length/verbosity, self-enhancement) with valid mitigations, correctly distinguishes a pairwise preference win rate from capability benchmarks, applies sound statistical reasoning (CIs/sample size), and invents no fake mechanisms. Full marks require identifying length bias as specifically dangerous given DPO's tendency to lengthen outputs.

Covers the full validation surface - judge-bias controls, statistical significance, contamination/representativeness, capability AND safety regression (alignment tax), and substance-vs-style - rather than fixating on one dimension. Partial credit scales with how many of these axes are addressed.

Explains WHY each risk threatens the 68% conclusion (e.g., why DPO's length increase confounds the judge, why chat win rate can't detect a reasoning regression) and ties the mitigations into a defensible, explicit ship/no-ship gate rather than listing checks in isolation.

Communicates as a prioritized set of risks each paired with a concrete mitigation, uses correct post-training vocabulary (DPO, LLM-as-judge, length-controlled win rate, alignment tax, IFEval), and ends with a clear recommendation suitable for a design review.

common_pitfalls: Accepts the 68% as self-evidently a real improvement and recommends shipping, treating the win rate as ground truth instead of a biased, noisy measurement.
Fixes only position/order bias while ignoring length/verbosity bias, which is the dominant confound because DPO reliably produces longer answers that judges prefer.

Stays entirely within chat win-rate framing and never checks capability regression (alignment tax) via benchmarks like MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval/IFEval, so a reasoning/knowledge regression could ship unnoticed.
Omits any statistical treatment - no confidence interval or sample-size reasoning - or conflates 'statistically significant' with 'practically meaningful.'
Proposes 'just use a stronger/bigger judge model' as if a better judge removes systematic biases like length and position, which it does not.
Assumes a 'held-out' set automatically means no contamination and representative coverage, without checking overlap with the DPO preference data or the production prompt distribution.

open.question:
Your team fine-tuned an 8B open-weight base model with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on ~200k instruction/response pairs assembled from three sources: (a) a purchased third-party instruction dataset, (b) transcripts of your live production assistant's real user conversations, and (c) synthetic examples generated by a larger frontier model. Internal evals looked strong, so you shipped. In production you now observe three problems:

1. The model occasionally emits long verbatim passages — including a competitor's marketing copy and, in one case, a real end user's email address and phone number.
2. On the public multiple-choice benchmark you also use as a release gate, the fine-tuned model beats the base model by 12 points, yet users report it 'feels dumber' on genuinely novel tasks than the base model did.
3. Its output formatting is inconsistent and it frequently ignores the system prompt.

You own the fine-tuning data pipeline. For each of the three symptoms, give the most likely data-quality/governance root cause(s) and the concrete curation and governance controls you would put in place before the next training run. Then describe the pipeline-level governance you would institute so these classes of problem are caught before training, not in production.
open.answer_format: A labelled, per-symptom written analysis — root cause(s) plus a concrete fix for each of the three symptoms — followed by a short section on pipeline-level governance. Roughly 400-650 words; naming specific techniques/tools (dedup, decontamination, PII redaction, loss masking, provenance) is expected.
open.reference_answer:
Symptom 1 (verbatim regurgitation + leaked PII): two distinct failures. The verbatim copy is memorization driven by duplicate and near-duplicate examples — the purchased set and production logs almost certainly contain repeated boilerplate, and memorization scales with a sequence's duplication count and with training epochs. Fixes: exact dedup (hash of normalized text) plus near-dup detection (MinHash+LSH or SimHash) run across all three sources jointly, cap per-cluster copies, and avoid many-epoch training on a small set. The leaked email/phone is a governance failure: production transcripts were never PII-scrubbed and may lack a lawful basis/consent for training use. Fixes: automated PII detection+redaction (regex + NER, e.g. Presidio/DLP) as a mandatory pre-train step, plus a consent/retention review of the logs. The competitor's marketing copy is a provenance/licensing problem — you don't know the rights on the purchased data or that it embedded copyrighted third-party text; track per-example source and license and filter disallowed content.

Symptom 2 (benchmark up 12, capability down): classic train/eval contamination plus capability regression. The gated benchmark (or near-duplicates of it) leaked into the training data — via the purchased set, or via the synthetic teacher, which may itself have seen the benchmark — inflating the score. Meanwhile real capability dropped because a narrow, low-diversity SFT distribution caused catastrophic forgetting / an alignment tax. Fixes: decontaminate — n-gram/substring overlap (e.g. 13-gram) plus embedding near-match between the entire training set and every held-out eval, remove hits, and keep a private held-out eval that provably never enters any data source. Never gate release on a public benchmark whose items could be in training. Preserve general ability with diversity/coverage targets, replay/mixing of broad instruction data, fewer epochs, lower LR, or PEFT/LoRA to limit parameter drift; measure on novel, diverse tasks, not just the leaked metric.

Symptom 3 (inconsistent format + ignores system prompt): the three sources use different chat templates/role markers, and loss was likely computed over prompt/system tokens rather than masked to response tokens only, so the model learned to model prompts instead of following them. Training examples probably also had missing or inconsistent system messages, so the model never learned to condition on them. Fixes: normalize every example to one canonical chat template with explicit roles; apply response-only loss masking; include varied, representative system prompts whose target responses genuinely depend on them; and validate each example's structure and length, dropping malformed or truncated records.

Pipeline-level governance: institute a mandatory pre-training QA gate that, for every dataset version, runs exact+near dedup, decontamination against all eval sets, PII/secret scanning, license/provenance validation, and format/schema validation, and emits a report that blocks the run on threshold breaches. Track per-example lineage (source, license, consent status, timestamp), version datasets (e.g. DVC) for reproducibility, publish a data card/datasheet, keep an audit trail and access controls, and hold eval-set custody entirely separate from training. This turns 'looked strong internally' into a defensible, repeatable release gate and aligns with data-governance obligations (e.g. EU AI Act Art. 10 for high-risk systems).

Identifies the leaked email/phone as a governance gap (unscrubbed production logs, missing lawful basis/consent) and prescribes automated PII detection+redaction (NER/regex, e.g. Presidio) plus consent/retention review.

open.question: Your team fine-tuned an open-weight LLM (Llama-3-8B) with a LoRA adapter to draft replies for a customer-support inbox. It beats the current production model on your offline eval set, and leadership wants it live this week. You own the deployment. In a design review, explain: (a) how you would roll the adapted model out to production instead of hard-swapping it for the current model, and (b) what you would monitor once it is live -- separating operational/system signals from output-quality signals -- and why quality monitoring for an adapted LLM needs more than the standard uptime dashboards.
open.answer_format: A short structured explanation, roughly 200-300 words: a progressive rollout plan (shadow/canary with rollback), then two clearly labeled lists of monitoring signals (operational vs output-quality), plus a one- or two-sentence justification for why quality monitoring is special here.
open.reference_answer:
Don't hard-swap; roll out progressively.

First shadow-deploy: mirror a copy of live traffic to the adapted model without returning its answers to users, and diff its outputs against the current model on real inputs. Then canary: route a small slice (e.g. 5%) of real traffic to the adapted model while the current model stays the 'champion', and ramp 5% -> 25% -> 100% only while metrics stay healthy. Pin the exact base-model and adapter versions and keep a one-click rollback / kill switch wired to alert thresholds, so a regression reverts in minutes.

Operational/system signals: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/sec, requests/sec), error and timeout rate, GPU memory and utilization, and cost per request. Serving the LoRA adapter unmerged adds a little per-request overhead; merging the weights removes it at the cost of multi-adapter flexibility.

Output-quality signals: task quality on a stream of labeled or human-reviewed canary samples (or an LLM-as-judge), output format/schema validity, refusal and hallucination rate, and output length/tone distribution versus the champion. Also watch for capability regression -- fine-tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting on general tasks -- and for drift as the input mix shifts, so quality evaluation must be ongoing, not a one-time gate. Feed in human spot-checks, thumbs up/down, and a downstream KPI such as escalation or human-edit rate.

Quality monitoring needs more than uptime dashboards because an LLM has no cheap ground-truth correctness signal: the service can be 100% 'up' and fast while silently producing worse replies. You only catch that with semantic/quality metrics and human-in-the-loop review, not HTTP 200s.
expected_answer_points: Rejects a hard cutover in favor of progressive rollout -- shadow deployment and/or a canary that routes a small traffic percentage and ramps up gradually while keeping the current model as champion for comparison
Includes a safety net: version-pin the base model and adapter, define acceptance thresholds from the offline eval, and keep an automated rollback / kill switch tied to alerts

Names concrete operational/system signals: latency percentiles (p95/p99), throughput (tokens/sec), error/timeout rate, GPU memory/utilization, and cost per request (optionally noting unmerged-adapter serving overhead)

Flags capability regression / catastrophic forgetting from fine-tuning and/or input drift over time, arguing quality evaluation must be continuous rather than a one-time pre-launch gate
Incorporates live feedback signals -- human spot-checks, thumbs up/down, or a downstream business KPI (escalation/edit/resolution rate) -- because offline eval cannot capture the live distribution

Explains why quality monitoring is special: LLM output has no cheap ground-truth correctness signal, so a service can be fully 'up' and fast yet silently degrade, requiring semantic metrics plus human-in-the-loop

No invented mechanisms or false claims (e.g., treating uptime as a quality signal, or claiming the offline win guarantees production quality).

Covers both asks: a progressive rollout plan with a rollback/version-pinning safety net, AND two distinct monitoring categories (operational vs output-quality) each with concrete signals, plus the regression/drift and live-feedback dimension. Full marks require both the rollout and the operational-vs-quality split; partial credit if one category or the rollback plan is thin or missing.

Trade-offs such as merged vs unmerged adapter serving, or offline-vs-live evaluation gap, strengthen the score.

open.question: Your team ships a customer-support chat feature backed by a self-hosted 7-billion-parameter transformer LLM. The prototype runs on general-purpose CPU instances (AWS c-family) and generates roughly 3-5 tokens/second per request under load, far short of the product's p95 first-token and streaming targets. Traffic averages about 15 concurrent conversations with peaks to about 60. In a design review you've been asked to decide whether to move inference to GPU instances and, if so, how to size and operate them. Walk through your recommendation. Address: (a) why CPU decoding is slow for this workload in terms of the underlying hardware bottleneck; (b) how you'd size GPU memory for a 7B model, including what besides the weights consumes VRAM; (c) how batching changes the latency/throughput trade-off; and (d) how you'd keep GPU cost and utilization reasonable given the spiky traffic. Finish with a concrete, justified instance choice.
open.answer_format: A structured written recommendation, roughly 250-400 words (prose or a labeled bullet walkthrough), that explicitly covers parts (a)-(d) and ends with a specific instance/GPU choice justified by memory, bandwidth, and concurrency reasoning.
open.reference_answer:
Recommendation: move to GPU; a single mid-range 24 GB GPU with a batching-aware server will meet the targets.

(a) Bottleneck. Autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound. Generating each token requires streaming the entire set of weights (plus the growing KV cache) from memory through the compute units, and only a single token's worth of work is done per pass, so arithmetic intensity is very low. CPU main-memory bandwidth is typically tens to low-hundreds of GB/s, whereas GPU HBM/GDDR bandwidth is many hundreds of GB/s to multiple TB/s (an A10G is ~600 GB/s; an A100 ~1.5-2 TB/s). That bandwidth gap, not raw FLOPs, is why CPU decode crawls and GPU decode is interactive.

(b) Memory sizing. 7B params at FP16 is ~14 GB for weights alone (2 bytes/param). On top of that: the KV cache, which scales with batch x sequence length x layers (~0.5 MB per token per sequence for a 7B-class model, so ~1 GB for a 2K-token conversation), plus CUDA/framework context and activation memory. A 16 GB card (T4) is too tight once KV cache and batching are included; you want ~24 GB of headroom. INT8/INT4 quantization (~7 GB / ~3.5 GB of weights) is a lever to fit a smaller GPU or leave more room for larger batches.

(c) Batching. A single request badly underutilizes the GPU because each token read of the weights is amortized over just one sequence. Batching many concurrent requests amortizes that weight read across many tokens, sharply increasing tokens/sec throughput and lowering cost-per-token, but it raises per-request latency (queueing + larger matmuls). Continuous / in-flight batching (vLLM, TGI) resolves this by inserting and evicting requests at the token level rather than waiting for a whole batch, and PagedAttention reduces KV-cache fragmentation. With continuous batching, one 24 GB GPU comfortably serves the 15-avg / 60-peak concurrency; you do NOT need one GPU per conversation.

(d) Cost/utilization. Keep a small autoscaling fleet with a warm minimum (1 instance) to cover baseline, scale out for peaks behind a request queue with backpressure and a concurrency cap, and right-size the hardware, don't buy an 80 GB A100/H100 for a 7B model. Spot/on-demand can absorb burst.

Concrete choice: AWS g5.xlarge (single NVIDIA A10G, 24 GB, ~600 GB/s) running vLLM with continuous batching, autoscaled 1->N behind a queue; FP16 weights, optionally INT8 to enlarge batch headroom. 24 GB fits the FP16 weights plus KV cache, the bandwidth gives interactive token rates, and batching lets one instance cover the concurrency far more cheaply than an A100. I'd validate p50/p95 with representative prompt and generation lengths before committing, and sanity-check the self-host economics against a managed endpoint (SageMaker/Bedrock/Vertex) at this volume.
expected_answer_points: Identifies autoregressive decode as memory-bandwidth bound (each token streams all weights + KV cache, low arithmetic intensity) and that GPU HBM/GDDR bandwidth greatly exceeds CPU DRAM bandwidth, which is the real reason CPU is slow and GPU is fast, not FLOPs.

Sizes VRAM correctly: ~14 GB for 7B FP16 weights (2 bytes/param) plus KV cache (scales with batch x sequence length x layers) plus framework/activation overhead, concluding ~24 GB is needed and 16 GB is too tight.

Explains batching amortizes weight reads to raise throughput and lower cost-per-token but adds per-request latency, and names continuous/in-flight batching (vLLM/TGI, PagedAttention) as the way to get throughput without forcing latency to the slowest request.
Concludes one batched GPU can serve the 15-avg/60-peak concurrency, i.e. rejects the one-GPU-per-request assumption.
Addresses cost/utilization under spiky traffic: autoscaling with a warm baseline, queue + backpressure/concurrency cap, right-sizing rather than over-buying, and possibly spot/serverless for burst.
Gives a concrete, justified instance pick (e.g. A10G/L4 24 GB, g5.xlarge or GCP g2) tied to memory + bandwidth + concurrency reasoning.
Mentions quantization (INT8/INT4) as a lever to fit a smaller GPU or enlarge batch headroom.
Recommends validating real p50/p95 with representative prompt/generation lengths and/or weighing self-host vs a managed endpoint at this volume.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly frames decode as memory-bandwidth bound with the CPU-vs-GPU bandwidth gap as the driver; accurate FP16 weight math (~14 GB for 7B) plus KV-cache/overhead pushing to ~24 GB; correct batching semantics (throughput up, per-request latency up) and a real continuous-batching stack; a technically sound instance choice. Deduct for wrong bottleneck (pure FLOPs/parallelism), bad memory arithmetic, or claiming batching has no latency cost.

Full marks: substantively covers all four asked parts (bottleneck, memory sizing, batching trade-off, cost/utilization) AND ends with a concrete justified instance. Deduct one point per omitted or only superficially treated part; missing quantization or the measure-p95 caveat costs at most a partial point.

Full marks: the instance choice and sizing follow logically from the bandwidth/memory/concurrency argument (e.g. 24 GB justified by weights + KV cache; single GPU justified by continuous batching; not over-buying an A100). Deduct when recommendations are asserted without linking to the mechanism or when the concurrency-to-hardware jump is unjustified.

Treats batching as a pure win that only raises throughput, without acknowledging the added per-request latency, and doesn't know continuous/in-flight batching.
Assumes one GPU serves one request, concluding they need dozens of GPUs to cover 60 concurrent conversations.

Pins an always-on large fleet and ignores utilization/cost for spiky traffic (no autoscaling, no warm baseline, no queue/backpressure), or gives no concrete instance at all.

open.question: Your team runs a customer-support RAG assistant behind an HTTP API. Each request retrieves passages from a knowledge base and calls a hosted LLM to generate an answer; traffic is high, many questions are near-duplicates, and both cost and p99 latency are under pressure. An engineer proposes a 'semantic cache': embed each incoming user query, do an approximate-nearest-neighbour lookup against a vector store of past query->answer pairs, and if cosine similarity to a stored query exceeds a fixed threshold (say 0.92), return that stored answer directly without retrieval or an LLM call. Critique this design. In your answer, contrast semantic caching with provider-side prompt/prefix (KV) caching, identify the main failure modes of the proposed cache, and describe concretely how you would deploy it safely and what you would measure.
open.answer_format: A written critique and design discussion, roughly 200-350 words. It should evaluate the proposal, explicitly contrast semantic caching with prompt/prefix (KV) caching, enumerate the main failure modes, and give concrete safeguards plus the metrics you would track. Prose or structured bullets are both fine.
open.reference_answer:
Semantic caching is attractive because, unlike exact-match caching, it can serve paraphrases of previously answered questions and skips the entire retrieval+generation pipeline, cutting both cost and latency for the matched requests. But it is fundamentally lossy/approximate, and that is where the risks live.

Contrast with prompt/prefix (KV) caching: provider or server-side prefix caching (Anthropic prompt caching, OpenAI/vLLM automatic prefix caching) reuses the computed attention key/value states for a shared exact prompt prefix -- typically the system prompt, few-shot examples, or long retrieved context -- so the prefill step is not recomputed. It is lossless (same output distribution), still runs decoding for every request, and mainly reduces TTFT and input-token cost. Semantic caching instead skips the model call entirely and returns a stored response, so it is approximate and can be wrong. The two are complementary: use prefix caching to make the calls you still make cheaper, and semantic caching to avoid some calls.

Main failure modes of the proposal: (1) False hits -- embeddings can be near for queries with opposite intent or different critical entities/numbers/negation ('cancel order 123' vs '456', 'how to enable' vs 'disable'), so a single fixed cosine threshold returns confidently wrong answers; threshold is a precision/recall trade-off. (2) Staleness -- when the knowledge base changes (policies, prices) cached answers go stale; changing the embedding model invalidates all stored vectors. (3) Personalization/multi-tenant leakage -- answers that depend on user, account state, permissions, or locale can leak PII or be wrong if cached across users.

Safe deployment: only cache generic, non-personalized, stable queries (never account-specific or action/tool queries); make the cache key = embedding plus explicit partition filters (tenant, locale, KB version, embedding-model version); choose the threshold empirically on a labeled set and add a cheap secondary check (cross-encoder or lightweight LLM verify) for borderline hits; fall through to the full pipeline on low confidence; apply TTL plus event-based invalidation on KB updates. Measure not just hit rate and cost/latency savings, but a quality guardrail -- sample cached-served answers and grade correctness (false-hit rate) -- and track hit vs miss latency separately.
expected_answer_points: Explains the semantic-cache mechanism (embed query, ANN lookup, serve stored answer above a similarity threshold) and its benefit -- serves paraphrases and skips the full retrieval+generation call, cutting cost and latency -- versus exact-match caching

Correctly contrasts prompt/prefix (KV) caching as lossless reuse of computed KV states for a shared exact prefix that reduces prefill/TTFT and input cost but still decodes every request, against semantic caching which skips the model entirely and is approximate/lossy; notes they are complementary

Identifies the false-hit risk: embeddings can be close for queries with opposite intent, negation, or different entities/numbers, so a single fixed threshold returns confidently wrong answers (precision/recall trade-off)

Identifies staleness/invalidation: cached answers go stale when the knowledge base changes, and changing the embedding model invalidates stored vectors; requires TTL plus version/event-based invalidation

Identifies personalization/multi-tenant/privacy risk: caching across users can leak PII or return wrong per-user answers, so the cache key must include user/tenant/locale/KB-version context and only non-personalized queries should be cached
Proposes concrete safeguards: empirically validated threshold, secondary verification for borderline hits, fallback to the full pipeline on low confidence, and scoping what is cacheable
Names the right metrics: hit rate AND a correctness/false-hit guardrail (sample and grade cached responses), cost/latency savings, and hit-vs-miss latency -- not hit rate alone

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly describes the semantic-cache mechanism, accurately distinguishes it from prompt/prefix (KV) caching (lossless prefix/KV reuse reducing prefill/TTFT vs approximate model-skipping), and states technically sound failure modes and fixes (false hits, staleness/embedding-model invalidation, cross-user leakage). Deduct for conflating the two caching types, calling semantic caching lossless, or asserting incorrect mechanics.

Full marks: covers the mechanism/benefit, the prefix-caching contrast, all three main risk classes (false hits, staleness/invalidation, personalization/multi-tenancy), concrete safeguards, and a metrics/measurement plan. Partial credit as classes are omitted.

Full marks: justifies choices with mechanisms -- why a fixed cosine threshold is a precision/recall trade-off, why prefix and semantic caching are complementary, why the cache key must be partitioned -- rather than asserting fixes. Deduct when recommendations are stated without a why or without acknowledging the trade-off.

Full marks: a well-organised critique that separates the contrast, the risks, and the safeguards/metrics, uses correct vocabulary (TTFT, prefill/KV, ANN, false-hit rate, invalidation), and stays within the length. Deduct for disorganised or vague phrasing.

common_pitfalls: Conflates semantic caching with prompt/prefix (KV) caching -- treating both as the same mechanism or claiming semantic caching is lossless like prefix caching
Endorses the design on hit rate and cost savings alone, never recognising the false-hit correctness risk of returning a semantically-near but wrong cached answer
Assumes a single global cache is fine, missing multi-tenant/personalization: PII leakage and per-user-context correctness (cache key needs tenant/user/locale/KB-version)
Forgets staleness -- that a knowledge-base update or a change of embedding model invalidates cached entries -- so proposes no TTL or invalidation
Offers only 'raise the threshold' with no empirical validation, secondary check, or fallback, or picks a threshold with no measurement basis
Proposes caching everything, including account-specific or action/tool-invoking queries that must never be served from a stale approximate cache

open.question:
You run an internal LLM gateway (FastAPI) that fronts one hosted model provider for ~40 downstream microservices. The call path is: service → gateway → provider SDK. Both the service's HTTP client and the gateway's provider SDK are independently configured to retry up to 3 times on failure. One afternoon the provider has a 90-second brownout: p99 latency jumps from 1s to 25s and it returns intermittent 429 (rate limit) and 529 (overloaded) responses. During the incident your gateway's outbound request rate to the provider climbs to ~8× baseline, every downstream service sees errors, and — critically — the gateway does NOT recover on its own after the provider fully heals 90 seconds later; you must restart the gateway fleet to restore service.

Explain (a) the failure mode: why outbound load spiked to ~8× and why the system stayed stuck ('metastable') after the provider recovered; and (b) design a retry-and-backoff strategy for the gateway that would have contained this incident. Be specific about backoff math, retry budgets, timeout/deadline propagation, which errors you do and don't retry, and how your design interacts with a circuit breaker.
open.answer_format: A written diagnosis-plus-design answer, roughly 300-450 words (a structured list is fine). Part (a) explains the failure mechanism concretely; part (b) specifies the retry/backoff design with concrete parameters and its interaction with timeouts and a circuit breaker.
open.reference_answer:
(a) Failure mode. Retries multiply across layers. The service retries up to 3× and the gateway's SDK retries up to 3×, so one logical request can fan out to roughly (1+3)×(1+3) ≈ 16 provider calls — and when failures are widespread this multiplier is what turns baseline traffic into the ~8× spike. Fixed backoff without jitter synchronizes retries into waves (thundering herd). Meanwhile p99 climbed to 25s with generous client timeouts, so in-flight requests, worker threads and connection-pool slots saturate and an unbounded queue builds.

The stuck state is a metastable failure. The brownout is only the trigger; the sustaining effect is work amplification — retries generate load, saturated pools make requests time out, and every timeout spawns more retries. That feedback loop holds offered load above capacity even after the provider heals, so the system sits in the bad equilibrium. There is no mechanism to drain the backlog, so it only escapes when load is externally removed — the fleet restart drops the queue.

(b) Design. (1) Retry at exactly one layer: disable SDK retries in the gateway (or client retries in services) so attempts stop multiplying; make one owner responsible. (2) Exponential backoff with full jitter: delay = random(0, min(cap, base·2^attempt)), a low attempt cap (e.g. 2–3 total) and a max-delay cap; full jitter decorrelates retries. Honor Retry-After on 429/503 and back off on 529. (3) Retry budget (token bucket): allow retries only while they stay under ~10% of request volume over a sliding window; when the budget is exhausted, fail fast. This bounds amplification to ~1.1× regardless of failure rate — the direct fix for the 8× spike. (4) Deadline propagation: set an overall deadline at the edge, propagate it, and never start an attempt (or retry) that can't finish within the remaining budget; bound provider concurrency (bulkhead) and shed load / drop past-deadline work instead of queuing unboundedly. (5) Classify errors: retry only transient/idempotent failures — connection errors, timeouts, 429, 500/502/503/504, 529; never retry 400/401/403/422. Guard non-idempotent effects (partial streams, already-executed tool calls) with idempotency keys. (6) Circuit breaker sharing state with retries: never retry through an OPEN breaker. On elevated error/latency the breaker trips, sheds load so queues drain, and HALF-OPEN probes test recovery before closing — that self-healing path is exactly what was missing, and it removes the need for a manual restart.

Afterward, validate with fault-injection load testing: inject 429/529/latency and confirm the amplification factor stays bounded and the gateway self-recovers.
expected_answer_points: Identifies multiplicative retry amplification across layers — service (×3) and gateway SDK (×3) compound to ~9–16 provider calls per request — as the cause of the ~8× outbound spike

Explains the metastable failure: a self-sustaining feedback loop (retries generate load, saturated pools/queues cause timeouts, timeouts respawn retries) keeps the system overloaded after the trigger clears, so only external load removal (restart) escapes it
Prescribes exponential backoff with full jitter (gives the formula/idea) with a low attempt cap, and honoring Retry-After / backing off on 429 and 529
Prescribes a retry budget / token-bucket cap (retries limited to a small fraction of traffic) and/or retrying at only one layer, to bound the amplification factor

Prescribes deadline/timeout propagation (overall deadline propagated, per-attempt timeout < remaining budget, no retry past the deadline) plus bounded concurrency / load shedding instead of unbounded queuing

Classifies retryable (429/500/502/503/504/529, connection errors, timeouts) vs non-retryable (400/401/403/422) and flags non-idempotent side effects (partial streams, already-run tool calls) needing idempotency keys

Integrates a circuit breaker that shares state with retries (no retry through an OPEN breaker), whose OPEN→HALF-OPEN→CLOSED cycle drains load and provides the self-healing path that removes the need for a manual restart

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Mechanisms are correct and precise: retry fan-out truly multiplies across layers; backoff-with-full-jitter and retry-budget/token-bucket are described accurately; Retry-After and 429/529 semantics are right; retryable vs non-retryable classification is correct; circuit-breaker states and their interaction with retries are stated correctly. No fabricated behavior (e.g., jitter alone bounding amplification, or retrying through an open breaker being fine).

Covers both halves — the (a) amplification + metastability diagnosis AND a (b) design touching all the demanded levers: backoff math, retry budget/single-layer, deadline propagation, error classification/idempotency, and circuit-breaker integration. Missing levers (e.g., no retry budget, or no deadline propagation, or no breaker) cost proportionally.

Connects each fix to the specific failure it addresses — e.g., retry budget bounds the 8× spike, breaker HALF-OPEN provides the drain/recovery that avoids the restart, deadline propagation stops 25s calls from piling up — rather than listing generic best practices. Explains WHY the system stayed stuck, not just that it did.

Clear structure separating diagnosis from design; correct use of domain vocabulary (retry amplification, full jitter, retry budget, deadline propagation, bulkhead/load shedding, half-open); concrete parameters rather than vague hand-waving; concise and readable.

common_pitfalls: Answers only 'add exponential backoff with jitter' and stops — misses that jitter decorrelates timing but does not bound the amplification factor, so without a retry budget or single-layer retry the ~8× spike still happens
Treats the incident as 'the provider was down' and never explains the metastable self-sustaining loop, so cannot say why a restart was needed after the provider healed
Ignores multi-layer compounding — reasons as if retries happen once, missing that the service and gateway both retry and the attempts multiply
Keeps retries and the circuit breaker independent (or retries through an OPEN breaker), so the breaker never actually sheds the retry-generated load and provides no recovery path
Sets per-attempt timeouts but omits overall deadline propagation, so retries still exceed the caller's budget and 25s calls keep piling up

Retries non-idempotent operations blindly (a 429 on a tool call that already executed, or a partially streamed response) causing duplicate side effects, or wastes load retrying deterministic 4xx like 400/422

open.question: You own a hosted LLM inference API (a streaming /chat endpoint plus a synchronous /embeddings endpoint). Leadership wants a formal reliability SLO and alerting that pages the on-call engineer only when user impact is real, not on every transient blip. The current setup is a single Datadog monitor: 'page if server-side p99 latency > 3s for 5 minutes', and it both floods on-call at night and missed a slow multi-hour degradation last week. Design the reliability program: define the SLI(s) you would measure and exactly what a 'good' and a 'valid' event is, set an SLO target with an error budget, define the error-budget policy, and specify a burn-rate alerting scheme to replace the current monitor. Justify each choice, and be specific about why a total-response-latency SLI is wrong for the streaming endpoint and why the static p99 monitor pages both too much and too little.
open.answer_format: A structured written design, roughly 300-450 words, covering: (1) the SLI definition(s) with explicit good/valid event criteria and where they are measured, (2) the SLO target and resulting error budget, (3) the error-budget policy, and (4) the burn-rate alerting scheme. Each part should carry a one- to two-sentence justification. Bullets or short paragraphs are both fine.
open.reference_answer:
SLI definition. An SLI should be a ratio of good events to valid events computed from raw request logs at the point closest to the user (load balancer / API gateway), never a pre-aggregated server-side average. I would define two families:

- Availability SLI: fraction of valid requests that return a successful response out of all valid requests. 'Valid' excludes client-caused 4xx such as 400/401 and 429 rate-limit rejections, because burning our budget on the caller's own quota or malformed input punishes us for things outside our control. 'Good' = 2xx, and for /chat specifically a stream that completes (first token AND clean end-of-stream), so half-finished streams count as bad.
- Latency SLI: for the streaming /chat endpoint the meaningful signal is time-to-first-token (TTFT) — fraction of requests whose first token arrives within a threshold (e.g. 2s). Total response time is the wrong SLI here because it grows with output length: a legitimate 2000-token answer takes longer than a 20-token one, so a total-latency SLI conflates model verbosity with degradation and will look 'slow' whenever answers are long. Optionally add an inter-token latency / tokens-per-sec SLI for steady-state throughput. /embeddings, being synchronous, can use ordinary request latency.

SLO and error budget. Set a target over a rolling window, e.g. 99.9% of valid requests good over 28 days. The complement (0.1%) is the error budget — the quantity of bad events we may spend. The point is the budget, not 'zero errors': it turns reliability into a measurable, spendable resource. Avoid 100% or 99.999% targets that leave no room to ship and guarantee constant paging.

Error-budget policy. Agree in advance what happens when the budget is exhausted: freeze risky launches / model-weight rollouts and redirect effort to reliability until it recovers. This ties the SLO to a decision rather than leaving it a vanity dashboard.

Burn-rate alerting. Alert on how fast the budget is being consumed (burn rate = observed bad-rate divided by the bad-rate that would exactly exhaust the budget over the SLO window). Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate: a fast/high-burn page (e.g. ~14.4x burn = 2% of a 30-day budget in 1h) gated by a short 5-minute second window so it fires only while the incident is live and resets quickly; plus a slow-burn ticket-only alert (~1-3x over 6h/24h) to catch gradual erosion.

Why the p99 monitor fails. 'p99 > 3s for 5 min' isn't tied to user impact or duration, so it pages on a harmless 2-minute spike (the nighttime noise) yet a sustained latency sitting just under 3s silently drained the budget for hours last week (the missed degradation). It also encourages invalid percentile-averaging across instances and leaves the aggregation window ambiguous. Burn-rate alerting scales urgency to actual budget consumption and gives predictable detection and reset behavior.
expected_answer_points: Defines the SLI as a ratio of good events to valid (total) events measured close to the user (LB/gateway) from raw events, not a server-side average or pre-aggregated percentile

Specifies 'valid' events to exclude client-caused errors (e.g. 4xx / 429 quota rejections) so the service is not penalised for callers' faults, and defines 'good' concretely (2xx, and a completed stream for /chat)

Argues the streaming latency SLI should be time-to-first-token (or inter-token latency), and explains that total response latency is wrong because it scales with output length and conflates verbosity with degradation
Sets a concrete SLO target over a rolling window (e.g. 99.9% / 28 days) and derives the error budget as the complement, framing the budget as a spendable resource; avoids 100%/unrealistic targets
Defines an error-budget policy: a concrete consequence when the budget is exhausted (e.g. freeze risky launches/rollouts, prioritise reliability) that ties the SLO to action
Proposes multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting, explaining burn rate as the rate of budget consumption, with a fast high-burn page (short+long window pair) and a slow-burn ticket alert
Explains why the static p99 monitor both over-pages (short harmless spikes, no duration/impact link, alert fatigue) and under-pages (sustained sub-threshold degradation drains budget undetected)

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: SLI is correctly a good/valid event ratio measured near the user; 'valid' correctly excludes client 4xx/429; TTFT (not total latency) is correctly chosen and justified for streaming; error budget is correctly the complement of the SLO; burn rate is correctly defined as budget-consumption rate and the multi-window scheme is technically sound. Deduct for wrong SLI math, treating total latency as fine, mislabelling SLI/SLO/SLA, or a broken/hand-wavy burn-rate definition.

Full marks: addresses all four required parts (SLI good/valid definition, SLO + error budget, error-budget policy, burn-rate alerting) AND explicitly explains both the too-much and too-little failure modes of the p99 monitor. Deduct for each missing part (e.g. no error-budget policy, no explicit good/valid criteria, only one of the two p99 failure modes).

Full marks: choices are justified by mechanism (why TTFT rather than total time; why exclude client errors; why a budget rather than zero-errors; why multi-window balances detection vs precision vs reset) rather than asserted. Deduct where recommendations are stated without a causal 'because'.

Full marks: organised by the four requested parts, uses correct vocabulary (SLI/SLO, error budget, burn rate, TTFT, valid vs good events) precisely, and is concise. Deduct for disorganised, ambiguous, or jargon-dropping-without-meaning prose.

common_pitfalls: Choosing total response latency (or total-time p99) as the streaming SLI, not recognising it scales with generated token count and so conflates a legitimately long answer with a degradation; the correct signal is time-to-first-token and/or inter-token latency

Keeping a static threshold alert ('page when latency/error-rate > X') without tying it to an error budget, so it stays disconnected from user impact and duration and reproduces the alert-fatigue problem
Counting client-caused errors (4xx, 429 quota rejections) as bad events in the SLI, burning the budget and paging on-call for faults the service did not cause

Conflating SLA (external, contractual, penalty-bearing) with SLO (internal target) and SLI (the measured metric), or setting a 100%/99.999% SLO that leaves no error budget and guarantees constant paging

Proposing a single-window burn-rate alert, which is either too slow to catch a fast outage or too noisy on brief spikes, instead of a multi-window multi-burn-rate scheme that balances detection time, reset time, and precision
Explaining only one side of the p99 monitor's failure (usually the over-paging) and missing that a sustained sub-threshold degradation silently drains the budget without ever tripping the monitor
