open.question: You own an LLM+RAG customer-support answer generator. Every prompt, model, or retrieval change must pass an automated pre-release gate: a frozen 300-example "golden set" is scored 1-5 by an LLM-as-judge, and a change is promoted only if the mean judge score does not drop by more than 0.1. A recent retrieval change sailed through the gate (mean 4.20 -> 4.25) and shipped to 100% of traffic. Within a day, escalations to human agents spiked sharply for one product line, while overall volume looked normal. Leadership asks you, in a design review, to (a) explain the statistical and methodological reasons a real regression passed this gate, and (b) design a pre-release plus continuous evaluation system that would have caught it. Be specific about mechanisms and trade-offs.
open.answer_format: A structured written design-review answer (~350-550 words): first diagnose why the gate passed a genuine regression, then design the pre-release + continuous evaluation system, naming concrete mechanisms and their trade-offs. No code required.
open.reference_answer:
The gate failed because it compresses everything into one noisy aggregate and never leaves the offline world.

Diagnosis. (1) No uncertainty: a 4.20->4.25 move on 300 items scored by a stochastic judge is almost certainly within noise, yet the gate reads a bare point estimate. Because the same items are scored before and after, use a paired comparison (paired bootstrap or Wilcoxon on per-item score deltas) and gate on the confidence interval, plus a power analysis defining a minimum detectable effect (e.g. -0.15); 300 items may lack the power to see a regression you care about. (2) Aggregation masks segments: a mean can rise while one subpopulation collapses (a Simpson-style effect). The failing product line is a slice whose few examples were swamped. (3) The frozen golden set is stale and unrepresentative -- it under-covers, or omits, that product line, so no amount of aggregate scrutiny could surface it. (4) LLM-as-judge validity: a single pointwise 1-5 holistic score is coarse, and the judge is itself a model with verbosity/position/self-preference bias and its own drift; it was never calibrated against human labels, and if the judge prompt/model isn't pinned, a 'improvement' could be judge drift. (5) Structural limit: offline eval measures a proxy on a fixed sample and cannot see live distribution shift or the true business outcome -- escalation rate -- which is an online signal.

Design. Pre-release: stratify the eval set by product line, query type, difficulty, language, and retrieval hit/miss; make it representative of (or reweighted to) live traffic; report per-slice deltas and gate on the worst regressing slice with multiple-comparison correction and enough items per slice for power. Replace the single score with decomposed, largely reference-based metrics -- faithfulness/groundedness to retrieved context, answer relevance, correctness, safety -- and pin+version the judge, whose agreement with human labels (correlation / Cohen's kappa) is tracked. Continuously refresh the set from production, mine hard/failure cases, and add every incident as a permanent regression case (this failure becomes a fixed test).

Continuous evaluation: never ship straight to 100%. Roll out via shadow or canary / A-B with automatic guardrail metrics -- escalation/handoff rate, thumbs-down, deflection -- and an online judge/human score on a sampled stream of real traffic, all sliced by the same segments, with alerting and automatic rollback on a guardrail breach. Add input/output drift detection and spend a human-review budget on sampled live traffic to keep the judge honest. On breach: roll back, root-cause, feed the case into the golden set, and guard against feedback-loop contamination if that data also trains the model.

Net trade-off: keep the pre-release gate but make it stratified, paired, powered, and judge-calibrated -- and accept it is a filter, not a guarantee. The escalation regression is ultimately caught in production by canarying against the real business metric with fast automatic rollback, which is cheaper and safer than trying to make an offline set omniscient.
expected_answer_points: The gate reads a point estimate with no uncertainty; a 0.05 move on 300 stochastic judge scores is likely within noise, so it needs a paired significance test / bootstrap confidence interval and a defined minimum detectable effect (power analysis).

A single aggregate mean masks per-segment regressions (Simpson-style effect); the fix is stratified evaluation by segment (esp. product line) with gating on the worst-slice delta, an eval set representative of production traffic, and multiple-comparison awareness.

The frozen golden set is stale and under-covers the failing product line; it must be continuously refreshed from production, mined for hard/failure cases, and grow a permanent regression case from every incident.

Critiques the LLM-as-judge: a coarse single pointwise score, judge biases (verbosity/position/self-preference) and judge drift; requires calibration against human labels, a pinned/versioned judge, and decomposition into faithfulness/groundedness/relevance/safety.

Argues offline pre-release evaluation is structurally insufficient -- a proxy on a fixed sample that cannot see live distribution shift or the true business outcome (escalation rate); the gate is a filter, not a guarantee.

Designs continuous/online evaluation: canary/shadow/A-B rollout instead of 100%, guardrail metrics (escalation, thumbs-down, handoff) sliced by segment, online judge/human sampling of live traffic, drift detection, alerting and automatic rollback.

Closes the loop and weighs trade-offs: incident -> root cause -> add to regression suite; notes feedback-loop contamination risk for retraining and balances rigor against release velocity and human-eval cost.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks for statistically and methodologically correct claims: signal-vs-noise on 300 judge scores handled with a paired test/CI and power/MDE; correct account of aggregate masking (Simpson-style) and worst-slice gating; accurate treatment of LLM-judge bias, calibration and versioning; correct offline-vs-online distinction; and sound canary/guardrail/rollback mechanics. Deduct for fabricated statistics, treating the judge as ground truth, or mischaracterising how canarying works.

Full marks cover both halves: a diagnosis spanning statistical invalidity, segment masking, stale/unrepresentative golden set, and judge validity; AND a design spanning stratified/powered pre-release gating plus continuous evaluation (canary, sliced guardrail metrics, online sampling, drift detection, automatic rollback, loop closure). Partial credit if either the diagnosis or the online-evaluation design is thin or missing.

Full marks explain WHY each flaw let this specific product-line regression slip through and why each proposed control would have caught it (e.g. worst-slice gating vs averaged mean, canary against escalation vs an offline proxy), and weigh real trade-offs (velocity/cost vs rigor, judge vs human, canary sample size vs detection time). Lower marks for asserted fixes without causal linkage to the observed failure.

Full marks for a well-organised diagnosis-then-design answer at a senior design-review register, using the vocabulary precisely (paired test, power/MDE, stratification, faithfulness/groundedness, judge calibration, canary, guardrail, drift, rollback). Lower marks for vague, disorganised, or jargon-dropping prose that does not make the mechanisms legible.

common_pitfalls: Treats 4.20 -> 4.25 as a genuine improvement and never asks whether the delta exceeds judge noise -- no confidence interval, significance test, or power analysis.
Proposes only a bigger golden set or a better judge prompt, without stratification, representativeness, or worst-slice gating, so the same segment-masking recurs.
Trusts the LLM-as-judge as ground truth: no human calibration, no acknowledgement of judge bias or drift, and no pinning/versioning of the judge model and prompt.
Keeps gating on an aggregate metric and merely tightens the 0.1 threshold, so a single-segment regression is still averaged away.

Stops at pre-release evaluation with no online/canary guardrail on the real business metric (escalation rate) and no automatic rollback, so nothing catches a distribution the offline set does not contain.
Recommends blocking every release behind full human evaluation, ignoring cost and velocity trade-offs and the fact that human review does not scale to continuous monitoring.

open.question: You operate a production LLM service that triages inbound support emails: it classifies each email into a routing category and generates a draft reply that a human agent reviews before sending. You have fine-tuned a new model, v2, which offline evaluation shows is ~3 macro-F1 points better than the live model v1. A previous careless rollout caused an incident, so leadership wants this one de-risked. Your platform has a traffic-routing / feature-flag layer that can both mirror and percentage-split traffic. Design a progressive rollout of v2 using shadow deployment and canary deployment. Explain precisely how each stage works and what it catches, define the concrete guardrail metrics and rollback triggers you would wire up, and state the single most important thing shadow mode CANNOT tell you about v2 for this system.
open.answer_format: A short written rollout design, ~250-350 words: a two-stage plan (shadow then canary) explaining the mechanism of each stage, the concrete guardrail metrics and rollback triggers, and the key limitation of shadow mode. Prose or structured bullets are both fine.
open.reference_answer:
Run the rollout in two stages behind the traffic-routing / feature-flag layer, keeping v1 as the always-warm default so rollback is instant.

Stage 1 - Shadow (traffic mirroring / dark launch). Send a copy of every live request to v2 in parallel with v1, but keep serving v1's category and draft to users; v2's output is only logged and compared. This exercises v2 on the real input distribution and catches what offline eval cannot: crashes/exceptions, malformed or schema-invalid outputs, p95/p99 latency and throughput under production load, and token/cost per request. I would track agreement rate vs v1 and, where delayed ground truth exists (the category an agent ultimately routed to), v2's macro-F1 on live traffic. Critically, side effects must be suppressed - the shadow draft must never actually be sent, and DB writes / downstream API calls stubbed - and I would budget for roughly double inference cost while shadowing.

Stage 2 - Canary. Once v2 is stable in shadow, actually serve it to a small, sticky slice of real traffic - e.g. 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% - with a bake period at each step, comparing the canary cohort against a v1 control. Only now can I measure user-facing quality: human re-route/correction rate, draft acceptance / edit-distance, and escalation/complaint rate, alongside the technical guardrails.

Guardrails and rollback. Wire explicit thresholds - error/timeout rate, p95 latency, cost per request, and misroute rate relative to control - to automated rollback plus a manual kill switch. Rollback is a flag flip routing 100% back to the warm v1 (a config change, not a redeploy), so recovery is seconds.

Key limitation of shadow: because users never act on v2's output, shadow cannot tell you whether v2 is actually better for users/business - only that it runs and roughly agrees with v1. That verdict requires canary (or reliable delayed labels).
expected_answer_points: Correctly distinguishes the mechanisms: shadow mirrors a copy of live traffic to v2 whose output is logged/compared but NOT served, while canary actually serves v2 to a small percentage of real users.
Sequences shadow first and justifies it: catches crashes/exceptions, malformed outputs, real-traffic p95/p99 latency and throughput, and cost/token usage before any user is exposed.
Then ramps canary in stages (e.g. 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with a bake period per stage and a v1 control cohort for comparison.
Defines concrete technical guardrails: p95/p99 latency, error/timeout (5xx) rate, and cost/tokens per request.

Defines quality guardrails appropriate to triage: agreement-with-v1 or delayed-label macro-F1 in shadow; human re-route/correction rate, draft acceptance/edit rate, and escalation/complaint rate in canary.
Specifies fast rollback via feature-flag flip to a warm v1 (config change, not redeploy), with explicit breach thresholds driving automated rollback plus a manual kill switch.
Names the key shadow limitation: it cannot measure real user/business quality because users never act on v2's output; that requires canary or delayed labels.
Flags shadow side-effect hazards: suppress duplicate user-facing actions (sending the drafted email), DB writes and downstream calls, and account for roughly doubled inference cost.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: shadow vs canary mechanics are stated correctly (shadow = mirrored copy, output logged not served; canary = small % of real users actually served v2); guardrail metrics named are real and appropriate; rollback is described as a flag flip to a warm v1 rather than a redeploy; side-effect suppression and doubled cost of shadow are handled correctly. Deduct for any mechanism error (e.g. shadow serving responses, canary being offline).

Full marks: covers both stages in the right order, includes BOTH technical and quality/business guardrails, a staged canary ramp with bake time and control cohort, concrete rollback triggers, and explicitly answers the 'what shadow cannot tell you' ask. Partial credit if one of these elements (e.g. quality metrics, or the shadow-limitation answer) is missing.

Full marks: justifies WHY shadow precedes canary (de-risk stability/latency/cost with zero user exposure, then measure real impact), ties metric choices to this triage system, and explains why shadow's discarded output caps what it can validate. Lower marks for an unjustified checklist of steps.

Full marks: clear staged structure, correct use of terms (shadow/traffic mirroring, canary, guardrail metric, bake time, sticky sessions, rollback), and unambiguous thresholds/triggers. Lower marks for muddled ordering or vague, hand-wavy metrics.

common_pitfalls: Conflates the two techniques - describes shadow as serving v2 to a subset of users, or thinks canary runs offline without real user exposure.
Claims shadow mode can validate user-facing or business quality (e.g. reply acceptance, resolution rate), when users never see v2's output so that signal is impossible from shadow alone.

Forgets that shadow duplicates side effects - fails to stub the drafted reply so it double-sends emails, double-writes to the DB, or double-charges the LLM API, and ignores the doubled inference cost.
Proposes rollback by rebuilding/redeploying v1 instead of an instant flag flip to a warm instance, or never keeps v1 warm, making recovery slow.
Lists only technical guardrails (latency, errors) with no quality/business metrics, or gives metrics with no concrete thresholds, bake time, or automated-rollback wiring.
Ignores sticky sessions and sample-size/significance in the canary, so users flip between v1 and v2 or conclusions are drawn from too little traffic.

open.question: You operate a deployed text-classification model (support-ticket routing) in production. Ground-truth labels arrive with an unavoidable ~30-day delay (they come from downstream human resolution). Your input monitoring computes the Population Stability Index (PSI) per feature against a fixed reference window, alarming at the conventional 0.2 threshold. This week three of your input features tripped 0.2, and product reports the model 'feels worse' — but you have no fresh labels to confirm. Write a design-review response that (a) states precisely what a PSI trip on input features does and does NOT tell you about model quality, distinguishing the kinds of drift involved; (b) explains how you would determine whether model quality has ACTUALLY degraded despite the 30-day label delay; and (c) explains how you would control false alarms and root-cause the signal before taking action. Name the specific statistical tests, methods, and tooling you would use and justify each choice.
open.answer_format: A structured written design-review answer, roughly 250-400 words, ideally organized around the three parts (a/b/c). Should name concrete methods/tools and justify them, not just list terms.
open.reference_answer:
The core error to avoid is equating input drift with quality loss. Three distinct shifts matter: covariate/data drift (P(X) changes), label/prior drift (P(Y) changes), and concept drift (P(Y|X) changes — the input→label mapping itself moves). PSI measures only P(X): it bins a reference and current window and sums (curr%-ref%)*ln(curr%/ref%) per bin, with >0.1 a moderate and >0.2 a large shift by convention. So a trip tells me a feature distribution moved — not that accuracy dropped. A robust model can absorb input drift with no quality loss, and pure concept drift can crater accuracy with zero input drift, so PSI is neither sufficient nor necessary evidence of degradation. PSI is also univariate (misses correlation/interaction shifts), binning- and threshold-heuristic, and with many features monitored the odds at least one trips by chance are high.

Because labels lag 30 days I cannot compute live accuracy/F1, so I add label-free signals: the model's output-score distribution and predicted class-prior, confidence and calibration drift (e.g. reliability/ECE over time), and embedding-level drift via the KS test, Jensen-Shannon divergence, or MMD on representations. For an actual quality estimate before labels land I would use confidence-based performance estimation (e.g. NannyML CBPE, or DLE) and buy fast partial ground truth — human-label a stratified sample of the drifted slice, or route a canary. When the delayed labels arrive I backfill true accuracy on the drifted cohorts and confirm the drop is statistically and practically significant.

To control false alarms I fix a clean, representative reference window, require the shift to persist across several consecutive windows rather than firing on one spike, apply multiple-comparison control (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR or Bonferroni) across features, account for known seasonality, and slice by segment instead of a single global alarm. For streaming I would consider ADWIN/DDM/Page-Hinkley. Root-cause discipline comes before action: rule out upstream pipeline/schema/feature-encoding changes (the most common false 'drift') before concluding a genuine population shift, then choose remediation — retrain, rollback, prompt/feature fix, or no-op. Reflexively retraining on an input-PSI alarm alone is the anti-pattern. Tools: Evidently or NannyML for drift/performance-estimation reporting, wired to alerting.
expected_answer_points: Distinguishes covariate/data drift (P(X)) from concept drift (P(Y|X)) and label/prior drift (P(Y)), and states PSI on inputs detects only P(X) — which is neither sufficient nor necessary for quality degradation (robust models absorb input drift; concept drift degrades quality with no input drift).

Explains PSI mechanics correctly (binned reference-vs-current comparison, ~0.1 moderate / ~0.2 large heuristic thresholds) and its limitations: univariate/ignores feature correlations, binning- and threshold-sensitive, and inflated false-alarm rate when many features are monitored.

Recognizes the 30-day label delay means live accuracy/F1 cannot be measured, so proposes label-free/proxy signals: output-score distribution and predicted class-prior shift, confidence/calibration drift, and embedding-level drift via KS test, Jensen-Shannon divergence, or MMD.

Proposes a label-free performance estimate (e.g. confidence-based performance estimation / NannyML CBPE or DLE) and/or fast partial ground truth via human-labeling a stratified sample of the drifted slice or a canary, to estimate quality before the delayed labels arrive.

Controls false alarms: clean reference window, require sustained/persistent shift over multiple windows (not a single spike), apply multiple-comparison correction (FDR/Bonferroni), account for seasonality, and slice by segment rather than one global alarm.
Closes the loop with the delayed labels: backfill true accuracy on drifted cohorts and confirm statistical and practical significance / business impact before acting.

Applies root-cause discipline: rule out upstream pipeline/schema/feature-encoding changes before concluding genuine population shift, and choose remediation (retrain, rollback, fix, or no-op) accordingly rather than reflexively retraining on an input-drift alarm.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly and precisely uses drift taxonomy (covariate P(X) vs concept P(Y|X) vs label/prior P(Y)); accurately describes what PSI measures and its 0.1/0.2 heuristic and limitations; and names valid label-free methods (KS/JS/MMD, confidence-based performance estimation, calibration) without technical errors such as claiming PSI detects concept drift or that accuracy can be computed live.

Covers all three requested parts — (a) what PSI does/doesn't imply, (b) determining real degradation under the label delay, (c) false-alarm control and root-causing — and includes the label-free estimation path, the delayed-label backfill/confirmation, and remediation decisioning rather than stopping at drift detection.

Justifies why input drift is not equivalent to degradation, why each chosen signal/test is appropriate given no fresh labels, and why false-alarm controls (persistence, FDR, seasonality, segmentation) and root-cause checks are needed before retraining; trade-offs are argued, not merely asserted.

Reads as a clear, well-organized design-review response with correct terminology used naturally; a reviewer can act on it. Structure around the three parts and concrete named tools/methods aids clarity.

common_pitfalls: Treats the PSI trip as equivalent to model degradation and recommends immediate retraining without any evidence accuracy actually dropped.
Assumes accuracy/F1 can be measured on current traffic, ignoring the 30-day label delay, and proposes computing supervised metrics on data that has no labels yet.
Only monitors inputs and never the model's output-score distribution, predicted-prior, or confidence/calibration — missing pure concept drift that leaves P(X) unchanged.
Confuses concept drift with covariate drift, or claims PSI (an input-distribution metric) can detect concept drift or a P(Y|X) change.

Ignores the multiple-comparisons/false-alarm problem: treats a single PSI spike on one of many features as conclusive, with no persistence requirement, FDR/Bonferroni correction, or seasonality check.
Skips root-causing — never checks for upstream pipeline/schema/feature-encoding changes that masquerade as 'drift' before concluding a genuine population shift.

open.question: You maintain a RAG agent whose steps are: embed the user query, vector-search Qdrant, build a prompt, call the LLM, optionally call a tool, then make a final LLM call. Today the service emits a single application log line per request that records only the final answer. Users report that some answers are wrong and that some requests take 8+ seconds, but from the logs you cannot tell which step is responsible. You are asked to add LLM/agent tracing (using something like LangSmith, Langfuse, or the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions). Explain how a trace-based approach differs from your current flat logging, describe how you would structure the trace and its spans for one request, and specify what you would capture on each span so you can diagnose BOTH the correctness problem and the latency problem. Justify your choices.
open.answer_format: A short written explanation (~180-260 words). Contrast tracing with flat logs, sketch the span hierarchy for one request, and give a per-span list of what to capture, tied back to diagnosing correctness vs latency.
open.reference_answer:
Flat logging gives one line per request; tracing gives one trace per request built from nested, individually-timed spans, so you can view the request as a waterfall and localize the failing or slow step instead of guessing.

Structure: a root span for the whole request carries a trace_id, with child spans for each step -- embed_query, vector_search, prompt_build, llm_call_1, tool_call, llm_call_2. Each span records start/end (duration), status, and its parent span_id, so the tree reconstructs the exact execution path. The trace context propagates across async boundaries and any service hops so spans stitch into one request.

Per-span capture:
- All spans: name, duration, status (ok/error), recorded exceptions, and attributes like request id, user id, and model/version.
- Retrieval span: the query plus returned doc ids, similarity scores, and count -- this exposes correctness failures from bad retrieval.
- LLM spans: model name, parameters (temperature, max_tokens), the rendered prompt/messages, the completion, and token usage (prompt/completion) plus cost.
- Tool span: tool name, arguments, and result or error.

Diagnosis: the span durations in the waterfall reveal which step eats the 8s (e.g. vector_search vs generation); the captured inputs/outputs on the retrieval and LLM spans reveal why an answer was wrong -- irrelevant retrieved docs, a malformed prompt, or a model error. Export spans asynchronously to a tracing backend (LangSmith/Langfuse or an OTel collector), sample to bound overhead, and redact PII in prompts/outputs before export.
expected_answer_points: A trace represents one end-to-end request and is composed of nested spans (one per step) that are individually timed, versus a single flat log line -- so per-step latency and structure become visible
Spans are correlated via a shared trace_id and parent span_id (context propagation across steps/async/service boundaries), letting you reconstruct the full request tree/waterfall

Capture inputs and outputs per span -- retrieval: query plus returned doc ids/scores/count; LLM: rendered prompt/messages and the completion -- which is what lets you diagnose WHY an answer was wrong (bad retrieval vs bad prompt vs model)
Capture timing/duration on every span, plus token usage/cost on LLM spans, to isolate the source of the 8s latency
Capture status and errors/exceptions plus metadata attributes (request id, user id, model name/version, temperature/params) on spans
Name a concrete standard/tool and export path -- LangSmith, Langfuse, or OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions to a collector -- that renders a span waterfall UI
Address overhead/safety: asynchronous export and/or sampling to limit latency impact, and redaction of PII in captured prompts/outputs

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly describes the trace/span model: a per-request trace, nested spans per step timed independently, trace_id/parent span_id correlation and context propagation, and accurate per-span attributes (durations, inputs/outputs, token usage, status/errors). Full marks require no incorrect claims (e.g. does not conflate tracing with aggregate metrics or with merely more verbose logs) and correct use of terms like span, trace, and attribute.

Covers both diagnostic goals: captures per-span timing/tokens for the latency problem AND per-span inputs/outputs (retrieval docs+scores, prompt, completion) for the correctness problem, plus status/errors and metadata. Full marks also mention a concrete backend/standard and the export/overhead consideration (async export or sampling).

Explicitly ties each captured field to what it lets you diagnose -- e.g. span durations localize the 8s, retrieved doc scores vs prompt vs completion distinguish a retrieval failure from a prompt or model failure -- rather than listing fields without connecting them to the two reported problems.
Explanation is well organized (clear tracing-vs-logging contrast, a legible span hierarchy, and a structured per-span capture list), uses correct vocabulary, and stays within a focused length.

common_pitfalls: Proposes just adding more or more verbose log lines (e.g. a log per step) instead of a hierarchical trace with correlated parent/child spans, so the answer never gains the structure that localizes the failing step
Captures only latency/durations and omits per-span inputs/outputs, so the slow step can be found but the wrong-answer cause cannot (or vice versa -- captures prompts but no timing)
Confuses tracing with aggregate metrics/dashboards (Prometheus counters, average latency), which cannot drill into a single bad request
Forgets trace_id/span_id correlation and context propagation, so spans cannot be stitched into one request across the tool call or async boundaries
Dumps full prompts/completions with no mention of PII redaction, cost/volume, or that export/sampling has overhead -- or claims tracing every request is free
Answers with an unrelated fix (set temperature=0, switch models, add retries) instead of adding observability

open.question: Your company ships a RAG-powered support assistant. Two teams deploy independently: Team A owns the orchestrator (a FastAPI backend that receives a user turn, retrieves context, and assembles the prompt), and Team B owns an internal generation service that wraps a hosted LLM and returns the answer. Today the two are coupled through a shared Python module and a shared database table, so any change to generation forces a lock-step deploy and a failure in one cascades into the other. In a design review you've been asked to define a proper service contract between the orchestrator and the generation service. Generation latency is typically 3-30s, calls are billed per token, and output is non-deterministic. Describe the contract you would propose and justify the key decisions: what the interface is, how requests, responses, and errors are shaped, how the two teams can evolve it without breaking each other, and how the contract copes with slow, expensive, non-deterministic LLM calls.
open.answer_format: A written design description, roughly 250-350 words (a short schema sketch is welcome but not required). It should name the interface mechanism, describe the request/response and error shapes, explain the evolution/versioning strategy, and address the LLM-specific realities (latency, cost, non-determinism) with justification for each major choice.
open.reference_answer:
Replace the shared module and table with an explicit network interface owned by a single versioned schema. I'd define an OpenAPI (or protobuf) spec as the source of truth and generate typed clients/stubs from it, so neither team reads the other's code or DB. That alone is the point of a service contract: it lets the two services deploy independently behind a stable boundary.

Interface and semantics: given 3-30s latency, a plain blocking request risks cascading timeouts and holds connections open, so I'd offer streaming (SSE / chunked responses) for the interactive path and/or an async submit-and-poll pattern (POST returns 202 + a job id, GET polls status) for batch. Requests carry only stable, provider-agnostic fields: assembled prompt or messages, max_tokens, a stop condition, a caller-supplied request_id, and an Idempotency-Key. The response carries the text (or stream), a finish_reason, token/usage counts for cost attribution, and the resolved model/version for observability. Crucially, vendor-specific knobs and the actual model choice stay hidden behind the contract so Team B can swap providers without breaking Team A — that is the component boundary.

Error contract: separate transport failures from a stable, typed domain-error envelope (e.g. code, message, retryable flag, request_id). Map to sane HTTP: 400/422 for bad input (non-retryable), 429/503 for rate-limit/overload (retryable with backoff), 504 for upstream timeout. Because retries on a non-idempotent, billed call would double-generate and double-charge, the Idempotency-Key lets the server dedupe.

Evolution: additive, backward-compatible changes only; breaking changes require a new version (URL or header) run side-by-side. Enforce with consumer-driven contract tests (e.g. Pact) in CI and a tolerant-reader posture (ignore unknown fields). Finally, bake non-functional terms into the contract: auth (scoped token/mTLS), latency and availability SLOs, rate limits, max payload/token budgets, and timeout expectations, so both teams share explicit, testable expectations.
expected_answer_points: Replace the shared module/DB with an explicit network interface governed by a single versioned schema (OpenAPI/protobuf/JSON Schema) as the source of truth, enabling independent deploys
Choose an interaction style suited to 3-30s latency: streaming (SSE/chunked) and/or async submit-and-poll (202 + job id) rather than a naive long blocking call, with explicit timeouts
Define a stable, typed error contract that separates transport errors from domain errors and distinguishes retryable (429/503/504) from non-retryable (400/422), carrying a request_id for tracing
Require idempotency keys so network retries of expensive, billed, non-deterministic calls do not double-generate or double-charge

Keep the contract provider-agnostic: hide vendor-specific params and the actual model choice behind stable fields so the generation team can swap models/providers without breaking the orchestrator (clean component boundary)
Evolve compatibly: additive-only changes, version bump for breaking changes, tolerant-reader behavior, and consumer-driven contract tests (e.g. Pact) enforced in CI
Include non-functional terms in the contract: auth (scoped token/mTLS), SLOs (latency/availability), rate limits, payload/token budgets, and usage/token counts returned for cost attribution

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: every mechanism named is used correctly — a schema-defined network interface as source of truth, an appropriate sync-streaming/async pattern for long latency, correct HTTP/error semantics with retryable vs non-retryable distinction, idempotency keys for safe retries, provider-agnostic fields, and compatible versioning. Deduct for technical errors such as retrying non-idempotent 4xx, claiming a blocking call is fine at 30s, or conflating transport status with domain errors.

Full marks: covers all four asked dimensions — the interface mechanism, request/response+error shaping, an evolution/versioning strategy, and the LLM realities (latency, cost/billing, non-determinism) — plus at least some non-functional terms (auth, SLOs, rate/token limits). Partial credit as dimensions are missing; omitting error contract, versioning, or idempotency each drops a point.

Full marks: each major choice is justified by the scenario's constraints — e.g. streaming/async chosen because of 3-30s latency and cascading-timeout risk, idempotency chosen because calls are billed and retried, provider-agnostic fields chosen to preserve the component boundary and independent deploys. Lower marks for asserting choices without tying them to the decoupling/latency/cost pressures.

Full marks: a well-organized answer that a design-review audience could act on — clearly separates interface, payload/error shape, evolution, and LLM concerns, uses precise vocabulary (contract, idempotency, backward-compatible, SLO, tolerant reader), and reads as a coherent proposal rather than a scattered list. Deduct for disorganized, vague, or jargon-without-meaning writing.

common_pitfalls: Describes only the happy-path request/response JSON and omits the error contract, versioning strategy, and non-functional terms — treating a data shape as if it were a full service contract
Proposes a single synchronous blocking call for a 3-30s generation with no streaming, async, or timeout strategy, ignoring cascading-timeout and held-connection risks
Conflates transport-level HTTP status with the domain error envelope, or recommends blanket retries that would retry non-retryable 4xx and double-generate/double-bill on a non-idempotent call
Bakes provider-specific fields or the concrete model name into the contract, leaking the implementation and recoupling the orchestrator to the generation team's internals
Keeps a shared library or shared database table (or introduces a shared schema-owning DB) as the 'contract,' which defeats independent deployability
Ignores versioning/compatibility, so any field change is a breaking change requiring a lock-step deploy — the exact problem the review is trying to fix — with no contract tests to catch drift
open.prompt: Your company ships a RAG-powered support assistant. Two teams deploy independently: Team A owns the orchestrator (a FastAPI backend that receives a user turn, retrieves context, and assembles the prompt), and Team B owns an internal generation service that wraps a hosted LLM and returns the answer. Today the two are coupled through a shared Python module and a shared database table, so any change to generation forces a lock-step deploy and a failure in one cascades into the other. In a design review you've been asked to define a proper service contract between the orchestrator and the generation service. Generation latency is typically 3-30s, calls are billed per token, and output is non-deterministic. Describe the contract you would propose and justify the key decisions: what the interface is, how requests, responses, and errors are shaped, how the two teams can evolve it without breaking each other, and how the contract copes with slow, expensive, non-deterministic LLM calls.

open.question:
You've inherited a production LLM agent service, `assistant-api`. Every request carries a `session_id`. Each worker keeps, in a process-local Python dict, the running conversation transcript, the agent's tool-call scratchpad, and a cached vector-retriever handle. Today it runs as a single container. Traffic has grown and you're asked to run N replicas behind an L7 load balancer with autoscaling, survive rolling deploys and crashes without dropping conversations, and keep the existing behaviour where some responses stream tokens over SSE for up to 90 seconds.

Write a design-review analysis that: (1) explains precisely why the current design breaks once you run multiple replicas and do rolling deploys; (2) redesigns the request tier to be stateless — what state moves out, where each kind belongs, and why; (3) addresses the SSE streaming and in-flight tool-execution wrinkle, which resists a naive stateless treatment; and (4) states the key trade-offs your design introduces and how you mitigate them. Assume common infrastructure (Redis, Postgres, Kubernetes) is available.
open.answer_format: A written design-review analysis, roughly 300-450 words (prose or structured bullet sections), that addresses all four asks: the failure diagnosis, the stateless redesign with a clear state taxonomy and store choice, the streaming/in-flight-tool wrinkle, and the trade-offs with concrete mitigations.
open.reference_answer:
1) Why it breaks. State lives in a process-local dict, so it is bound to one replica's memory. With N replicas behind an L7 load balancer doing round-robin/least-conn routing, a session's follow-up request usually lands on a replica that never saw the first turn — the transcript/scratchpad lookup misses and the conversation is lost. The dict is also volatile: a rolling deploy, crash, OOM, or autoscaler scale-in terminates the container and every in-flight transcript with it. There is no durability and no shared view. Sticky sessions are not the fix: pinning a session_id to a replica (cookie/consistent-hash affinity) makes each replica stateful — load skews toward hot instances, autoscaling can't rebalance, and when that replica is drained or dies its pinned sessions are still lost.

2) Stateless redesign. Separate authoritative from rebuildable state. The transcript and agent scratchpad are authoritative — externalize them to a shared low-latency store keyed by session_id: Redis for hot state, optionally write-through to a durable DB (Postgres) if losing a conversation is unacceptable. Each request becomes load(session_id) → run turn → persist, so any replica is fungible and the LB needs no affinity. The retriever handle, model/HTTP client, and connection pools are derived and rebuildable — a cache, not source of truth — so they legitimately stay per-process. The principle: statelessness doesn't eliminate state, it relocates it to a purpose-built data tier and makes the compute tier interchangeable. Concurrency: two requests for one session can race read-modify-write on the transcript; since a conversation is sequential, serialize per session (per-session lock or optimistic-concurrency version/CAS) and use an idempotency key so a client retry after a timeout doesn't append a turn twice or re-run a tool.

3) Streaming / in-flight tools. An SSE response is a live TCP connection pinned to one socket on one replica for up to 90s; you cannot transparently migrate it, so 'stateless' applies to session state, not the transport. Handle deploys with graceful shutdown / connection draining: on SIGTERM stop accepting new work and let in-flight streams finish within a drain timeout (preStop hook, PodDisruptionBudget) before the pod exits. Checkpoint incrementally — persist the partial assistant message and tool results as they're produced — so if a connection still drops the client reconnects (SSE Last-Event-ID) and resumes/replays from the last checkpoint instead of losing the turn. Side-effecting tool calls must be idempotent or recorded as a step/run so a retry doesn't double-execute; for very long agent runs, prefer an async job + status-poll/webhook pattern over holding a synchronous request.

4) Trade-offs. (a) Latency: every request now pays a store round-trip — mitigate with a co-located in-region Redis, connection pooling, compact state (a rolling token window, not full history), and a short-TTL read-through cache. (b) Consistency vs throughput: per-session serialization prevents lost updates but serializes that session — acceptable because concurrent same-session requests are rare. (c) Durability vs cost: Redis alone is volatile; pairing with a durable DB costs money and write latency — choose by how catastrophic a lost conversation is. (d) New failure domain: the store must be HA and the app should degrade gracefully if it's briefly unavailable.
expected_answer_points: Diagnoses that process-local state means a follow-up request the LB routes to a different replica loses the conversation, and that rolling deploys/crashes/scale-in destroy volatile in-memory state (no durability, no shared view).

Explains that sticky sessions / session affinity are not a real fix — they re-introduce statefulness, cause load imbalance, block autoscaler rebalancing, and still lose state when the pinned replica is drained or dies.

Externalizes the authoritative session state (transcript + agent scratchpad) to a shared low-latency store keyed by session_id (e.g. Redis, optionally write-through to a durable DB) with a load→run→persist per-request flow, making the compute tier fungible/stateless.

Distinguishes authoritative session state from rebuildable per-process caches (retriever handle, model/HTTP client, connection pools) that legitimately stay local, and frames statelessness as relocating state rather than eliminating it.

Handles concurrent same-session read-modify-write races via per-session serialization or optimistic concurrency (versioning/CAS) plus idempotency keys for retried requests, to avoid lost updates or duplicated turns/tool runs.

Recognizes an SSE stream / in-flight tool run is pinned to one replica and cannot be migrated, and handles deploys with connection draining / graceful shutdown (SIGTERM, preStop, drain timeout) plus incremental checkpointing so a dropped stream can resume/replay (Last-Event-ID) without re-executing side-effecting tools.
Names concrete trade-offs — per-request store round-trip latency, consistency vs throughput of session locking, durability vs cost, and the new failure domain — each with a specific mitigation.

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly explains why process-local state fails under LB routing, rolling deploys, and scale-in; accurately externalizes authoritative session state to a shared store while keeping rebuildable caches local; correctly handles same-session concurrency (locking/CAS/idempotency) and the pinned-connection nature of SSE streams (draining + checkpoint resume). Full marks require no false claims — e.g. calling sticky sessions 'stateless', asserting a live stream can migrate, or treating a rebuildable cache as authoritative state.

Addresses all four asks: failure diagnosis (routing + durability), stateless redesign with a state taxonomy and store choice, the streaming/in-flight-tool wrinkle with drain + resume, and concrete trade-offs with mitigations. Full marks require the streaming/tool-idempotency nuance and the concurrency handling, not merely 'put the transcript in Redis'.

Justifies each choice by mechanism rather than assertion — why round-robin loses state, why affinity is a poor fix, why per-session serialization is cheap here, why a live stream can't be migrated, why a rebuildable handle need not be externalized — and weighs alternatives (e.g. async job vs synchronous stream) instead of naming one tool.

Reads as an organized design review with a clear authoritative-vs-rebuildable state taxonomy and precise vocabulary (statelessness, session affinity, connection draining, optimistic concurrency/CAS, idempotency, checkpoint/resume), so a reviewer can follow the argument without inferring missing links.

common_pitfalls: Proposes sticky sessions / session affinity as the solution and calls the result stateless, missing that it imbalances load, blocks autoscaling, and still loses state when the pinned replica is drained or crashes.

Moves everything — including rebuildable caches like the retriever handle, model client, and connection pools — into the shared store, treating a cache as authoritative state and adding round-trip latency for zero durability benefit.

Ignores concurrency: assumes one request per session at a time and appends to the shared transcript with no lock, versioning, or idempotency key, allowing lost updates or duplicated turns/tool executions on client retries.

Claims externalizing state makes SSE streaming stateless or that a live stream can be moved to any replica, ignoring that the connection is pinned to one socket and needs connection draining plus checkpoint-resume.
Treats 'stateless' as an absolute goal and tries to eliminate all state, rather than relocating it to a durable/shared data tier while keeping compute replicas interchangeable.

Hand-waves the trade-offs — says 'just use Redis' without acknowledging the added per-request latency, the durability-vs-cost choice, or that the store is a new failure domain that needs HA and graceful degradation.

open.question:
You are the first engineer at an early-stage startup adding an AI feature that summarizes incoming customer-support tickets. You must decide between two options: (a) BUY — call a hosted, managed LLM API (e.g. Anthropic/OpenAI) and pay per token, or (b) BUILD — self-host an open-weight model (e.g. a Llama/Mistral variant) on your own GPU infrastructure. Today the feature would see only a few hundred requests per day, but the founders expect usage to grow if the product succeeds, and product-market fit is not yet proven.

Walk through how you would make this build-versus-buy decision. Compare the two options across the dimensions that actually matter here, state which one you would ship for the MVP, justify it, and name at least one concrete signal that would later make you switch to the other option.
open.answer_format: A short written recommendation with justification, roughly 150-250 words: a brief comparison across the key dimensions, a clear MVP choice, the reasoning behind it, and at least one concrete 'switch' trigger. Prose or a short structured list are both fine.
open.reference_answer:
For an unproven MVP at a few hundred requests/day, I would BUY: use a hosted LLM API for the summarization feature.

The dimensions that matter here are engineering effort / time-to-market, cost structure, quality, and control. A hosted API needs almost no infrastructure work — no GPU provisioning, autoscaling, batching, or on-call — so we ship in days and validate whether users even want the feature. Its cost is variable (pay-per-token) and scales with usage, which is ideal when volume is low and uncertain: at a few hundred requests/day the bill is tiny, whereas self-hosting means paying for GPUs that mostly sit idle, plus the ongoing ops/MLOps burden. A frontier managed model also gives strong summary quality out of the box, while a small open-weight model may need prompt tuning, evaluation, and possibly fine-tuning to match it.

Build wins later, not now. The two costs cross over: API cost grows roughly linearly with volume, self-hosting is mostly fixed, so above some sustained, steady volume the amortized infra becomes cheaper. Other pulls toward build are hard data-residency/compliance requirements, vendor lock-in, rate limits, or a need for a specialized fine-tuned model.

So: ship on the API behind a thin provider-agnostic interface and an eval harness. I would revisit build when sustained volume makes the monthly API bill clearly exceed amortized GPU + engineering cost, or if a compliance requirement forbids sending ticket data to a third party.
expected_answer_points: Recommends BUY (hosted API) for the low-volume, unproven MVP, and gives a clear recommendation rather than hedging
Argues time-to-market / low engineering effort: a hosted API removes GPU provisioning, scaling, batching, and ops/on-call, so the team ships fast and validates product-market fit before investing
Contrasts cost structures: API is variable pay-per-token that scales with usage (cheap at low volume), while self-hosting is largely fixed cost with GPUs idle at a few hundred requests/day
Notes a cost break-even / crossover: because variable API cost grows with volume and self-hosting is mostly fixed, build becomes cheaper only above some sustained, steady volume
Addresses quality/effort: a managed frontier model gives strong summaries out of the box, whereas a small open-weight model may need eval, prompt tuning, or fine-tuning to match
Identifies non-cost factors that can pull toward build: data residency/privacy/compliance, vendor lock-in, rate limits, model deprecation, or need for a custom fine-tuned model
Recommends keeping the decision reversible — a provider-agnostic abstraction layer and an eval harness — so switching later is cheap
Names a concrete switch trigger, e.g. sustained volume where the amortized self-host cost undercuts the API bill, or a compliance rule barring sending ticket data to a third party

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly characterizes buy as low-fixed-cost, variable, fast-to-ship with strong out-of-the-box quality, and build as high-fixed-cost infra that only amortizes at sustained high volume; the cost, latency, effort, and control claims are all true. Deduct for factual errors such as treating open-weight models as 'free', claiming self-hosting is automatically cheaper or faster, or misstating how the cost structures scale.

Full marks: covers effort/time-to-market, cost structure (variable vs fixed + break-even), quality, and at least one control/compliance factor, AND supplies a concrete switch trigger. Deduct for each major dimension omitted or for giving no reconsideration signal.

Full marks: ties the recommendation explicitly to the scenario's specifics — low, uncertain volume and unproven PMF — and reasons about the volume-dependent crossover rather than asserting a blanket preference. Deduct if the choice is stated without justification or ignores the given context.

Full marks: a well-organized, senior-register answer with a clear decision up front and clean use of the real vocabulary (variable vs fixed cost, break-even, time-to-market, vendor lock-in). Deduct for rambling, contradictory recommendations, or vague hand-waving.

common_pitfalls: Assumes self-hosting is cheap or free because open-weight model licenses cost nothing, ignoring GPU provisioning, idle capacity, and ongoing ops/MLOps cost
Chooses BUILD to 'save money' at low volume without recognizing that variable API cost is tiny at a few hundred requests/day and that build only pays off above a break-even volume
Treats the decision as purely about per-token price and never weighs engineering effort, time-to-market, quality, or the fact that PMF is unproven
Recommends build for 'data privacy' reflexively without noting that hosted providers offer enterprise/no-training data terms, or without checking whether the MVP actually has a compliance requirement
Gives no concrete switch trigger, or an unmeasurable one, so the decision is not revisitable
Hedges with no clear recommendation, or recommends build and buy simultaneously without resolving the trade-off

items.sub_competency: C10.4 · System quality attributes & failure analysis

open.question:
You are in a design review for a production customer-support tool. Its `POST /assist` endpoint synchronously (a) retrieves passages from a vector DB and (b) calls a hosted LLM API to synthesize an answer. The LLM call has p50 ~800ms but its p99 can spike above 30s when the provider is degraded. Current design: a 60s server-side request timeout; on any LLM error the client retries 3 times immediately; and every endpoint in the service is served from one shared worker pool. During last week's provider slowdown, the WHOLE service went down — even endpoints that never call the LLM started returning 503s. A teammate proposes the fix: ‘add two more retries and raise the timeout to 120s so slow calls have time to finish.’

Do a failure-mode analysis. Explain the mechanism by which one degraded dependency took down the entire service, say why the teammate's proposal makes it worse, and design the changes that would contain the blast radius to the `/assist` feature. Be specific about timeouts, retry policy, resource isolation, and degradation behavior, and note the key trade-offs.
open.answer_format: A short design-review write-up (~250–400 words): first a diagnosis of the cascading-failure mechanism, then a prioritized set of mitigations, each tied to its effect on availability/blast radius and its trade-offs. Enumerated points are fine.
open.reference_answer:
The provider outage is the trigger, but the real defect is that one slow dependency is allowed to consume resources shared by the whole service — a classic cascading failure.

Mechanism: when LLM p99 latency spikes, each `/assist` request holds its worker (thread/async task) and upstream connection until the 60s timeout. The ‘retry 3x immediately’ turns one slow request into up to four sequential slow calls AND adds a retry storm that further overloads the already-degraded provider. Because all endpoints share one worker pool, these long-held workers exhaust the pool; requests to unrelated endpoints can't acquire a worker and 503. That is head-of-line blocking / resource-pool exhaustion through a shared bulkhead.

Why the proposal is wrong: raising the timeout to 120s makes each stuck worker hold longer, so the pool saturates faster and stays saturated longer; two more retries multiply load on the failing provider and burn more worker-time. Both amplify the exact mechanism that caused the outage; neither addresses the shared-resource coupling.

Fixes (prioritized):
1. SLO-aligned timeouts. Replace 60s with a per-attempt timeout near the acceptable p99 (single-digit seconds) plus an overall deadline, so a hung call fails fast and releases the worker.
2. Disciplined retries. Retry only retryable failures (timeouts, 429, 5xx) with exponential backoff + jitter, a small cap (1–2), honoring `Retry-After`, governed by a retry budget so retries can't multiply load during an incident.
3. Bulkhead isolation. Give the LLM path its own bounded concurrency limit / thread pool / connection pool so its saturation cannot starve endpoints that don't call the LLM — this caps the blast radius to `/assist`.
4. Circuit breaker. Trip on sustained errors/latency and fail fast (with half-open probes to recover) instead of queuing doomed calls against a dead provider.
5. Graceful degradation. Make the feature fail-open: on LLM failure return retrieval results without synthesis, a cached/templated answer, or an explicit ‘AI temporarily unavailable’ state, so the product keeps working.
6. Detection & shedding. Monitor per-dependency latency/error rate and pool saturation against SLOs/error budgets; add load shedding, and consider moving generation off the request path (queue + `202` + poll) if latency can't be bounded.

Trade-off: fail-open preserves availability but can serve lower-quality answers; tight timeouts may abort some slow-but-valid calls. The net principle is: isolate the dependency, fail fast, degrade gracefully, and make retries safe — so a provider incident degrades one feature instead of the whole service.
expected_answer_points: Identifies the mechanism as a cascading failure: slow LLM calls hold workers/connections until the long timeout, and because all endpoints share one worker pool, the pool is exhausted and unrelated endpoints starve (head-of-line blocking / resource exhaustion)
Explains that immediate 3x retries amplify the failure — they multiply load on the degraded provider (retry storm) and multiply worker-hold time per request

Argues the teammate's fix is counterproductive: raising the timeout makes stuck workers hold longer (saturating the pool faster), and more retries add more load — both amplify the root cause without touching the shared-resource coupling
Recommends tight, SLO/p99-aligned timeouts (plus an overall deadline) so hung calls fail fast and release workers
Recommends a disciplined retry policy: retry only retryable errors, with exponential backoff + jitter, a small cap, honoring Retry-After, and/or a retry budget
Recommends bulkhead/isolation — a separate bounded pool or concurrency limit for the LLM path so its saturation cannot starve non-LLM endpoints, capping the blast radius
Recommends a circuit breaker that fails fast on sustained errors/latency (with half-open recovery) instead of piling up calls against a down dependency

Recommends graceful degradation / fail-open behavior (retrieval-only answer, cached/templated response, or explicit 'AI unavailable' state) and names a trade-off (e.g. availability vs answer quality, fail-open vs fail-closed)

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly explains the cascading-failure mechanism (shared worker/connection-pool exhaustion, head-of-line blocking) and the amplifying role of naive retries and the oversized timeout, and applies each mitigation with correct semantics: SLO-aligned timeouts, backoff+jitter/retry-budget retries, bulkhead isolation, circuit breaker, and graceful degradation. No technically wrong claims (e.g. that adding workers or raising the timeout resolves the coupling).

Delivers both a diagnosis (why one dependency downed the whole service) and mitigations spanning the required axes — timeout, retry policy, resource isolation, circuit breaking, and fallback/degradation — plus a critique of the teammate's proposal, rather than fixing only one dimension.

Ties each recommendation to its effect on blast radius/availability and surfaces trade-offs (e.g. fail-open vs fail-closed, availability vs answer quality, why more retries/longer timeouts worsen saturation), rather than listing resilience patterns without connecting them to the observed failure.

Reads as a coherent design-review narrative: states the failure mechanism first, then presents organized, prioritized mitigations using correct terminology (cascading failure, bulkhead, circuit breaker, backoff, graceful degradation).

common_pitfalls: Blames the LLM provider outage and stops there, without explaining the internal amplification (shared pool exhaustion + retry storm) that turned a dependency issue into a full-service outage
Endorses or only mildly tweaks the teammate's fix — treats it as a capacity problem to be solved by more workers, longer timeouts, or more retries, all of which worsen or merely delay pool saturation

Proposes retries without qualification: retrying on all errors (including non-retryable 4xx), with no backoff/jitter, no cap, and no retry budget — which produces a retry storm against a degraded provider
Adds a circuit breaker but no fallback, so users still get hard errors — confusing 'the service stays up' with 'the feature still does something useful' (missing graceful/fail-open degradation)
Omits resource isolation/bulkheading entirely, leaving the shared worker pool as a single point of coupling so any one slow dependency can still starve every endpoint
Sets a timeout but leaves it far larger than the SLO/p99, so hung calls still hold workers long enough to exhaust the pool

open.question: Your team shipped a research-assistant feature as a single ReAct agent wired to 25 tools (web search, several SQL connectors, a code sandbox, a summariser, a chart generator, etc.). In production it is degrading: it frequently picks the wrong tool, latency per request keeps climbing, the context window regularly fills before the task finishes, and evaluation is nearly impossible because every failure is buried in one long trajectory. A colleague proposes refactoring to a multi-agent orchestrator/worker topology (a lead agent that delegates to specialised sub-agents). You are the reviewer on this design. Assess the proposal: explain WHY the monolith is degrading, what an orchestrator/worker topology would and would NOT fix, the concrete context-passing contract you would require between the lead and the sub-agents, the cost/latency/reliability trade-offs the refactor introduces, and the specific conditions under which you would reject multi-agent in favour of a cheaper single-agent fix. Be concrete about mechanisms, not just labels.
open.answer_format: A structured written design assessment, roughly 350-550 words. Should contain: (1) a diagnosis of the monolith's failure mode, (2) a recommended topology and the specific benefit it delivers, (3) an explicit context-passing contract between lead and workers, (4) an honest cost/latency/reliability trade-off analysis, and (5) named conditions under which multi-agent is the wrong call plus the cheaper alternatives. Prose or headed sections both acceptable; must reason about mechanisms rather than assert that multi-agent is simply 'better'.
open.reference_answer:
Diagnosis first. The monolith degrades for two compounding, structural reasons, not because the code is untidy. (1) Decision-space blowup: all 25 tool descriptions live in the system prompt, so at every step the model must discriminate among 25 options — tool-selection accuracy falls and the prompt is large before any work begins. (2) Trajectory bloat: a single long thread accumulates every observation, so effective context grows unbounded, diluting attention, hurting instruction-following, and driving up both latency and token cost until the window fills. Evaluation is hard because there is exactly one opaque trajectory to attribute failures to.

Recommended topology: an orchestrator (supervisor)/worker pattern. A lead agent decomposes the request and delegates sub-tasks to specialised sub-agents — e.g. a search agent, a SQL agent, a writer — each with a scoped system prompt and a small, relevant subset of the 25 tools. The primary benefit is context isolation: each worker reasons over a narrow tool set and only its slice of context, which restores tool-choice accuracy and shortens trajectories, and each worker becomes independently evaluable. It does NOT, by itself, fix bad retrieval, ambiguous tool descriptions, or a genuinely sequential task.

Context-passing contract (this matters more than the box diagram). Each sub-agent receives only the slice it needs, and must return a condensed, structured result (a summary or artifact), not its raw transcript — otherwise the orchestrator's context re-bloats with every worker's full trace and you have recreated the monolith one level up. Large artifacts (tables, documents, images) are passed by reference/handle through a shared store or blackboard and only the handle is inlined. Do not broadcast the whole message history to every agent.

Trade-offs. Multi-agent is not free. Each hop re-reads instructions and context, and orchestration adds round-trips, so token spend multiplies — often several-fold (Anthropic reported ~15x versus a single chat for their research system). You only earn that back when sub-tasks are independent enough to run in parallel, cutting wall-clock latency; purely sequential delegation just adds latency and cost. Reliability compounds multiplicatively across hops (end-to-end success is roughly the product of per-step success rates), so the orchestrator must validate worker outputs, apply timeouts/retries, and contain a failing sub-agent rather than let a hallucinated or malformed result propagate downstream. You also now need per-agent plus end-to-end tracing and eval.

When to reject multi-agent. If the task is tightly coupled and stateful — later steps depend on earlier reasoning — agents coordinate badly because they share nothing implicitly and communicate only by messages, producing conflicting or duplicated work; here a single-threaded agent with context compression is the better call. And if the real failure is tool ambiguity or retrieval, cheaper fixes come first: sharper tool descriptions, grouping/namespacing tools, retrieving tools by relevance (tool-RAG), or a routing classifier inside one agent. Reach for multi-agent only when sub-tasks are genuinely separable, parallelisable, or require different context or policies.
expected_answer_points: Diagnoses the monolith's failure as structural: 25 tools enlarge the per-step tool-selection space (degrading tool choice and inflating the system prompt) AND the single long trajectory bloats the context window, diluting attention and raising latency/cost.

Recommends an orchestrator/supervisor-worker topology where a lead agent decomposes and delegates to specialised sub-agents, each scoped to a small relevant tool subset, and identifies context isolation (and per-agent evaluability) as the core benefit.

Specifies a context-passing contract: workers get only their relevant slice and return condensed structured results/artifacts (not raw transcripts); large artifacts passed by reference/handle via a shared store; no broadcasting of full message history.

Quantifies the cost/latency trade-off: multi-agent multiplies token usage because each hop re-reads context/instructions and adds round-trips (often several-fold, e.g. Anthropic's ~15x), and parallelism only helps wall-clock latency when sub-tasks are independent — sequential delegation adds latency.

Addresses reliability/failure isolation: end-to-end reliability compounds across hops, so the orchestrator must validate outputs, use timeouts/retries, and contain sub-agent failures so errors/hallucinations don't propagate downstream.

States explicit conditions to reject multi-agent: tightly coupled/stateful sequential tasks coordinate poorly through message passing (favouring a single-threaded agent with context compression), and tool-ambiguity/retrieval problems are better solved by cheaper fixes (better tool descriptions, tool grouping/namespacing, tool-RAG, or an intra-agent routing classifier).
Notes the added evaluation/observability burden: per-agent plus end-to-end tracing and eval are now required, and the system is harder to debug and more non-deterministic.

No false claims (e.g. that multi-agent is inherently cheaper, that agents share state implicitly, or that parallelism always cuts latency). Deduct for each mechanism that is vague, mislabelled, or wrong.

Full marks: covers all five required strands — diagnosis, recommended topology and its benefit, an explicit lead/worker context-passing contract, cost/latency/reliability trade-offs, and named conditions for rejecting multi-agent with cheaper alternatives. Full marks: recommendations are justified by mechanism and tied to the symptoms in the scenario (fills window -> isolate context; wrong-tool -> narrow tool sets), trade-offs are weighed rather than asserted, and the decision to split or not is contingent on task coupling/parallelisability rather than a blanket preference. Full marks: organised as a reviewable assessment, uses correct vocabulary (orchestrator/supervisor, worker/sub-agent, context isolation, blackboard/shared store, tool-RAG, ReAct) precisely, and is concise and unambiguous. common_pitfalls: Treats multi-agent as strictly better or 'more scalable' and ignores the token/latency multiplier and the new coordination failure modes it introduces.

open.question: Your team runs a production LLM assistant whose retrieval layer is a self-managed, single-node vector index (FAISS behind a Python service) holding ~200M embeddings. It is tightly coupled inside the monolithic inference service, and an ingestion pipeline continuously mutates the index (~5M upserts/deletes per day). Leadership wants you to (a) extract retrieval into its own horizontally-scalable service and (b) move the data onto a managed, clustered vector database (e.g. Qdrant/Milvus/Pinecone) — with zero user-facing downtime, no regression in retrieval quality, and a safe rollback path. Design the migration architecture. Be specific about: the migration pattern and topology; how you keep the old and new stores consistent while ingestion never stops; how you validate the new backend before it serves users; and how you detect and instantly roll back a quality regression.
open.answer_format: A structured design narrative (~350-550 words) organised into named phases (interface/abstraction, backfill + catch-up, shadow validation, progressive cutover, rollback/decommission). Name concrete mechanisms (dual-write vs event log, high-water mark, canary %, guardrail metrics) and justify the key trade-offs. A short prose topology sketch is welcome; a one-line 'flip DNS and pray' answer is not.
open.reference_answer:
Pattern & topology (strangler fig, one variable at a time). First reduce blast radius by decoupling the two changes. Introduce a stable retrieval interface (a facade/gateway) at the monolith's call site so callers don't know the backend. Extract retrieval behind that interface as its own service while it still talks to FAISS — this proves the service boundary with no data risk. Then make the store pluggable behind the same interface, with old (FAISS) and new (managed cluster) implementations selectable per-request via a feature flag/router. This lets both run in parallel and makes cutover and rollback a routing decision, not a redeploy.

Data consistency under continuous ingestion. A one-time dump-and-load is wrong because ingestion never stops. Do a bulk backfill first: export the 200M embeddings and idempotent-upsert them into the new store keyed by document id, snapshotting at a known log offset/timestamp. Then catch up the tail. Prefer feeding both stores from a single durable, ordered event stream (Kafka/CDC) with idempotent consumers per store, rather than app-level dual-writes — dual-writes fail partially and lose ordering, whereas a replayable log lets a lagging store catch up and be re-driven after any fault. Track a high-water mark per store to confirm the new one has reached parity, and run periodic reconciliation (counts, checksums, sampled nearest-neighbour comparison, tombstone/deletion propagation) to catch drift. Keep the embedding model/version identical across stores so you're changing one variable; re-embedding is a separate migration.

Validation before serving. Shadow (mirror) live queries to both backends: serve from FAISS, log the new store's results, and compare offline — recall@k / result overlap, nDCG on a labelled golden query set, and p50/p99 latency — plus downstream answer quality (LLM-judge or human eval). This surfaces silent recall regressions with zero user impact.

Progressive cutover. Once shadow metrics are green, canary real traffic through the flag: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%, watching online guardrails at each step. Blue-green gives an instant flip but bets everything at once; canary is safer for a quality-sensitive change, so I default to canary.

Detect & roll back. Define guardrail thresholds — recall proxy (overlap vs old), p99 latency, error rate, and a downstream quality signal (answer eval / thumbs-down rate) — and wire automated rollback: on breach, the flag routes 100% back to FAISS instantly. Crucially, keep the old store hot and dual-fed from the event stream through a bake period so there is always a consistent fallback; decommission FAISS (and the monolith coupling) only after sustained confidence. Call out the costs made explicit by this plan: running two stores in parallel, index-build resource contention, and metadata/dimension parity.
expected_answer_points: Uses an incremental strangler-fig approach with a stable retrieval interface/facade so both store implementations run behind one call site, and sequences the two changes (service extraction vs store swap) to change one variable at a time rather than a big-bang cutover

Handles never-stopping ingestion with a bulk idempotent backfill (upsert by doc id from a known offset) plus a catch-up mechanism, preferring a single durable ordered event log with idempotent per-store consumers over app-level dual-writes, and tracks a high-water mark
Includes reconciliation/drift detection (counts, checksums, sampled NN comparison) and correct deletion/tombstone propagation to both stores

Validates quality before serving via shadow/mirror traffic and an offline eval harness (recall@k / overlap / nDCG on a golden set) plus downstream answer-quality eval, keeping the embedding model/version constant to isolate the variable
Progressive canary cutover (1%->5%->25%->100%) via feature flag/router with online guardrails, and contrasts it against blue-green with the trade-off stated

Defines explicit guardrail metrics with thresholds (recall proxy, p99 latency, error rate, downstream quality/user feedback) and wires instant automated rollback as a routing/flag change, not a redeploy or re-migration

Keeps the old store hot and dual-fed through a bake period as the fallback and decommissions only after sustained confidence, while acknowledging the cost/operational overhead of running two stores in parallel

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: mechanisms are correct and used precisely — strangler-fig extraction behind a stable interface, idempotent backfill from a snapshot offset, event-log-driven catch-up with idempotent consumers and a high-water mark, shadow traffic + offline recall/nDCG eval, canary with guardrails, and flag-based instant rollback. Correctly identifies why app dual-writes are riskier than a replayable log, why embedding-model parity matters, and why deletions/tombstones must propagate. Deduct for technically wrong claims (e.g. treating the vector store as static, claiming dual-writes are consistent by default, or asserting latency health alone proves no quality regression).

Full marks: covers all four required areas — migration pattern/topology, consistency under continuous ingestion (backfill + catch-up + reconciliation), pre-serving validation (shadow + offline eval), and detection + instant rollback — and notes the parallel-run cost and a decommission/bake step. Deduct for each missing area, especially omitting the continuous-ingestion catch-up or the rollback/fallback design.

Full marks: justifies the key choices — why incremental over big-bang, why an event log over dual-writes, why canary over blue-green for a quality-sensitive change, why the old store stays hot until a bake period completes, and why the embedding model is held constant. Weaker answers assert steps without explaining the trade-offs or the failure modes they prevent.

Full marks: organised into clear phases with a legible topology, correct vocabulary (facade/gateway, backfill, high-water mark, shadow/canary, guardrail, tombstone), and an unambiguous end-to-end sequence a reviewer could act on. Deduct for disorganised, vague, or jargon-dropping prose that never forms a coherent plan.

common_pitfalls: Proposes a big-bang cutover — freeze ingestion, dump-and-load, flip DNS — treating a continuously-mutated store as a static one-time copy, with no shadow validation and no instant rollback
Does only a one-time backfill and assumes the two stores stay consistent, missing the catch-up/replay mechanism, high-water-mark parity check, and reconciliation needed to prevent drift
Relies on naive application-level dual-writes without acknowledging partial-failure and ordering hazards, instead of a replayable event log with idempotent consumers
Validates only that the new service responds with low latency and no errors, conflating 'healthy' with 'no quality regression', so a silent recall/nDCG drop ships to users
Swaps the embedding model at the same time as the store, confounding the comparison so any regression cannot be attributed to the migration
Rollback plan requires a redeploy or re-migration rather than a flag/traffic flip, and/or decommissions the FAISS store before a bake period, leaving no consistent fallback to roll back to
