open.question:
You are reviewing a pull request during a design review for a new event-ingestion service. The lead has decided to adopt Apache Kafka (via managed MSK) over a managed cloud queue such as AWS SQS. A teammate's PR adds an Architecture Decision Record whose entire content is:

    Status: Accepted
    Decision: We will use Kafka because it is the industry standard and scales well.

As the reviewer, explain what is deficient about this ADR and how you would fix it. Your answer should: (a) diagnose what is missing and why the stated justification is weak; (b) describe the sections a solid ADR must contain and why each matters to an engineer reading it a year later; (c) produce an improved ADR for this specific Kafka-vs-SQS decision; and (d) explain how this record should be handled if a future team later decides to migrate off Kafka.
open.answer_format: A structured written critique plus a rewritten ADR, roughly 250-400 words. It should cover: what the record is missing and why 'industry standard / scales well' is a weak justification; the sections a good ADR contains and their purpose; a concrete improved ADR for the Kafka-vs-SQS decision including trade-offs; and how to treat the record when the decision is later reversed (superseding, not editing).
open.reference_answer:
The record captures only the outcome plus a slogan. 'Industry standard' and 'scales well' are appeals to authority, not reasoning tied to this service's requirements. A future engineer cannot tell why Kafka beat SQS, what was traded away, or under what conditions the decision should be revisited, so the record has almost no value.

A solid ADR (Nygard/MADR style) contains:
- Metadata: a unique sequential id (e.g. ADR-014), date, status (Proposed then Accepted), and deciders/reviewers, so it is discoverable and its state is legible.
- Context / problem: the forces and constraints at decision time (event volume, need for replay, multiple independent consumers, ordering guarantees, retention, existing infra and team skills). This is what makes the record interpretable later.
- Considered options: the real alternatives compared on the axes that mattered.
- Decision: the choice, stated plainly.
- Consequences: both positive and negative, i.e. the trade-offs the team accepted.

Improved ADR:
ADR-014 - Event ingestion transport. Status: Accepted (2026-07). Deciders: platform team.
Context: ~50k events/s that several independent services must consume, some needing to reprocess history after bug fixes. We need per-key ordering and multi-day retention.
Considered options: (1) Kafka/MSK - durable partitioned log, replay, multiple consumer groups, partition ordering; heavy operational surface. (2) SQS - fully managed and trivial to operate, but point-to-point, no replay/log semantics, no multi-consumer fan-out without SNS, limited retention.
Decision: Adopt Kafka (MSK) as the ingestion transport.
Consequences: + replayable log, independent consumer groups, ordered high-throughput ingestion. - broker operations/patching or MSK cost, added client complexity, steeper learning curve than SQS.

Lifecycle: ADRs are immutable once accepted. If a future team migrates off Kafka, they do not edit or delete ADR-014. They write a new ADR (e.g. ADR-032) with the new context and decision and mark ADR-014 'Superseded by ADR-032' (ADR-032 referencing ADR-014). This preserves the decision history so readers understand what was believed and why it changed.
expected_answer_points: Identifies that the record is missing the core ADR sections: context/problem, considered options (the alternatives), consequences (trade-offs), and full metadata (id, date, deciders) - it has only a status and a one-line decision

Explains that 'industry standard' and 'scales well' are appeals to authority, not justification tied to this system's specific requirements, so a future reader cannot reconstruct the reasoning or know when to revisit it

States that Context must record the forces/constraints at decision time (e.g. event volume, replay needs, multiple consumers, ordering, retention, team skills) because decisions are context-bound and the context is what makes the record useful later
States that Consequences must include the negative trade-offs accepted (Kafka's operational burden/broker patching or MSK cost, added complexity vs SQS's managed simplicity), not just benefits

Compares Kafka vs SQS on the axes that actually differ - durable replayable log, multiple independent consumer groups, partition ordering, high throughput vs SQS being point-to-point with no replay/log semantics and simpler operations
Produces a concrete improved ADR that ties the Kafka choice to this service's needs rather than generic claims

Explains the immutability/superseding lifecycle: an accepted ADR is not edited or deleted when the decision changes; a NEW ADR is written and the old one is marked 'Superseded by ADR-N' to preserve decision history
Notes ADR governance/metadata: unique sequential id, date, status field (Proposed then Accepted), deciders/reviewers, versioned in-repo and reviewed via PR like code

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Correctly names the standard ADR sections (context, decision, considered options, consequences, status/metadata); the Kafka-vs-SQS trade-offs are accurate (log/replay/multiple consumer groups/partition ordering vs managed point-to-point simplicity); and the superseded lifecycle is described correctly. No factual errors such as claiming you edit or delete an accepted ADR, or that SQS natively provides replay/fan-out.

Addresses all four asks: diagnosis of what is missing, the section list with purpose, a concrete rewritten ADR, and the handling of the record when the decision is later reversed. Loses marks for omitting the rewrite, the negative consequences, or the superseding lifecycle.

Ties each ADR section to why a future reader needs it, justifies the Kafka choice against this system's specific forces (replay, multiple consumers, ordering, throughput vs operational cost) rather than generic claims, and explains why immutability plus superseding preserves the decision history.

Well organized and uses correct ADR vocabulary (status, context, considered options, consequences, superseded); the improved ADR is readable and coherent enough to stand as a real record rather than a loose list of ideas.

common_pitfalls: Lists ADR template section names without explaining why each matters or applying them to the Kafka/SQS case, so the critique stays generic

Re-justifies Kafka with the same vague 'industry standard / scales well' framing instead of concrete forces like replay, multiple independent consumer groups, per-partition ordering, and throughput weighed against operational cost

Claims the fix when the team later migrates is to edit or overwrite the accepted ADR, instead of writing a new ADR and marking the original 'Superseded by ADR-N', which breaks the immutable decision log
Presents only Kafka's benefits and omits the negative consequences/trade-offs (broker operations, patching or MSK cost, added complexity) that a proper ADR must record
Confuses the ADR (a focused, durable decision record) with the design-review meeting itself or with a full RFC/design doc, and bloats it accordingly
Forgets the metadata (unique id, date, status, deciders) that make the record discoverable and its lifecycle state legible

items.sub_competency: C10.8 · Reusable platform components & engineering standards

open.question:
You're a staff engineer at a 200-person company where six product teams have each independently wired up LLM access. The result: retry/backoff and rate-limit handling is re-implemented in every service, prompt versions live in scattered code and Git branches, there's no shared way to trace a request or attribute token spend, every team hand-rolls its own eval scripts, provider API keys are copied into multiple repos, and swapping a model or adding Anthropic alongside OpenAI means editing six codebases. Leadership asks you to design a reusable internal 'AI platform' — a shared LLM gateway plus supporting libraries — and, critically, the engineering standards that make teams adopt it instead of quietly bypassing it.

Write a design-review-quality proposal that: (a) enumerates the reusable platform components you would build and what each one owns; (b) draws an explicit boundary between what lives in the shared platform layer and what stays product-specific; (c) specifies the cross-system engineering standards and governance — interface/versioning, backward-compatibility and deprecation policy, observability and cost-attribution conventions, and the 'golden path' — that keep the platform durable and widely adopted; and (d) analyzes the central trade-off of centralization versus team autonomy, naming the concrete failure modes (e.g., the gateway as a bottleneck or single point of failure, a leaky lowest-common-denominator abstraction, noisy neighbors) and how you mitigate each.
open.answer_format: A structured design-review response, ~350-500 words, organized into four parts: (1) an enumerated set of reusable platform components with the responsibility each owns; (2) an explicit platform-vs-product boundary with a decision rule; (3) the engineering standards and governance (versioning, backward-compat/deprecation, observability/cost conventions, golden path, adoption strategy); and (4) an analysis of the centralization-vs-autonomy trade-off naming concrete failure modes and their mitigations. Prose or tight bullets are both acceptable; senior design-review register.
open.reference_answer:
**Reusable components (the shared platform).** (1) LLM gateway/proxy — one provider-agnostic endpoint that normalizes request/response across OpenAI, Anthropic and self-hosted models and centralizes auth/key management, rate limiting, retries with exponential backoff + jitter, timeouts, provider failover/routing, and response caching. It passes provider-native features (streaming, tool/function calling, structured outputs) through rather than hiding them. (2) A thin client SDK — the golden-path library teams import; it propagates trace context, gives typed requests and sane defaults, and holds no business logic. (3) Observability + cost layer — structured logging of prompt/response with PII redaction, distributed tracing, and per-request token/cost accounting tagged by team/feature/model, with budgets and alerts. (4) A versioned prompt registry — prompts/templates as reviewable artifacts (semver or content hash) with history and rollback, decoupled from code deploys. (5) A shared eval/regression harness — golden datasets and CI gates so every team measures quality and regressions the same way. (6) Guardrails and a secrets vault — centralized moderation/PII handling so keys never sprawl into repos.

**Boundary.** The platform owns undifferentiated, cross-cutting concerns: provider abstraction, resilience, security/compliance, observability, and cost governance. Product teams own the differentiated work: actual prompt content, orchestration/agent logic, business rules, UX, and their own eval datasets. Rule of thumb — if it's the same for everyone and getting it wrong is a reliability, security, or cost problem, it's platform; if it encodes product behavior, it's the team's.

**Standards & governance.** Treat the gateway as an internal product with an SLA. Ship a stable, versioned (semver) provider-agnostic API with a written backward-compatibility contract and a deprecation policy: announce, dual-run, migration window, and contract tests that fail CI when a change breaks a client. New providers/models onboard behind the same interface without breaking callers; roll changes out via canary + feature flags. Mandate conventions, not implementations — trace-id propagation, cost tags, structured logs. Make the golden path the easiest path (better DX than rolling your own) with documented escape hatches (raw passthrough), and inner-source the platform so teams contribute instead of forking.

**Centralization vs autonomy.** Bottleneck: a central team gatekeeping every change stalls teams — mitigate with self-service, inner-source contributions, and middleware/extension points. SPOF: all traffic flows through the gateway — mitigate with HA/multi-region, circuit breakers, a client fallback to direct provider calls on outage, a tight proxy latency budget, and caching. Noisy neighbors: one team's spike starves others — mitigate with per-tenant quotas and bulkhead isolation. Leaky abstraction: a lowest-common-denominator API that hides streaming/tool-use drives teams to bypass it — mitigate with native passthrough and fast-follow on new capabilities. Adoption is won by DX and trust, not mandate: if bypassing is easier than compliance, the platform fails.
expected_answer_points: Enumerates concrete reusable components with clear ownership: an LLM gateway (provider abstraction, key/auth management, rate limiting, retries/backoff, failover, caching), a thin client SDK, an observability + per-request token/cost-accounting layer, a versioned prompt registry, a shared eval/regression harness, and guardrails/secrets management

Draws an explicit platform-vs-product boundary with a decision rule: platform owns undifferentiated cross-cutting concerns (resilience, provider abstraction, security, observability, cost); teams own prompt content, orchestration/business logic, UX, and their own eval data

Specifies interface and versioning standards: a stable, versioned (semver) provider-agnostic API with a backward-compatibility contract, a deprecation policy (migration window, contract tests), the ability to add providers/models without breaking clients, and safe rollout via canary/feature flags

Defines cross-system observability and cost-attribution conventions to mandate (trace-context propagation, cost tags per team/feature/model, structured logging with PII redaction) — mandating conventions rather than implementations

Treats adoption as a developer-experience / paved-road problem rather than a mandate: the golden path is the easiest path, with documented escape hatches/passthrough and inner-source contribution to prevent the central team becoming a bottleneck

Addresses the gateway as a single point of failure and noisy-neighbor risk: HA/failover, circuit breakers, client fallback to direct provider calls, per-tenant quotas/bulkheads, and a proxy latency/caching budget
Avoids a leaky lowest-common-denominator abstraction by passing through provider-native features (streaming, tool/function calling, structured outputs) and fast-following new capabilities
Analyzes the centralization-vs-autonomy trade-off explicitly, pairing each concrete failure mode with a mitigation rather than asserting a single 'right' design

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly identifies genuine cross-cutting AI-platform concerns (provider-abstraction gateway, resilience via retries/backoff/failover, observability with token+cost attribution and trace propagation, versioned prompt registry, shared eval harness, guardrails/secrets) and places each correctly relative to product code; interface and evolution claims are sound (semver, backward-compat contract, deprecation window, provider-native passthrough); reliability claims (SPOF/HA, circuit breakers, per-tenant quotas/bulkheads, proxy latency, caching) are accurate. Deduct for invented mechanisms, mislabeled responsibilities, or a design that would break clients or leak provider features.

Full marks require all four requested dimensions: (1) the reusable component set with ownership, (2) the explicit platform/product boundary, (3) the standards & governance including a versioning/backward-compat/deprecation story and observability/cost conventions, and (4) the centralization-vs-autonomy trade-off with failure modes and mitigations. Also requires an adoption strategy and at least one escape-hatch/extension mechanism. Partial credit scales with dimensions meaningfully covered.

Full marks: justifies why each concern belongs in the shared layer versus the product (undifferentiated/reliability-security-cost vs product behavior), frames adoption as a DX/paved-road problem rather than a mandate, and weighs the centralization trade-off by tying concrete consequences (bottleneck, SPOF, noisy neighbors, leaky abstraction) to specific mitigations instead of asserting one correct design. Deduct for unsupported assertions or ignoring the tension between central control and team autonomy.

Full marks: cleanly separates components, boundary, standards, and trade-offs; uses platform-engineering vocabulary precisely (golden path/paved road, inner-source, contract testing, canary, feature flags, bulkhead, deprecation window, SLA); reads as a senior design-review proposal. Deduct for disorganized structure, vague hand-waving, or misused terminology.

common_pitfalls: Answers by naming a vendor or library (e.g., 'just deploy LiteLLM / an API gateway') without defining component boundaries, ownership, or the engineering standards that make it adopted
Over-centralizes: routes all traffic through a rigid gateway with no escape hatches or extension points, ignoring team autonomy — which in practice drives shadow/bypass implementations
Ignores the gateway as a single point of failure and the noisy-neighbor problem (no HA, no client fallback, no per-tenant quotas), turning the platform into a reliability liability
Designs a lowest-common-denominator API that hides provider-native features (streaming, tool/function calling, structured outputs) — the classic leaky abstraction that pushes teams off the platform

Blurs the boundary by putting product-specific concerns (business prompt content, domain orchestration) into the shared layer, or pushing cross-cutting concerns like key management down into each team
Treats adoption as a compliance mandate and omits any versioning, backward-compatibility, or deprecation policy, so the platform silently breaks downstream teams and loses their trust
open.prompt:
You're a staff engineer at a 200-person company where six product teams have each independently wired up LLM access. The result: retry/backoff and rate-limit handling is re-implemented in every service, prompt versions live in scattered code and Git branches, there's no shared way to trace a request or attribute token spend, every team hand-rolls its own eval scripts, provider API keys are copied into multiple repos, and swapping a model or adding Anthropic alongside OpenAI means editing six codebases. Leadership asks you to design a reusable internal 'AI platform' — a shared LLM gateway plus supporting libraries — and, critically, the engineering standards that make teams adopt it instead of quietly bypassing it.

Write a design-review-quality proposal that: (a) enumerates the reusable platform components you would build and what each one owns; (b) draws an explicit boundary between what lives in the shared platform layer and what stays product-specific; (c) specifies the cross-system engineering standards and governance — interface/versioning, backward-compatibility and deprecation policy, observability and cost-attribution conventions, and the 'golden path' — that keep the platform durable and widely adopted; and (d) analyzes the central trade-off of centralization versus team autonomy, naming the concrete failure modes (e.g., the gateway as a bottleneck or single point of failure, a leaky lowest-common-denominator abstraction, noisy neighbors) and how you mitigate each.
